# round3_q1: lattice approach to case (R). Partial result; (R) is still open ## 1. The definite 4-manifold (proved, with the orientations written out) Setting: Y = S^3_p(K), p = rs = 2g-1, and Y = L1 # L2 # Y3 as in (R). W = X_p(K) is positive definite with form

and boundary ∂W = Y. - Each lens space L_j bounds a negative-definite linear plumbing P_j, and P_j is sharp. [lit: Ozsvath–Szabo, "On the Heegaard Floer homology of plumbed three-manifolds"; this is the input Greene uses.] - Let C' = (Y3 x I) boundary-summed with P1 and P2 at the top end. Then C' is a cobordism from Y3 to Y. - Set N = W ∪_Y (-C'). We have ∂(-C') = Y3 ⊔ (-Y), so gluing along Y gives ∂N = Y3. The pieces W and -P_j are positive definite, so N is positive definite with b2 = n = 1 + rk P1 + rk P2. - Hence -N is negative definite with ∂(-N) = -Y3. Its lattice Λ is unimodular because Y3 is a homology sphere. Λ contains

⊕ Λ(-P1) ⊕ Λ(-P2) as a sublattice of index p, the same index as in Greene's gluing. The Ozsvath–Szabo inequality says c^2 + n ≤ 4 d(-Y3) for every characteristic c of the negative-definite form. Suppose d(Y3) = -2. This is the value forced by the computer evidence for p ≤ 45, but I have not proved it in general. Then 4 d(-Y3) = 8, so every characteristic vector of the positive-definite lattice Λ has norm ≥ n - 8. This is exactly Elkies' "long shadow" condition. ## 2. A constraint from root systems (proved) - The P_j are sharp linear plumbings, and the standard lens-space lattice embeds Λ(P_j) into some Z^m. - Every norm-2 vector of Z^m has the form ±e_i ± e_j. So the root system of Λ(P1) ⊕ Λ(P2) contains only components of types A and D. - Consequence: if Λ = E8 ⊕ Z^{n-8} and the E8-part of the image of the

generator is a root, then its orthogonal complement in E8 is E7. E7 cannot sit inside Λ(P1) ⊕ Λ(P2). - This rules out only that sub-case. A generic E8-part has a root-free orthogonal complement, so the argument stops there. ## 3. The decisive step is not done To get a contradiction one would need to: 1. Show the bound n - 8 is attained, i.e. Λ is not Z^n. Characteristic vectors split rationally as c_W + c_P1 + c_P2. The P-parts reach their minima by sharpness. The rank-1 W is not sharp: Ni–Wu gives a defect of -2 max(V_i, V_{p-i}), and in (R) this max is ≥ 1 for every i. Carrying out the bookkeeping needs a careful sign check that I have not completed. Depending on the signs, the minimum characteristic norm comes out as either n or n - 8. If it is n, then Λ = Z^n by Elkies, and the long-shadow route gives nothing. 2. Run Elkies' list (E8, D12, E7^2, A15, D8^2, ... plus Z^k), cited from memory with low confidence about the full list. For each entry, carry out a changemaker-type analysis of where the norm-p vector can go. I did neither, and I did not run the requested p = 15 lattice test. ## Status - **Proved:** the construction of N and the orientation bookkeeping (§1); the long-shadow inequality, conditional on d(Y3) = -2; the A/D root constraint and the E7 exclusion (§2). - **Rests on cited theorems:** sharpness of lens-space plumbings; the Ozsvath–Szabo d-invariant inequality; Elkies' theorems. - **Open:** - (R) itself, so the original question is not settled. - d(Y3) = -2 in general. - Whether the bound n - 8 is attained. - The Elkies-list case analysis. - Whether the lattice data are consistent, i.e. whether a fake model of the shape E8 ⊕ Z^m exists. === END OF ANSWER round3_q1 ===

# Round 3 summary (after round 2 results) ## Problem and goal Does every 3-manifold obtained by Dehn surgery on an L-space knot have at most two prime summands? Goal = ledger entry 1 ([GOAL], OPEN): the posed claim (expected answer YES), or a counterexample. Convention: after mirroring, K is a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g, invariants V_s (V_s >= 0, steps 0/1, V_s = 0 iff s >= g, V_{-s} = V_s + s). ## Established (in the run's own right, modulo cited standard Heegaard Floer tools) Cited HF tools used: Ozsvath–Szabo integer surgery mapping cone (plus and hat, relatively graded, with truncation), for L-space knots A_s = B_s = T^+ with v_s = U^{V_s}, h_s = U^{V_{-s}}; Kunneth/connected-sum formula; Ni–Wu d formula; HF of lens spaces. 1. (round2_q1 §3, ledger 6) Hat ranks per Spin^c class: rank HF-hat(S^3_p(K), i) = 1 for all i if p >= 2g-1; = 2n_i - 1 for 0 < p <= 2g-2; = 2n_i + 1 for p < 0; n_i = #{s ≡ i mod |p| : |s| <= g-1}. Proof: hat cone is a line graph with F at each vertex, edges iso exactly where V_s = 0 (s >= g) or H_s = 0 (s <= -g). 2. (round2_q1 §1-3, ledger 7) Coset invariance: if S^3_p(K) = L # Y' with L a lens space of order a >= 2, the rank function and the ungraded HF^+ type are invariant under translation by b = |p|/a (fibres of Spin^c(L)); since {i: n_i = q+1} is an interval of Z/|p| when 2g-1 = q|p| + r, 0 < r < |p|, this forces p >= 2g-1 or |p| divides 2g-1. Also p = ±1 impossible. 3. (round2_q3, ledger 8) THEOREM: for p a nonzero integer < 2g-1 (either sign), S^3_p(K) is never L # Y' with L an L-space of order |p| >= 3 and Y' an integer homology sphere. Proof: all classes would carry the same relatively graded HF^+ (= HF^+(Y')). p > 0: cone reduces (D surjective, edge equations solve outside [-(g-1), g-1]) to a path of n_i towers; "level" model: valley bottoms x(s) = s(s-p)/(2p) - V_s, peak levels y = s(s+p)/(2p) = (m^2 - p^2/4)/(2p), m = s + p/2, INDEPENDENT of K; finite summands have tops at {y - 1}; number of finite summands n_i - 1, so equal n_i forces p | 2g-1, n = (2g-1)/p >= 3 odd; class 0 has every peak level with even multiplicity (m and -m), class 1 all distinct (needs p >= 3) -> contradiction. p = -q < 0: truncated zigzag with n_i valleys, n_i + 1 peaks incl. two ground edges; B-peaks at b(t) = -(u^2 - q^2/4)/(2q), u = t + q/2; coker part = one tower at the max peak M, ker part finite with tops {y-1} minus one copy of M-1; equal n_i forces q | 2g-1; n >= 3: class 0 has a repeated top, class 1 none; n = 1: offset tower-bottom-to-finite-top is 1 in class 0 and 2 in class 1. Planner spot-checked the level formulas algebraically (x(s+p) - x(s) = V_s + s - V_{s+p}; y = x(s) + V_{-s}) and the n = 1 negative computation; all consistent. 4. (ledger 9) Consequence: L1 # L2 # Y3 (three summands, orders r, s >= 2 coprime, rs = |p|, Y3 a homology sphere) requires p >= 2g-1, so Y and Y3 are L-spaces. With Matignon–Sayari (non-cable => |p| <= 2g-1, cited) p = 2g-1 exactly. Also round2_q4 (d) gives the same divisibility independently. ## Topological reduction (round1_q3, round2_q2 §1, round2_q4 (a)-(c); all cited from memory, ledger 4 still OPEN) Unknot, slope infinity, slope 0 (Gabai), non-integral slopes (Gordon–Luecke 1987), torus knots (Moser: unique reducible slope ab, L(a,b)#L(b,a)), cables at cabling slope (L(m,n) # S^3_{n/m}(J), two summands), satellites (Scharlemann 1990 + Gabai braid theorem; S^3_p(K) = S^3_{p/w^2}(J), induct on JSJ pieces; companions of satellite L-space knots are L-space knots — Baker–Motegi, Hom) => reduce to K hyperbolic, p integral. Hyperbolic: at most 3 summands, three-summand shape L1 # L2 # Y3 (Howie 2002 / Valdez-Sanchez / Sayari; "two lens spaces + ZHS" attribution only moderate-low confidence; round2_q4 notes cyclicity of H_1 alone gives only coprime orders — but the GL96 lens summand plus Howie's Scott–Wiegold consequence is what's needed), Matignon–Sayari |p| <= 2g-1 (proof only sketched in round2_q4 (c)). Exact statements must be pinned down for the final proof. ## Remaining case (ledger 12, OPEN; the whole goal now hinges on it) K hyperbolic positive L-space knot, p = 2g-1, S^3_p(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3, Y3 an L-space integer homology sphere != S^3. ## Planner computation this round (round3_plan; scripts were in /tmp/w, not preserved) d-equation: d(L(p,1), i) - 2 V_{min(i,p-i)} = d(L1,.) + d(L2,.) + c, c = d(Y3) in 2Z, under a torsor-compatible CRT bijection. Exhaustive search over ALL formal staircases for p = 2g-1 in {15, 21, 33, 35, 39, 45}: exactly ONE solution each, namely V_j = V_j(T(r,s)) + 1 for 0 <= j <= g-1 (g = (rs+1)/2), with c = -2 and L1 # L2 the lens spaces of S^3_{rs}(T(r,s)) (e.g. p=15: V = [3,2,2,2,1,1,1,1], L(3,2)#L(5,2) in OS convention). Equivalently Delta_K = Delta_{T(r,s)} + t^g - t^{g-1} - t^{1-g} + t^{-g}; the extra term is t^{-g}(t-1)(t^p - 1), vanishing at p-th roots of unity, so Reidemeister torsion of Y also matches. The d-invariants (hence all of HF^+(Y), as Y is an L-space) coincide with those of S^3_{rs}(T(r,s)) # S^3_{+1}(T(2,3)) (Y3 = Poincare sphere oriented with d = -2). For p > 2g-1 (g <= 7, p < 70) only c = 0 solutions (torus/cable patterns) except a c = -2 one at p = 2g = 14 (V = V(T(2,7)) + 1), which Matignon–Sayari excludes. CONCLUSION: no argument using only HF(Y), d, Casson–Walker or torsion of Y can close the remaining case; one needs the dual knot / cobordism / lattice / topology. ## Dead ends - Citing Hom–Lidman–Zufelt from memory (round 1): not a proof. - "Reducible slope = 2g-1" for all L-space knots: false for cables. - Ungraded HF^+ / hat ranks / Ni–Wu d to settle the two-summand claim "reducible => p >= 2g-1" (round2_q1 §5: g=5, p=3 formal staircase passes all). Not needed for the goal anyway (two-summand case is fine). - Casson–Walker for the L-space regime: equivalent to summed d (round2_q2 §3). - Any invariant of Y alone in the remaining case (planner computation above). - Greene changemaker directly: needs Y3 to bound a negative-definite manifold; d(Y3) = -2 < 0 forbids that (Elkies). Possibly salvageable with orientation reversal (-Y3 has d = +2) — see q1 of round 3. ## Open gaps A. (ledger 12) the remaining case. B. (ledger 11) prove the d-characterization (useful: pins d(Y3) = -2 and Delta_K). C. The proof uses the intersection graphs G_P (n vertices, each of valence |p|) and G_F (one vertex, valence n|p|). Because there are no trivial loops and no Scharlemann cycles of length 2 (those would give a cabling annulus), each family of parallel edges in G_F holds at most n edges. The reduced graph G_F lives on a surface of genus g with one vertex, so it has at most 6g - 3 edge classes. A refinement of this bound gives n|p|/2 <= n(2g-1)/2 + ..., and from that |p| <= 2g - 1. If one could show that the equality configuration produces Scharlemann cycles on both sides of some P_i, one side would have to be the homology sphere Y3, which is a contradiction. I could not prove that both sides carry Scharlemann cycles. - Fibredness gives a circle's worth of fibres F_t. The dual knot K* is Floer simple, but that does not localise it For p = 2g-1 >= 2g-1, Y = S^3_p(K) is an L-space. The dual knot K* has rank HFK-hat(Y,K*) = p = |H_1(Y)|. (This follows from the rational surgery / dual-knot formula, cited from memory from Hedden and Rasmussen.) So K* is Floer simple. Its exterior is the exterior of K, which is irreducible and fibred with genus-g fibre. So every reducing sphere S for L1 # L2 # Y3 must meet K* in at least 2 points. Floer simplicity gives one generator in each Spin^c class, but I know of no Künneth-type formula for a knot that meets a reducing sphere essentially. A Künneth formula only covers knots lying inside one summand, and K* cannot be isotoped into one summand: its exterior would then be reducible. **Dead end:** the hypothesis that would make Floer simplicity usable (K* lies in a single summand) is exactly what irreducibility rules out. ## 2. The Alexander polynomial / torsion of K* The Turaev torsion of the exterior of K* is the same as that of the exterior of K: it is Delta_K/(t-1) up to units. In H_1(Y) = Z/p, the class of the meridian of K maps to the generator. Reducing modulo t^p - 1 gives the torsion of Y, and by the background computation that torsion agrees with the split model. The torsion of the exterior itself is determined by Delta_K. In the candidate solution, Delta_K = Delta_{T(r,s)} + t^{-g}(t-1)(t^p-1). I found no constraint that this polynomial violates: - the coefficients are ±1 and alternate; - the second coefficient is -1 (Hedden–Watson condition, cited from memory); - the formal semigroup is not closed under addition, but that closure is only known for algebraic knots and fails for many L-space knots (e.g. some hyperbolic Berge knots, from memory). Cobordism maps The trace X_p(K) is positive definite with b_2 = 1, and each map F_{X,t} hits the bottom of a tower with grading shift fixed by V. On L-spaces these maps are determined by d-invariants and the Spin^c labelling. I believe, but did not prove, that they give nothing beyond the d-equation already solved. Stated precisely: is there a hyperbolic positive L-space knot with p = 2g-1 = rs and S^3_p(K) = L(r,·) # L(s,·) # Y3, where Y3 is an L-space homology sphere with d(Y3) = -2? The cabling conjecture would imply this, and so would any proof that the dual knot of a reducible surgery lies "simply" relative to the decomposition. - **What any proof of (R) needs:** genuinely 3-dimensional input. Possible routes are a bordered Floer computation of the exterior glued across the reducing sphere, or Scharlemann-type combinatorics of the planar surface. === END OF ANSWER round3_q3 === === q4 # round3_q4 answer ## Answer: Yes. If K is a nontrivial L-space knot and S^3_p(K) is reducible, then: - p = 2g(K) - 1, up to mirroring; - S^3_p(K) has exactly two prime summands, one of them a lens space. Write out every lattice computation; test any combinatorial lattice claim on the smallest case p = 15 (r = 3, s = 5, g = 8) before relying on it. Suggested lead (not established; check it). Let W = X_p(K) be the trace of p-surgery (positive definite, H_2 = Z with form

, boundary Y = S^3_p(K)). Lens spaces in either orientation bound negative-definite linear plumbings P1, P2 which are sharp. (check the sign: you want a "long shadow" condition). Elkies (Math. Res. Lett. 1995: "A characterization of the Z^n lattice"; and "Lattices and codes with long shadows") classify unimodular definite lattices whose characteristic vectors all have norm >= n - 8 (they are Z^{n-k} ⊕ L for L in a short explicit list including E8, D12, E7^2, A15, D8^2, ...). Use sharpness of W (L-space knot, p >= 2g-1) and of P1, P2 to argue that the maximum is attained, so Λ is NOT diagonal and must be one of Elkies' lattices plus Z^m; then show <-p> ⊕ Λ(P1) ⊕ Λ(P2) cannot sit with index p in such a lattice in the required way (changemaker-type analysis of where the class of the <-p> generator goes), or show that the configuration forces K to share V with an explicit knot and derive a contradiction. Alternatively use different fillings: -Y3 versus Y3, or use that Y3 = summand means Y3 bounds (Y minus lens summands) etc. Explain clearly which 4-manifold is negative definite and why each sharpness claim holds. Also: if you find that the lattice data are consistent (e.g. the configuration is realized by Λ = E8 ⊕ Z^m glued exactly as for the split-link model S^3_{rs}(T(r,s)) # S^3_{+1}(T(2,3))), say so precisely — that is a valuable negative result. ## Shared background (facts marked [lit] are standard published results you may cite, stating exactly what you use; [cited, moderate confidence] means pin down the exact statement or avoid it; everything else below was proved earlier in this attempt, modulo [lit]) Conventions. An L-space knot is a knot K in S^3 with some nontrivial surgery an L-space. After mirroring (S^3_r(K) becomes -S^3_{-r}(mirror K), same number of prime summands) K is a positive L-space knot: S^3_r(K) is an L-space iff r >= 2g(K)-1 [lit]. Equivalently the Alexander polynomial has coefficients ±1 alternating and V_s = #{n not in S_K : n >= g + s}, where S_K (the "formal semigroup") is determined by Delta_K. Ni–Wu [lit]: for p > 0, d(S^3_p(K), i) = d(L(p,1), i) - 2 max(V_i, V_{p-i}), 0 <= i < p, with d(L(p,1), i) = ((2i-p)^2 - p)/(4p) (Ozsvath–Szabo convention S^3_p(U) = L(p,1); recursive formula d(L(p,q),i) = -1/4 + (2i+1-p-q)^2/(4pq) - d(L(q, p mod q), i mod q)). The extra term is t^{-g}(t-1)(t^p - 1), which vanishes at every p-th root of unity, so the Reidemeister–Turaev torsion of Y also agrees. In short: every invariant of the closed manifold Y computable from HF^+(Y) (Y is an L-space, so HF^+ is determined by the d-invariants), Casson–Walker, or torsion, coincides with that of S^3_{rs}(T(r,s)) # S^3_{+1}(T(2,3)), where S^3_{+1}(T(2,3)) is the Poincare sphere oriented with d = -2. Therefore NO argument using only such invariants of Y can exclude (R): one needs the knot (dual knot, 4-dimensional trace, cobordism maps) or 3-dimensional topology. (For p = 2g, a similar c = -2 solution exists, e.g. V = V(T(2,7)) + 1 at p = 14, g = 7; Matignon–Sayari excludes p = 2g for non-cables.) State clearly at the end: what is fully proved, what rests on cited theorems (with exact statements), and what remains open. ====== # Answer to round2_q3 **Theorem.** Let K be a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g, and let p be a nonzero integer with p < 2g-1 (p may be negative). Then S^3_p(K) is not homeomorphic to L # Y', where L is an L-space with |H_1(L)| = |p| >= 3 and Y' is an integer homology sphere. In particular it is not of the form L1 # L2 # Y3 with L1, L2 lens spaces of coprime orders r, s >= 2 (here rs = |p| >= 6) and Y3 an integer homology sphere. Below, "[lit]" means a standard result that I cite from memory. ## 0. Reduction to an algebraic statement Let Y = S^3_p(K) ≅ L # Y'. Write CF^-(L,s) ≃ F[U] for each s (L is an L-space). By the Ozsvath–Szabo connected-sum formula [lit], CF^-(L#Y', s#t) ≃ CF^-(L,s) ⊗_{F[U]} CF^-(Y',t) ≃ CF^-(Y') up to a grading shift. Tensoring with F[U,U^{-1}]/U·F[U] gives the same for CF^+. Since H_1(Y') = 0, every one of the |p| spin^c structures on Y has HF^+(Y, i) ≅ HF^+(Y') as relatively Z-graded F[U]-modules (up to a degree shift). (*) So it suffices to find two spin^c classes i, i' of S^3_p(K) whose HF^+ are **not** isomorphic up to a degree shift. I compare the classes i = 0 and i = 1. These are different classes because |p| >= 3. **Invariants used.** A finitely generated graded F[U]-module of the form T^+ ⊕ (finite part) is determined up to isomorphism by (a) the degree of the bottom of the tower and (b) the multiset of degrees of the tops of its cyclic summands. For (b), the number of summands whose top lies in degree k is dim (M/UM)_k. After a degree shift, two isomorphic modules have the same number of finite summands, and their multisets of top degrees agree up to a translation. In particular the multiplicity pattern of the multiset is the same for both. ## 1. Cone model in "level" form (both signs) I use the Ozsvath–Szabo integer surgery formula [lit]. For a positive L-space knot, A_s^+ ≅ B_s^+ ≅ T^+, with v_s = U^{V_s} and h_s = U^{H_s}, where H_s = V_{-s}. The V_s satisfy V_s >= 0, V_s - V_{s+1} ∈ {0,1}, V_s = 0 iff s >= g, and V_{-s} = V_s + s. Model each tower by levels k ∈ Z: the tower has F in each level k >= (its bottom), and U lowers the level by 1. If U^e maps A to B and the bottom of A is at level x, then preserving levels puts the bottom of B at level x + e. The real grading of a B-level is a uniform shift of the A-level (by the cone's degree-1 shift), and this shift is the same for all classes. The only exponents that appear below are V_s with s <= g-1 and H_s = V_{-s} with s >= -(g-1). All of these are >= 1. So every B-bottom (a "peak") lies strictly above the adjacent A-bottoms ("valleys"). At level k the cone map is the coboundary δ of a graph G_k: - vertices: the A's whose bottom is <= k; - edges: the B's whose bottom is <= k; - (Da)_B is the sum of the values at the A's adjacent to B. A B adjacent to only one retained A acts as an edge to a "ground" vertex, where the value is fixed to 0. ## 2. The case p > 0 **Truncation.** Fix a class i and let s_1 < … < s_n be the elements s ≡ i (mod p) with |s| <= g-1. D: ⊕A → ⊕B is surjective. Indeed, every map is U^e on T^+, which is surjective, and one can solve inductively along the zigzag. So H_*(cone) ≅ ker D, up to a uniform shift. For a kernel element: for s >= g we have V_s = 0, which forces a_s = U^{H_{s-p}} a_{s-p}. For s - p <= -g we have H_{s-p} = 0, which forces a_{s-p} = U^{V_s} a_s. So every a_s outside [-(g-1), g-1] is determined by the a_{s_j}. Hence ker D ≅ { (a_1,…,a_n) : U^{H_{s_j}} a_j = U^{V_{s_{j+1}}} a_{j+1}, j = 1,…,n-1 }. This is a path graph with valleys x_j (the bottom of A_{s_j}) and peaks y_{j+1} = x_j + H_{s_j} = x_{j+1} + V_{s_{j+1}}. If n = 0 the module is T^+. **Positions.** Solving x(s+p) - x(s) = V_{-s} - V_{s+p} = V_s + s - V_{s+p} gives x(s) = s(s-p)/(2p) - V_s, and therefore the peak between s and s+p is at y = x(s) + V_{-s} = s(s+p)/(2p) = (m^2 - p^2/4)/(2p), where m = s + p/2. The peak levels do not depend on K. **Module structure.** At level k, ker D is the space of functions on the vertices of G_k that are constant along its edges, i.e. functions on the connected components of G_k. U acts by restriction from G_k to G_{k-1}. - For large k, G_k is connected, so the module has one tower, with bottom at min_j x_j. - Restriction from level k+1 to level k fails to be surjective by exactly the number of edges (peaks) at level k+1. G_k is a subforest of a path, so each new edge joins two different components. - Hence the finite summands have their tops at the levels {y - 1 : y a peak}. There are n-1 of them, counted with multiplicity. **Number of summands.** The number of finite summands is max(n_i - 1, 0), where n_i = #{s ≡ i mod p : |s| <= g-1}. The integers in [-(g-1), g-1] are 2g-1 consecutive integers. Since 0 < p < 2g-1, every n_i >= 1, and the n_i are all equal iff p | 2g-1. By (*) they must be equal. So p | 2g-1, p is odd, and n := (2g-1)/p >= 3. The class of t (|t| <= (p-1)/2) is then {t + kp : |k| <= (n-1)/2}, and its peaks are at m = t + (k + 1/2)p for k = -(n-1)/2, …, (n-3)/2. - **Class 0:** m ∈ {±p/2, ±3p/2, …, ±(n-2)p/2}. Each peak level occurs with even multiplicity. - **Class 1:** two of the m's would give equal m^2 only if m = -m', i.e. 2 + (k + k' + 1)p = 0, which is impossible for p >= 3. So all n-1 >= 2 top levels are distinct. A translation cannot turn a multiset with all multiplicities even into one with all multiplicities 1. This contradicts (*). ## 3. The case p = -q < 0 **Truncation.** I use the Ozsvath–Szabo truncation of the cone [lit]: cancel A_s against B_s for s >= g (v_s is an isomorphism there), and A_s against B_{s-q} for s <= -g (h_s is an isomorphism there). In class i, let s_1 < … < s_n be the elements with |s| <= g-1. What remains is the zigzag B_{s_1-q} ← A_{s_1} → B_{s_1} ← A_{s_1+q} → … → B_{s_n}. It has n A's (valleys) and n+1 B's (peaks); the two end B's are ground edges. - If n = 0, exactly one B survives and the module is T^+. - Every A carries even (A-)parity and every B odd parity, and U preserves parity. So H = ker D ⊕ coker D as F[U]-modules. **Positions.** Solving x(s+q) - x(s) = V_s - V_{-(s+q)} gives x(s) = -s(s+q)/(2q) - V_s, and the bottom of B_t is at b(t) = -t(t+q)/(2q) = -(u^2 - q^2/4)/(2q), where u = t + q/2. Again the peak levels do not depend on K. **Module structure.** G_k together with the ground vertex is a subgraph of a single cycle. - **Coker.** coker δ_k = H^1(G_k ∪ ground, ground) = H^1(G_k ∪ ground), which is 0 until the cycle closes at level M = max peak and F from then on. So the B-parity part is a single tower with bottom at M. - **Ker.** ker δ_k is the space of functions on the components of G_k that do not touch ground; it is entirely finite. Its tops lie at {y - 1 : y a peak}, with one copy of M - 1 removed: the edge that closes the cycle does not merge two components. - **Number of summands.** dim ker U on the ker part is n_i: one summand is born at each valley. By (*) the n_i must be equal. That forces q | 2g-1, because if q > 2g-1 some classes have n_i = 0 and others n_i = 1. So n = (2g-1)/q is odd and q >= 3 is odd. The class of t has the B-midpoints u = t + (k + 1/2)q for k = -(n+1)/2, …, (n-1)/2. The invariant used here is the multiset of top levels of the finite summands, measured relative to the tower bottom. Both live in fixed parities, and these relative offsets are preserved by any graded isomorphism. - **Class 0:** u ∈ {±q/2, …, ±nq/2}. The maximal peak (|u| = q/2) occurs twice, so its value survives once after removing one copy; every other value occurs twice. - **Class 1:** all |u| are distinct (as in §2), so all values are distinct. - **If n >= 3:** class 0 has a repeated top level and class 1 does not. Contradiction. - **If n = 1:** both classes have a single finite summand. Its top lies 1 level below the tower bottom in class 0, but |b(1-q) - b(1)| + 1 = 2 levels below in class 1, since the two u's differ in u^2 by 2q. Contradiction. (For n = 1 the finite summand of class s is F[U]/U^{V_{|s|}}, and its top is |s| + 1 levels below the tower bottom. The sizes V_{|s|} alone might coincide across classes; the positions cannot.) This proves the Theorem in both cases. ∎ ## Status - **Proved here:** the Theorem, assuming the cited tools. - **Cited from memory [lit]:** - the integer surgery formula, as an isomorphism of relatively graded F[U]-modules, together with its truncation; - the facts about V_s for L-space knots; - the connected-sum formula for CF^-. - **Remark:** the proof only uses that one summand is an L-space with |H_1| = |p| >= 3. The p > 0 rank formula hinted in the task, rank HF-hat = 2n_i - 1, also follows: dim ker U = n_i. - **Not addressed here:** the regime p >= 2g-1 (p > 0), where S^3_p(K) is an L-space; this is where cables give two summands. It is not part of this task. === END OF ANSWER round2_q3 === ===== # round2_q4 answer Conventions: K is a positive L-space knot of genus g ≥ 1 (we may mirror). Citations are from memory, and the confidence in each is stated. ## (a) Reductions - **Unknot.** S^3_r(U) is S^3, S^1×S^2 or a lens space. Each of these is prime. - **Slope ∞.** This gives S^3, which is prime. - **Slope 0.** By Gabai (high confidence), S^3_0(K) is irreducible for nontrivial K. Since it is not S^3, it is prime. - **Non-integral slopes.** By Gordon–Luecke 1987 (high confidence), a reducible surgery on a nontrivial knot has integral slope. So non-integral surgeries are irreducible, hence prime: an irreducible manifold other than S^1×S^2 is prime, and S^1×S^2 only arises at slope 0 (Gabai). - **Torus knots.** By Moser (high confidence), the only reducible surgery on T(a,b) is at slope ab, and it gives L(a,b) # L(b,a). That is two summands. - **Satellites.** Known facts: - Baker–Motegi and Hom (moderate-to-high confidence): the companion J of a satellite L-space knot is an L-space knot, and the pattern is braided. - Scharlemann 1990 (moderate confidence on exact form): if a satellite K with companion torus T has a reducible surgery, then either K is a cable C_{m,n}(J) and the slope is mn, or T compresses in the surgered solid torus V(K). The second summand is a non-integral surgery on the nontrivial knot J, so it is irreducible (Gordon–Luecke) and not S^3. This gives exactly two summands. - In the other case, S^3_p(K) ≅ S^3_{p'}(J). Here J is an L-space knot (Baker–Motegi/Hom) whose exterior has fewer JSJ pieces. By induction, S^3_{p'}(J) has at most 2 summands. This holds whether or not p' is integral, since non-integral slopes give prime manifolds. - The base cases are torus knots (Moser) and hyperbolic knots. I cannot derive it from cyclicity of H_1 alone: cyclicity only gives coprime orders. - Given that statement: the remaining summand has H_1 of order |p|/(rs) = 1. It is not S^3, since it is prime. - Result: the only open case is S^3_p(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3 with |L1| = r, |L2| = s coprime, r, s ≥ 2, rs = |p|, and Y3 a homology sphere ≠ S^3. ## (c) Matignon–Sayari bound Statement (moderate confidence): if K is not a cable and S^3_p(K) is reducible, then |p| ≤ 2g(K) − 1. This gives a planar surface P in the exterior with n boundary components of slope p. 2. Take a minimal-genus Seifert surface F. 3. Intersect P and F and count arcs. Each boundary component of P meets ∂F in |p| points. 4. An Euler characteristic count on the graphs in P and F, together with the absence of Scharlemann cycles of certain lengths (Scharlemann cycles here produce lens-space summands or cable structure), gives n|p| ≤ n(2g − 1) + (correction terms). 5. The non-cable hypothesis removes the correction terms. I can only sketch this; it is not verified here. 1	kind: attempt
2	Open question attempted: the missing statement (M) below (ledger entry 12: no hyperbolic positive L-space knot K has S^3_{2g-1}(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3 with Y3 an L-space integer homology sphere other than S^3). It is the single statement on which a complete "yes" answer to the problem now rests.
3	
4	Your task: give a complete written proof of exactly (M), or else an explicit counterexample to it. Write out every step; state precisely every published theorem you invoke (you may invoke standard theorems; do not merely recall that "someone proved (M)" — a citation of the problem's answer from memory is not a proof and will not be accepted). If you cannot settle (M), reduce it to a precise, strictly easier statement and prove the reduction, and say exactly what remains.
5	
6	## THE MISSING STATEMENT (call it (M); it is the one statement standing between the material below and a complete answer)
7	
8	(M) Let K ⊂ S^3 be a hyperbolic knot of genus g such that S^3_n(K) is an L-space for some integer n > 0 (so K is fibred, S^3_r(K) is an L-space iff r >= 2g-1, and CFK^∞(K) is a staircase), and let p = 2g-1. Then S^3_p(K) is not homeomorphic to L1 # L2 # Y3 where L1, L2 are lens spaces of coprime orders r, s >= 2 with rs = p and Y3 is an integer homology sphere other than S^3 (Y3 is then automatically an L-space). Equivalently: no hyperbolic positive L-space knot has S^3_{2g-1}(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3 with Y3 an L-space integer homology sphere other than S^3.
9	
10	A proof of (M) for only some of the cases it covers — a sub-class of the knots (e.g. only when Y3 has finite fundamental group, only for particular (r, s), only for knots with extra structure) or a sub-range of the parameters — does NOT answer the question, though it should be reported if it is all that was found. A disproof must be an explicit knot (or a rigorous existence argument) with all the properties listed in (M).
11	
12	## How (M) completes the answer (the chain; check it, and say so if any step is flawed)
13	
14	1. Mirror so K is a positive L-space knot (mirroring preserves the number of prime summands). The unknot, slopes ∞ and 0, non-integral slopes, torus knots, cables and satellites are settled by the cited topological reduction (spliced below as "Reduction", from an earlier answer): each gives a prime manifold, or exactly two summands, or reduces to a hyperbolic L-space knot with integral slope.
15	2. For K hyperbolic and p integral with at least three prime summands, the cited Howie / Valdez-Sanchez / Sayari result gives S^3_p(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3, lens spaces of coprime orders r, s >= 2, rs = |p|, Y3 an integer homology sphere != S^3.
16	3. Then |p| = rs >= 6, and L1 # L2 is an L-space of order |p|, so the Theorem proved below ("Proved theorem (ledger 8)") forces p >= 2g-1. Hence Y = S^3_p(K) is an L-space (p >= 2g-1), and so is Y3 (Kunneth: HF-hat(Y) has rank |H_1(Y)| iff each summand is an L-space). By Matignon–Sayari (cited: a non-cable knot with reducible surgery slope p has |p| <= 2g-1) p = 2g-1.
17	4. (M) excludes exactly this configuration. Hence every surgery on an L-space knot has at most two prime summands.
18	
19	## Shared background (facts marked [lit] are standard published results you may cite, stating exactly what you use; [cited, moderate confidence] means pin down the exact statement or avoid it; everything else below was proved earlier in this attempt, modulo [lit])
20	
21	Conventions. An L-space knot is a knot K in S^3 with some nontrivial surgery an L-space. After mirroring (S^3_r(K) becomes -S^3_{-r}(mirror K), same number of prime summands) K is a positive L-space knot: S^3_r(K) is an L-space iff r >= 2g(K)-1 [lit]. Then K is fibred, CFK^infty(K) is a staircase, and the integers V_s satisfy V_s >= 0, V_s - V_{s+1} in {0,1}, V_s = 0 iff s >= g (K nontrivial), V_{-s} = V_s + s. Equivalently the Alexander polynomial has coefficients ±1 alternating and V_s = #{n not in S_K : n >= g + s}, where S_K (the "formal semigroup") is determined by Delta_K. Ni–Wu [lit]: for p > 0, d(S^3_p(K), i) = d(L(p,1), i) - 2 max(V_i, V_{p-i}), 0 <= i < p, with d(L(p,1), i) = ((2i-p)^2 - p)/(4p) (Ozsvath–Szabo convention S^3_p(U) = L(p,1); recursive formula d(L(p,q),i) = -1/4 + (2i+1-p-q)^2/(4pq) - d(L(q, p mod q), i mod q)).
22	
23	Topological reduction [cited; high confidence: Gabai (0-surgery irreducible), Gordon–Luecke 1987 (reducible slopes are integral), Moser (torus knots); moderate confidence: Scharlemann 1990 + Gabai's braid theorem for satellites, Baker–Motegi/Hom (companions of satellite L-space knots are L-space knots), Gordon–Luecke 1996 (a reducible surgery has a lens-space summand), Howie 2002 / Valdez-Sanchez / Sayari (at most three summands; with three, the shape is L1 # L2 # Y3, L1, L2 lens spaces of coprime orders r, s >= 2, rs = |p|, Y3 an integer homology sphere != S^3), Matignon–Sayari (a non-cable knot with reducible surgery slope p has |p| <= 2g-1)]. Cables at the cabling slope give L(m,n) # S^3_{n/m}(J): exactly two summands. So everything reduces to: K hyperbolic, p an integer, S^3_p(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3.
24	
25	Proved earlier in this attempt (Heegaard Floer, using the Ozsvath–Szabo relatively graded mapping cone):
26	(a) Hat ranks: rank HF-hat(S^3_p(K), i) = 1 for p >= 2g-1, 2n_i - 1 for 0 < p <= 2g-2, 2n_i + 1 for p < 0, where n_i = #{s ≡ i mod |p| : |s| <= g-1}.
27	(b) Theorem: for a nonzero integer p < 2g-1 (either sign), S^3_p(K) is never L # Y' with L an L-space of order |p| >= 3 and Y' an integer homology sphere. (All Spin^c classes would carry the same relatively graded HF^+; the cone gives K-independent "peak levels" whose multiplicity patterns differ between Spin^c classes 0 and 1.)
28	(c) Hence in the three-summand case p >= 2g-1 > 0, Y = S^3_p(K) and Y3 are L-spaces; with Matignon–Sayari, p = 2g-1 exactly, so p = rs is odd.
29	
30	THE REMAINING CASE (the only obstacle to answering the question "yes"):
31	  (R) K a hyperbolic positive L-space knot of genus g, p = 2g-1 = rs (r, s >= 2 coprime, both odd), S^3_p(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3 with L1, L2 lens spaces of orders r, s and Y3 an L-space integer homology sphere, Y3 != S^3.
32	
33	Computer evidence (exact rational arithmetic, exhaustive over all formal staircases V of genus g, all lens spaces of orders r, s and all torsor-compatible identifications of Spin^c structures) for p = 2g-1 in {15, 21, 33, 35, 39, 45}: the d-equation d(S^3_p(K), i) = d(L1, .) + d(L2, .) + d(Y3) has EXACTLY ONE solution, namely
34	   V_j(K) = V_j(T(r,s)) + 1 for 0 <= j <= g-1, d(Y3) = -2, and L1 # L2 = the lens-space pair of S^3_{rs}(T(r,s)) (= L(r,s) # L(s,r) up to orientation conventions; for p = 15 it is L(3,2) # L(5,2) in the OS convention).
35	Equivalently Delta_K = Delta_{T(r,s)} + t^g - t^{g-1} - t^{-(g-1)} + t^{-g} with g = (rs+1)/2 (for p = 15: Delta_K = t^8 - t^7 + t^4 - t^3 + t - 1 + t^{-1} - t^{-3} + t^{-4} - t^{-7} + t^{-8}, formal semigroup {0,4,7,9,10,12,13,14,16,...}, which is not closed under addition). The extra term is t^{-g}(t-1)(t^p - 1), which vanishes at every p-th root of unity, so the Reidemeister–Turaev torsion of Y also agrees. In short: every invariant of the closed manifold Y computable from HF^+(Y) (Y is an L-space, so HF^+ is determined by the d-invariants), Casson–Walker, or torsion, coincides with that of S^3_{rs}(T(r,s)) # S^3_{+1}(T(2,3)), where S^3_{+1}(T(2,3)) is the Poincare sphere oriented with d = -2. Therefore NO argument using only such invariants of Y can exclude (R): one needs the knot (dual knot, 4-dimensional trace, cobordism maps) or 3-dimensional topology. (For p = 2g, a similar c = -2 solution exists, e.g. V = V(T(2,7)) + 1 at p = 14, g = 7; Matignon–Sayari excludes p = 2g for non-cables.)
36	
37	## New facts found by the planner since the background was written (checked by hand / computer, not by a separate proof)
38

52	**Theorem.** Let K be a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g, and let p be a nonzero integer with p < 2g-1 (p may be negative). In particular it is not of the form L1 # L2 # Y3 with L1, L2 lens spaces of coprime orders r, s >= 2 (here rs = |p| >= 6) and Y3 an integer homology sphere.

56	## 0. Reduction to an algebraic statement

Since H_1(Y') = 0, every one of the |p| spin^c structures on Y has
58	  HF^+(Y, i) ≅ HF^+(Y') as relatively Z-graded F[U]-modules (up to a degree shift). (*)
59	So it suffices to find two spin^c classes i, i' of S^3_p(K) whose HF^+ are **not** isomorphic up to a degree shift. I compare the classes i = 0 and i = 1. These are different classes because |p| >= 3.

61	**Invariants used.** A finitely generated graded F[U]-module of the form T^+ ⊕ (finite part) is determined up to isomorphism by (a) the degree of the bottom of the tower and (b) the multiset of degrees of the tops of its cyclic summands. For (b), the number of summands whose top lies in degree k is dim (M/UM)_k. After a degree shift, two isomorphic modules have the same number of finite summands, and their multisets of top degrees agree up to a translation. In particular the multiplicity pattern of the multiset is the same for both.

If U^e maps A to B and the bottom of A is at level x, then preserving levels puts the bottom of B at level x + e. The real grading of a B-level is a uniform shift of the A-level (by the cone's degree-1 shift), and this shift is the same for all classes.

71	- vertices: the A's whose bottom is <= k;

57	Let Y = S^3_p(K) ≅ L # Y'. Write CF^-(L,s) ≃ F[U] for each s (L is an L-space). Since H_1(Y') = 0, every one of the |p| spin^c structures on Y has
58	  HF^+(Y, i) ≅ HF^+(Y') as relatively Z-graded F[U]-modules (up to a degree shift). (*)
59	So it suffices to find two spin^c classes i, i' of S^3_p(K) whose HF^+ are **not** isomorphic up to a degree shift. I compare the classes i = 0 and i = 1. These are different classes because |p| >= 3.

61	**Invariants used.** A finitely generated graded F[U]-module of the form T^+ ⊕ (finite part) is determined up to isomorphism by (a) the degree of the bottom of the tower and (b) the multiset of degrees of the tops of its cyclic summands. For (b), the number of summands whose top lies in degree k is dim (M/UM)_k. After a degree shift, two isomorphic modules have the same number of finite summands, and their multisets of top degrees agree up to a translation. In particular the multiplicity pattern of the multiset is the same for both.

50	# Answer to round2_q3
51	
52	**Theorem.** Let K be a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g, and let p be a nonzero integer with p < 2g-1 (p may be negative). Then S^3_p(K) is not homeomorphic to L # Y', where L is an L-space with |H_1(L)| = |p| >= 3 and Y' is an integer homology sphere. In particular it is not of the form L1 # L2 # Y3 with L1, L2 lens spaces of coprime orders r, s >= 2 (here rs = |p| >= 6) and Y3 an integer homology sphere.
53	
54	Below, "[lit]" means a standard result that I cite from memory.
55	
56	## 0. Reduction to an algebraic statement
57	Let Y = S^3_p(K) ≅ L # Y'. Write CF^-(L,s) ≃ F[U] for each s (L is an L-space). By the Ozsvath–Szabo connected-sum formula [lit], CF^-(L#Y', s#t) ≃ CF^-(L,s) ⊗_{F[U]} CF^-(Y',t) ≃ CF^-(Y') up to a grading shift. Tensoring with F[U,U^{-1}]/U·F[U] gives the same for CF^+. Since H_1(Y') = 0, every one of the |p| spin^c structures on Y has
58	  HF^+(Y, i) ≅ HF^+(Y') as relatively Z-graded F[U]-modules (up to a degree shift). (*)
59	So it suffices to find two spin^c classes i, i' of S^3_p(K) whose HF^+ are **not** isomorphic up to a degree shift. I compare the classes i = 0 and i = 1. These are different classes because |p| >= 3.
60	
61	**Invariants used.** A finitely generated graded F[U]-module of the form T^+ ⊕ (finite part) is determined up to isomorphism by (a) the degree of the bottom of the tower and (b) the multiset of degrees of the tops of its cyclic summands. For (b), the number of summands whose top lies in degree k is dim (M/UM)_k. After a degree shift, two isomorphic modules have the same number of finite summands, and their multisets of top degrees agree up to a translation. In particular the multiplicity pattern of the multiset is the same for both.
62	
63	## 1. Cone model in "level" form (both signs)
64	I use the Ozsvath–Szabo integer surgery formula [lit]. For a positive L-space knot, A_s^+ ≅ B_s^+ ≅ T^+, with v_s = U^{V_s} and h_s = U^{H_s}, where H_s = V_{-s}. The V_s satisfy V_s >= 0, V_s - V_{s+1} ∈ {0,1}, V_s = 0 iff s >= g, and V_{-s} = V_s + s.
65	
66	Model each tower by levels k ∈ Z: the tower has F in each level k >= (its bottom), and U lowers the level by 1. If U^e maps A to B and the bottom of A is at level x, then preserving levels puts the bottom of B at level x + e. The real grading of a B-level is a uniform shift of the A-level (by the cone's degree-1 shift), and this shift is the same for all classes.
67	
68	The only exponents that appear below are V_s with s <= g-1 and H_s = V_{-s} with s >= -(g-1). All of these are >= 1. So every B-bottom (a "peak") lies strictly above the adjacent A-bottoms ("valleys").
69	
70	At level k the cone map is the coboundary δ of a graph G_k:
71	- vertices: the A's whose bottom is <= k;
72	- edges: the B's whose bottom is <= k;
73	- (Da)_B is the sum of the values at the A's adjacent to B. A B adjacent to only one retained A acts as an edge to a "ground" vertex, where the value is fixed to 0.
74	
75	## 2. The case p > 0
76	**Truncation.** Fix a class i and let s_1 < … < s_n be the elements s ≡ i (mod p) with |s| <= g-1.
77	
78	D: ⊕A → ⊕B is surjective. Indeed, every map is U^e on T^+, which is surjective, and one can solve inductively along the zigzag. So H_*(cone) ≅ ker D, up to a uniform shift.
79	
80	For a kernel element: for s >= g we have V_s = 0, which forces a_s = U^{H_{s-p}} a_{s-p}. For s - p <= -g we have H_{s-p} = 0, which forces a_{s-p} = U^{V_s} a_s. So every a_s outside [-(g-1), g-1] is determined by the a_{s_j}. Hence
81	  ker D ≅ { (a_1,…,a_n) : U^{H_{s_j}} a_j = U^{V_{s_{j+1}}} a_{j+1}, j = 1,…,n-1 }.
82	This is a path graph with valleys x_j (the bottom of A_{s_j}) and peaks y_{j+1} = x_j + H_{s_j} = x_{j+1} + V_{s_{j+1}}. If n = 0 the module is T^+.
83	
84	**Positions.** Solving x(s+p) - x(s) = V_{-s} - V_{s+p} = V_s + s - V_{s+p} gives
85	  x(s) = s(s-p)/(2p) - V_s,
86	and therefore the peak between s and s+p is at
87	  y = x(s) + V_{-s} = s(s+p)/(2p) = (m^2 - p^2/4)/(2p), where m = s + p/2.
88	The peak levels do not depend on K.
89	
90	**Module structure.** At level k, ker D is the space of functions on the vertices of G_k that are constant along its edges, i.e. functions on the connected components of G_k. U acts by restriction from G_k to G_{k-1}.
91	- For large k, G_k is connected, so the module has one tower, with bottom at min_j x_j.
92	- Restriction from level k+1 to level k fails to be surjective by exactly the number of edges (peaks) at level k+1. G_k is a subforest of a path, so each new edge joins two different components.
93	- Hence the finite summands have their tops at the levels {y - 1 : y a peak}. There are n-1 of them, counted with multiplicity.
94	
95	**Number of summands.** The number of finite summands is max(n_i - 1, 0), where n_i = #{s ≡ i mod p : |s| <= g-1}. The integers in [-(g-1), g-1] are 2g-1 consecutive integers. Since 0 < p < 2g-1, every n_i >= 1, and the n_i are all equal iff p | 2g-1. By (*) they must be equal. So p | 2g-1, p is odd, and n := (2g-1)/p >= 3.
96	
97	The class of t (|t| <= (p-1)/2) is then {t + kp : |k| <= (n-1)/2}, and its peaks are at m = t + (k + 1/2)p for k = -(n-1)/2, …, (n-3)/2.
98	- **Class 0:** m ∈ {±p/2, ±3p/2, …, ±(n-2)p/2}. Each peak level occurs with even multiplicity.
99	- **Class 1:** two of the m's would give equal m^2 only if m = -m', i.e. 2 + (k + k' + 1)p = 0, which is impossible for p >= 3. So all n-1 >= 2 top levels are distinct.
100	
101	A translation cannot turn a multiset with all multiplicities even into one with all multiplicities 1. This contradicts (*).
102	
103	## 3. The case p = -q < 0
104	**Truncation.** I use the Ozsvath–Szabo truncation of the cone [lit]: cancel A_s against B_s for s >= g (v_s is an isomorphism there), and A_s against B_{s-q} for s <= -g (h_s is an isomorphism there).
105	
106	In class i, let s_1 < … < s_n be the elements with |s| <= g-1. What remains is the zigzag
107	  B_{s_1-q} ← A_{s_1} → B_{s_1} ← A_{s_1+q} → … → B_{s_n}.
108	It has n A's (valleys) and n+1 B's (peaks); the two end B's are ground edges.
109	- If n = 0, exactly one B survives and the module is T^+.
110	- Every A carries even (A-)parity and every B odd parity, and U preserves parity. So H = ker D ⊕ coker D as F[U]-modules.
111	
112	**Positions.** Solving x(s+q) - x(s) = V_s - V_{-(s+q)} gives
113	  x(s) = -s(s+q)/(2q) - V_s,
114	and the bottom of B_t is at
115	  b(t) = -t(t+q)/(2q) = -(u^2 - q^2/4)/(2q), where u = t + q/2.
116	Again the peak levels do not depend on K.
117	
118	**Module structure.** G_k together with the ground vertex is a subgraph of a single cycle.
119	- **Coker.** coker δ_k = H^1(G_k ∪ ground, ground) = H^1(G_k ∪ ground), which is 0 until the cycle closes at level M = max peak and F from then on. So the B-parity part is a single tower with bottom at M.
120	- **Ker.** ker δ_k is the space of functions on the components of G_k that do not touch ground; it is entirely finite. Its tops lie at {y - 1 : y a peak}, with one copy of M - 1 removed: the edge that closes the cycle does not merge two components.
121	- **Number of summands.** dim ker U on the ker part is n_i: one summand is born at each valley. By (*) the n_i must be equal. That forces q | 2g-1, because if q > 2g-1 some classes have n_i = 0 and others n_i = 1. So n = (2g-1)/q is odd and q >= 3 is odd. The class of t has the B-midpoints u = t + (k + 1/2)q for k = -(n+1)/2, …, (n-1)/2.
122	
123	The invariant used here is the multiset of top levels of the finite summands, measured relative to the tower bottom. Both live in fixed parities, and these relative offsets are preserved by any graded isomorphism.
124	- **Class 0:** u ∈ {±q/2, …, ±nq/2}. The maximal peak (|u| = q/2) occurs twice, so its value survives once after removing one copy; every other value occurs twice.
125	- **Class 1:** all |u| are distinct (as in §2), so all values are distinct.
126	- **If n >= 3:** class 0 has a repeated top level and class 1 does not. Contradiction.
127	- **If n = 1:** both classes have a single finite summand. Its top lies 1 level below the tower bottom in class 0, but |b(1-q) - b(1)| + 1 = 2 levels below in class 1, since the two u's differ in u^2 by 2q. Contradiction.
128	
129	(For n = 1 the finite summand of class s is F[U]/U^{V_{|s|}}, and its top is |s| + 1 levels below the tower bottom. The sizes V_{|s|} alone might coincide across classes; the positions cannot.)
130	
131	This proves the Theorem in both cases. ∎
132	
133	## Status
134	- **Proved here:** the Theorem, assuming the cited tools.
135	- **Cited from memory [lit]:**
136	  - the integer surgery formula, as an isomorphism of relatively graded F[U]-modules, together with its truncation;
137	  - the facts about V_s for L-space knots;
138	  - the connected-sum formula for CF^-.
139	- **Remark:** the proof only uses that one summand is an L-space with |H_1| = |p| >= 3. The p > 0 rank formula hinted in the task, rank HF-hat = 2n_i - 1, also follows: dim ker U = n_i.
140	- **Not addressed here:** the regime p >= 2g-1 (p > 0), where S^3_p(K) is an L-space; this is where cables give two summands. It is not part of this task.
141	
142	
143	### Reduction (topological, cited theorems): the full earlier answer
144	
145	# round2_q4 answer
146	
147	Conventions: K is a positive L-space knot of genus g ≥ 1 (we may mirror). Citations are from memory, and the confidence in each is stated.
148	
149	## (a) Reductions
150	- **Unknot.** S^3_r(U) is S^3, S^1×S^2 or a lens space. Each of these is prime.
151	- **Slope ∞.** This gives S^3, which is prime.
152	- **Slope 0.** By Gabai (high confidence), S^3_0(K) is irreducible for nontrivial K. Since it is not S^3, it is prime.
153	- **Non-integral slopes.** By Gordon–Luecke 1987 (high confidence), a reducible surgery on a nontrivial knot has integral slope. So non-integral surgeries are irreducible, hence prime: an irreducible manifold other than S^1×S^2 is prime, and S^1×S^2 only arises at slope 0 (Gabai).
154	- **Torus knots.** By Moser (high confidence), the only reducible surgery on T(a,b) is at slope ab, and it gives L(a,b) # L(b,a). That is two summands.
155	- **Satellites.** Known facts:
156	  - Baker–Motegi and Hom (moderate-to-high confidence): the companion J of a satellite L-space knot is an L-space knot, and the pattern is braided.
157	  - Scharlemann 1990 (moderate confidence on exact form): if a satellite K with companion torus T has a reducible surgery, then either K is a cable C_{m,n}(J) and the slope is mn, or T compresses in the surgered solid torus V(K). In the second case Gabai's theorem (surgery on a braid in a solid torus giving a solid torus forces a 0- or 1-bridge braid) applies, V(K) is a solid torus, and S^3_p(K) = S^3_{p'}(J) for a slope p' with K' integral (p' = p/w², where w is the winding number).
158	
159	  **Induction** on the number of JSJ tori of the exterior:
160	  - In the cable case, S^3_{mn}(C_{m,n}(J)) = L(m,n) # S^3_{n/m}(J). The second summand is a non-integral surgery on the nontrivial knot J, so it is irreducible (Gordon–Luecke) and not S^3. This gives exactly two summands.
161	  - In the other case, S^3_p(K) ≅ S^3_{p'}(J). Here J is an L-space knot (Baker–Motegi/Hom) whose exterior has fewer JSJ pieces. By induction, S^3_{p'}(J) has at most 2 summands. This holds whether or not p' is integral, since non-integral slopes give prime manifolds.
162	  - The base cases are torus knots (Moser) and hyperbolic knots.
163	
164	  So everything reduces to **K hyperbolic and p integral**.
165	
166	## (b) Shape of the summands
167	- By Howie (2002, via Scott–Wiegold), also Valdez-Sanchez and Sayari (moderate confidence), there are at most 3 prime summands.
168	- By Gordon–Luecke 1996 (moderate confidence), some summand is a lens space.
169	- H_1(S^3_p(K)) = Z/|p| is cyclic. The H_1 of the summands are direct summands of it, so their orders are pairwise coprime and multiply to |p|.
170	- In the three-summand case, the step "two of the summands are lens spaces, the third is a homology sphere" is what I recall as the statement of Howie / Valdez-Sanchez (moderate–low confidence on the attribution). I cannot derive it from cyclicity of H_1 alone: cyclicity only gives coprime orders.
171	- Given that statement: the remaining summand has H_1 of order |p|/(rs) = 1. It is not S^3, since it is prime.
172	- Result: the only open case is S^3_p(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3 with |L1| = r, |L2| = s coprime, r, s ≥ 2, rs = |p|, and Y3 a homology sphere ≠ S^3.
173	
174	## (c) Matignon–Sayari bound
175	Statement (moderate confidence): if K is not a cable and S^3_p(K) is reducible, then |p| ≤ 2g(K) − 1.
176	
177	Proof sketch:
178	1. Take a reducing sphere meeting the attached solid torus in a minimal number n of meridian disks. This gives a planar surface P in the exterior with n boundary components of slope p.
179	2. Take a minimal-genus Seifert surface F.
180	3. Intersect P and F and count arcs. Each boundary component of P meets ∂F in |p| points.
181	4. An Euler characteristic count on the graphs in P and F, together with the absence of Scharlemann cycles of certain lengths (Scharlemann cycles here produce lens-space summands or cable structure), gives n|p| ≤ n(2g − 1) + (correction terms).
182	5. The non-cable hypothesis removes the correction terms.
183	
184	I can only sketch this; it is not verified here.
185	
186	So for hyperbolic K: |p| ≤ 2g − 1.
187	
188	## (d) Heegaard Floer constraints in the three-summand case
189	By Künneth, HF-hat(L1 # L2 # Y3) in every spin^c class has rank k := rank HF-hat(Y3), which is odd. Moreover Y3 is an L-space iff k = 1. So **the rank must be the same in every class**.
190	
191	**p > 0.** By the hint formula (stated in the task, not proved here; the mechanism is the same as in the p < 0 computation below), the rank in class i is 2n_i − 1 if n_i ≥ 1 and 1 if n_i = 0, where n_i = #{s ≡ i mod p : |s| ≤ g−1}. The window [−g+1, g−1] has length 2g − 1.
192	- If p > 2g − 1: some n_i = 0 and all others are at most 1, so all ranks are 1. In this case Y3 is an L-space homology sphere. This contradicts Matignon–Sayari, so it does not occur.
193	- If p ≤ 2g − 1: all n_i ≥ 1. The ranks 2n_i − 1 are constant iff p divides 2g − 1. Then k = 2(2g−1)/p − 1.
194	- Conclusion: p | 2g − 1. Either p = 2g − 1 and Y3 is an L-space homology sphere ≠ S^3, or p is a proper divisor of 2g − 1 and Y3 is not an L-space.
195	
196	**p < 0, write p = −q.** Hat mapping cone in class i:
197	- Each Â_s has rank 1. The edges are v̂: Â_s → B̂_s, nonzero iff s ≥ g, and ĥ: Â_s → B̂_{s−q}, nonzero iff s ≤ −g.
198	- Cancel Â_s with B̂_s for s ≥ g, and Â_s with B̂_{s−q} for s ≤ −g.
199	- What survives: Â_s for |s| ≤ g−1 (n_i of them), and B̂_t for −g−q < t < g.
200	- The interval [−g−q+1, g−1] is [−g−q+1, −g] (length q, containing exactly one t ≡ i) together with [−g+1, g−1]. So there are n_i + 1 surviving B̂_t.
201	- All surviving maps vanish, so the rank in class i is 2n_i + 1.
202	- This is constant iff q | 2g − 1 (with q ≤ 2g − 1 forced). Then k = 2(2g−1)/q + 1 ≥ 3, so Y3 is not an L-space.
203	
204	**Proposition (proved modulo the cited HF facts and the hint formula).** In the three-summand case, |p| divides 2g − 1. If moreover p > 0 and p = 2g − 1, then Y3 is an L-space integer homology sphere ≠ S^3. This also answers the task's question: yes, |p| ≤ 2g − 1 in that case. It follows both from Matignon–Sayari for non-cables and, independently, from the divisibility.
205	
206	## Status
207	- **Proved here:** the reductions in (a), given the cited theorems; the divisibility |p| divides 2g − 1 and the per-class rank count for negative p in (d).
208	- **Rests on citations:** Gordon–Luecke 1987, Gabai and Moser (high confidence); Scharlemann 1990 / Gabai braid theorem, Baker–Motegi/Hom, Howie, Gordon–Luecke 1996, Matignon–Sayari (moderate confidence); the "two lens spaces" part of the shape (moderate–low confidence).
209	- **Not verified:** the per-class rank formula for p > 0 is used as stated in the hint; its proof is only indicated, via the same cancellation as in the p < 0 case.
210	- **Open:**
211	  1. Exclude L1 # L2 # Y3 when |p| divides 2g − 1. For example, use the d-invariant identity d(S^3_p(K), i) = d(L1) + d(L2) + d(Y3) together with the Ni–Wu formula, or the absolute grading of the HF^+ tower.
212	  2. Rule out p = 2g − 1 with an L-space homology sphere Y3 (for instance the Poincaré sphere).
213	
214	  So the original question (at most two prime summands) is reduced but **not settled** here.
215	
216	
217	## What to report at the end
218	State clearly: (1) whether (M) is proved in full, refuted, or reduced (to what, exactly); (2) every step that rests on a cited published theorem, with its exact statement; (3) whether the chain above, from (M) to the answer, is sound — and if not, which step fails; (4) what remains open.

1	kind: attempt
2	Open question attempted: the missing statement (M) below (ledger entry 12), by a NAMED APPROACH not yet tried in this attempt: the fibration of the knot exterior and circle-valued Morse position of the reducing planar surfaces (Thurston/Roussarie), combined with properties of the monodromy (pseudo-Anosov since K is hyperbolic; right-veering, as the monodromy of an L-space knot is; fractional Dehn twist coefficient; Gabai's degeneracy slope and the results on Dehn fillings far from it carrying pseudo-Anosov flows / taut foliations — state exactly any such theorem you use).
3	
4	Your task: prove (M) by this approach, or produce an explicit counterexample, or reduce (M) to a precise strictly easier statement (and prove the reduction). You may depart from the approach if you explain why. Concretely, work out in full: (i) the Morse-position normal form for the planar surface P (n boundary curves of slope p = 2g-1, n even, n >= 4) relative to the fibration, with its n - 2 saddles; (ii) the resulting arc systems P ∩ F_t (np/2 arcs) and how they change through one circuit, ending in h(A_0); (iii) how the 1/p boundary rotation per circuit constrains the fractional Dehn twist coefficient of h, and whether p = 2g-1 is extremal; (iv) what changes when there are two disjoint non-parallel reducing spheres (three summands), with Y3 a homology sphere containing no Scharlemann-cycle disc — and whether this yields a contradiction. Test any counting inequality on the smallest case p = 15 (r = 3, s = 5, g = 8) before relying on it.
5	
6	## THE MISSING STATEMENT (call it (M); it is the one statement standing between the material below and a complete answer)
7	
8	(M) Let K ⊂ S^3 be a hyperbolic knot of genus g such that S^3_n(K) is an L-space for some integer n > 0 (so K is fibred, S^3_r(K) is an L-space iff r >= 2g-1, and CFK^∞(K) is a staircase), and let p = 2g-1. Then S^3_p(K) is not homeomorphic to L1 # L2 # Y3 where L1, L2 are lens spaces of coprime orders r, s >= 2 with rs = p and Y3 is an integer homology sphere other than S^3 (Y3 is then automatically an L-space). Equivalently: no hyperbolic positive L-space knot has S^3_{2g-1}(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3 with Y3 an L-space integer homology sphere other than S^3.
9	
10	A proof of (M) for only some of the cases it covers — a sub-class of the knots (e.g. only when Y3 has finite fundamental group, only for particular (r, s), only for knots with extra structure) or a sub-range of the parameters — does NOT answer the question, though it should be reported if it is all that was found. A disproof must be an explicit knot (or a rigorous existence argument) with all the properties listed in (M).
11	
12	## How (M) completes the answer (the chain; check it, and say so if any step is flawed)
13	
14	1. Mirror so K is a positive L-space knot (mirroring preserves the number of prime summands). The unknot, slopes ∞ and 0, non-integral slopes, torus knots, cables and satellites are settled by the cited topological reduction (spliced below as "Reduction", from an earlier answer): each gives a prime manifold, or exactly two summands, or reduces to a hyperbolic L-space knot with integral slope.
15	2. For K hyperbolic and p integral with at least three prime summands, the cited Howie / Valdez-Sanchez / Sayari result gives S^3_p(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3, lens spaces of coprime orders r, s >= 2, rs = |p|, Y3 an integer homology sphere != S^3.
16	3. Then |p| = rs >= 6, and L1 # L2 is an L-space of order |p|, so the Theorem proved below ("Proved theorem (ledger 8)") forces p >= 2g-1. Hence Y = S^3_p(K) is an L-space (p >= 2g-1), and so is Y3 (Kunneth: HF-hat(Y) has rank |H_1(Y)| iff each summand is an L-space). By Matignon–Sayari (cited: a non-cable knot with reducible surgery slope p has |p| <= 2g-1) p = 2g-1.
17	4. (M) excludes exactly this configuration. Hence every surgery on an L-space knot has at most two prime summands.
18	
19	## Shared background (facts marked [lit] are standard published results you may cite, stating exactly what you use; [cited, moderate confidence] means pin down the exact statement or avoid it; everything else below was proved earlier in this attempt, modulo [lit])
20	
21	Conventions. An L-space knot is a knot K in S^3 with some nontrivial surgery an L-space. After mirroring (S^3_r(K) becomes -S^3_{-r}(mirror K), same number of prime summands) K is a positive L-space knot: S^3_r(K) is an L-space iff r >= 2g(K)-1 [lit]. Then K is fibred, CFK^infty(K) is a staircase, and the integers V_s satisfy V_s >= 0, V_s - V_{s+1} in {0,1}, V_s = 0 iff s >= g (K nontrivial), V_{-s} = V_s + s. Equivalently the Alexander polynomial has coefficients ±1 alternating and V_s = #{n not in S_K : n >= g + s}, where S_K (the "formal semigroup") is determined by Delta_K. Ni–Wu [lit]: for p > 0, d(S^3_p(K), i) = d(L(p,1), i) - 2 max(V_i, V_{p-i}), 0 <= i < p, with d(L(p,1), i) = ((2i-p)^2 - p)/(4p) (Ozsvath–Szabo convention S^3_p(U) = L(p,1); recursive formula d(L(p,q),i) = -1/4 + (2i+1-p-q)^2/(4pq) - d(L(q, p mod q), i mod q)).

23	Topological reduction [cited; high confidence: Gabai (0-surgery irreducible), Gordon–Luecke 1987 (reducible slopes are integral), Moser (torus knots); moderate confidence: Scharlemann 1990 + Gabai's braid theorem for satellites, Baker–Motegi/Hom (companions of satellite L-space knots are L-space knots), Gordon–Luecke 1996 (a reducible surgery has a lens-space summand), Howie 2002 / Valdez-Sanchez / Sayari (at most three summands; with three, the shape is L1 # L2 # Y3, L1, L2 lens spaces of coprime orders r, s >= 2, rs = |p|, Y3 an integer homology sphere != S^3), Matignon–Sayari (a non-cable knot with reducible surgery slope p has |p| <= 2g-1)]. 25	Proved earlier in this attempt (Heegaard Floer, using the Ozsvath–Szabo relatively graded mapping cone):
26	(a) Hat ranks: rank HF-hat(S^3_p(K), i) = 1 for p >= 2g-1, 2n_i - 1 for 0 < p <= 2g-2, 2n_i + 1 for p < 0, where n_i = #{s ≡ i mod |p| : |s| <= g-1}.
27	(b) Theorem: for a nonzero integer p < 2g-1 (either sign), S^3_p(K) is never L # Y' with L an L-space of order |p| >= 3 and Y' an integer homology sphere. (All Spin^c classes would carry the same relatively graded HF^+; the cone gives K-independent "peak levels" whose multiplicity patterns differ between Spin^c classes 0 and 1.)
28	(c) Hence in the three-summand case p >= 2g-1 > 0, Y = S^3_p(K) and Y3 are L-spaces; with Matignon–Sayari, p = 2g-1 exactly, so p = rs is odd.
29	
30	THE REMAINING CASE (the only obstacle to answering the question "yes"):
31	  (R) K a hyperbolic positive L-space knot of genus g, p = 2g-1 = rs (r, s >= 2 coprime, both odd), S^3_p(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3 with L1, L2 lens spaces of orders r, s and Y3 an L-space integer homology sphere, Y3 != S^3.
32	
33	Computer evidence (exact rational arithmetic, exhaustive over all formal staircases V of genus g, all lens spaces of orders r, s and all torsor-compatible identifications of Spin^c structures) for p = 2g-1 in {15, 21, 33, 35, 39, 45}: the d-equation d(S^3_p(K), i) = d(L1, .) + d(L2, .) + d(Y3) has EXACTLY ONE solution, namely
34	   V_j(K) = V_j(T(r,s)) + 1 for 0 <= j <= g-1, d(Y3) = -2, and L1 # L2 = the lens-space pair of S^3_{rs}(T(r,s)) (= L(r,s) # L(s,r) up to orientation conventions; for p = 15 it is L(3,2) # L(5,2) in the OS convention).
35	Equivalently Delta_K = Delta_{T(r,s)} + t^g - t^{g-1} - t^{-(g-1)} + t^{-g} with g = (rs+1)/2 (for p = 15: Delta_K = t^8 - t^7 + t^4 - t^3 + t - 1 + t^{-1} - t^{-3} + t^{-4} - t^{-7} + t^{-8}, formal semigroup {0,4,7,9,10,12,13,14,16,...}, which is not closed under addition). 38	
39	- Why the formal solution of the d-equation works: for p = 2g-1 every index min(i, p-i) is <= g-1, so the staircase V = V(T(r,s)) + 1 shifts every d(Y, i) by exactly -2 relative to S^3_{rs}(T(r,s)). So invariants of Y alone cannot exclude (M).

Elkies (some characteristic vector has |c|^2 <= n, equality only for Z^n) then gives d(Y3) <= -2, and if d(Y3) = -2 then Λ ≅ Z^n and the data are exactly Greene's lens-space realisation data for the staircase V - 1. So the 4-dimensional lattice is CONSISTENT with the split model S^3_{rs}(T(r,s)) # S^3_{+1}(T(2,3)); lattice arguments alone are not expected to prove (M).
41	- WARNING: the dual knot K* (core of the surgery solid torus) of (2g-1)-surgery on an L-space knot is NOT Floer simple in general: for T(2,3) and p = 1 the dual is a genus-one knot in the Poincare sphere, whose knot Floer homology has rank >= 3. Do not use "K* is Floer simple, hence rational-genus minimising (Ni–Wu)" at p = 2g-1. (Its rational genus is (2g-1)/(2p) = 1/2; a core#core knot in L1 # L2 has rational genus 1/2 - 1/(2r) - 1/(2s) with the -χ convention; turning this into a contradiction would need K* to be rational-genus minimising in its homology class, which is not known.)

43	## Planner's sketch of why (M) should hold (a suggestion only; discard it if you see a better route)
44	No invariant of Y alone sees (M), and the lattice reproduces the split model, so a proof must use the exterior M_K = S^3 \ N(K): fibred with fibre F of genus g (one boundary component), monodromy h pseudo-Anosov (K hyperbolic) and right-veering (L-space knot). A reducing sphere meeting the surgery solid torus minimally gives an incompressible, ∂-incompressible planar surface P ⊂ M_K with n boundary curves of slope p; n is even and n >= 4 (n = 2 would give an essential annulus, impossible for hyperbolic K). By Thurston/Roussarie, P can be isotoped so the fibration θ: M_K → S^1 restricted to P is Morse with only saddles, n - 2 of them. Each ∂-component of P meets each fibre F_t in p points, so P ∩ F_t is a system of np/2 disjoint essential arcs (at most 6g-3 = 3p isotopy classes when p = 2g-1), and after one circuit the system returns as h(A_0) after only n - 2 band moves. Arcs untouched by saddles form chains α, h(α), ..., h^{L-1}(α) of pairwise disjoint, pairwise non-isotopic arcs (h has no periodic arcs), at most 2(n-2) chains in total; the endpoints rotate by exactly 1/p of a turn per circuit, which must be reconciled with the fractional Dehn twist coefficient of h. With three summands there are two disjoint non-parallel reducing spheres, hence two such planar surfaces simultaneously in Morse position, both in the tight Matignon–Sayari regime p = 2g-1. The hoped-for contradiction: the counting plus right-veering forces Scharlemann-cycle faces on both sides of one of the P's, which would place a punctured lens space inside the homology-sphere side Y3. This is a conjectured mechanism, not a proof.

46	## Earlier results you may rest on (spliced verbatim from earlier answers)
