Again the peak levels do not depend on K.

**Module structure.** G_k together with the ground vertex is a subgraph of a single cycle.
- **Coker.** coker δ_k = H^1(G_k ∪ ground, ground) = H^1(G_k ∪ ground), which is 0 until the cycle closes at level M = max peak and F from then on. So the B-parity part is a single tower with bottom at M.
- **Ker.** ker δ_k is the space of functions on the components of G_k that do not touch ground; it is entirely finite. Its tops lie at {y - 1 : y a peak}, with one copy of M - 1 removed: the edge that closes the cycle does not merge two components.
- **Number of summands.** dim ker U on the ker part is n_i: one summand is born at each valley. By (*) the n_i must be equal. That forces q | 2g-1, because if q > 2g-1 some classes have n_i = 0 and others n_i = 1. So n = (2g-1)/q is odd and q >= 3 is odd. The class of t has the B-midpoints u = t + (k + 1/2)q for k = -(n+1)/2, …, (n-1)/2.

The invariant used here is the multiset of top levels of the finite summands, measured relative to the tower bottom. Both live in fixed parities, and these relative offsets are preserved by any graded isomorphism.
- **Class 0:** u ∈ {±q/2, …, ±nq/2}. The maximal peak (|u| = q/2) occurs twice, so its value survives once after removing one copy; every other value occurs twice.
- **Class 1:** all |u| are distinct (as in §2), so all values are distinct.
- **If n >= 3:** class 0 has a repeated top level and class 1 does not. Contradiction.
- **If n = 1:** both classes have a single finite summand. Its top lies 1 level below the tower bottom in class 0, but |b(1-q) - b(1)| + 1 = 2 levels below in class 1, since the two u's differ in u^2 by 2q. Contradiction.

(For n = 1 the finite summand of class s is F[U]/U^{V_{|s|}}, and its top is |s| + 1 levels below the tower bottom. The sizes V_{|s|} alone might coincide across classes; the positions cannot.)

This proves the Theorem in both cases. ∎

content.text:
Round 5 is planned and I did not conclude. I wrote 8 query files, all of them attempt queries.

**Target:** the new missing statement, the cover bound (CB). If K is a fibred knot of genus g and S^3_p(K) = A # B with B an integer homology sphere other than S^3, then |p| ≤ g.

**Why this changed:** the main line had stalled on ledger 12. Round4_q9 proved two facts about the |p|-fold cyclic cover of the surgery but did not compare them. First, the cover is an open book with page F, so its fundamental group has at most 2g generators. Second, it contains |p| copies of B, so its fundamental group needs at least 2|p| generators. Putting the two together is my own observation; no result file has written it up yet. With entry 8 (p ≥ 2g−1, now checked by round4_q10), it gives 2g−1 ≤ p ≤ g, a contradiction. The new chain no longer needs the hyperbolic reduction, Matignon–Sayari, the satellite results or Moser.

**The wave:**
- q1, q2, q3, q8: identical closing task on (CB).
- q4: tries to refute (CB).
- q5: the covering-space identification on its own.
- q6: (CB) via Heegaard genus instead of group rank.
- q7: the Heegaard Floer step needed by an alternative chain B. That chain avoids citing "the two non-homology-sphere summands are lens spaces", which three round-4 files flagged as uncertain.

**Ledger:** entries 16–25 are added. Entry 12 is retracted as the missing statement, replaced by entry 23 (CB). The claim that formal semigroups of L-space knots contain twice their least positive element is refuted by P(−2,3,7).

9	
10	Let K ⊂ S^3 be a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g (so V_s >= 0, V_s - V_{s+1} ∈ {0,1}, V_s = 0 iff s >= g, V_{-s} = V_s + s), and let p be a nonzero integer (either sign) such that |p| divides 2g-1 and |p| < 2g-1. 12	## Intended proof (planner's suggestion; free to discard)

126	# Answer to round2_q3
127	
128	**Theorem.** Let K be a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g, and let p be a nonzero integer with p < 2g-1 (p may be negative). Then S^3_p(K) is not homeomorphic to L # Y', where L is an L-space with |H_1(L)| = |p| >= 3 and Y' is an integer homology sphere. In particular it is not of the form L1 # L2 # Y3 with L1, L2 lens spaces of coprime orders r, s >= 2 (here rs = |p| >= 6) and Y3 an integer homology sphere.
129	
130	Below, "[lit]" means a standard result that I cite from memory.
131	
132	## 0. Reduction to an algebraic statement
133	Let Y = S^3_p(K) ≅ L # Y'. Write CF^-(L,s) ≃ F[U] for each s (L is an L-space). By the Ozsvath–Szabo connected-sum formula [lit], CF^-(L#Y', s#t) ≃ CF^-(L,s) ⊗_{F[U]} CF^-(Y',t) ≃ CF^-(Y') up to a grading shift. Tensoring with F[U,U^{-1}]/U·F[U] gives the same for CF^+. Since H_1(Y') = 0, every one of the |p| spin^c structures on Y has
134	  HF^+(Y, i) ≅ HF^+(Y') as relatively Z-graded F[U]-modules (up to a degree shift). (*)
135	So it suffices to find two spin^c classes i, i' of S^3_p(K) whose HF^+ are **not** isomorphic up to a degree shift. I compare the classes i = 0 and i = 1. These are different classes because |p| >= 3.
136	
137	**Invariants used.** A finitely generated graded F[U]-module of the form T^+ ⊕ (finite part) is determined up to isomorphism by (a) the degree of the bottom of the tower and (b) the multiset of degrees of the tops of its cyclic summands. For (b), the number of summands whose top lies in degree k is dim (M/UM)_k. After a degree shift, two isomorphic modules have the same number of finite summands, and their multisets of top degrees agree up to a translation. In particular the multiplicity pattern of the multiset is the same for both.
138	
139	## 1. Cone model in "level" form (both signs)
140	I use the Ozsvath–Szabo integer surgery formula [lit]. For a positive L-space knot, A_s^+ ≅ B_s^+ ≅ T^+, with v_s = U^{V_s} and h_s = U^{H_s}, where H_s = V_{-s}. The V_s satisfy V_s >= 0, V_s - V_{s+1} ∈ {0,1}, V_s = 0 iff s >= g, and V_{-s} = V_s + s.
141	
142	Model each tower by levels k ∈ Z: the tower has F in each level k >= (its bottom), and U lowers the level by 1. If U^e maps A to B and the bottom of A is at level x, then preserving levels puts the bottom of B at level x + e. The real grading of a B-level is a uniform shift of the A-level (by the cone's degree-1 shift), and this shift is the same for all classes.
143	
144	The only exponents that appear below are V_s with s <= g-1 and H_s = V_{-s} with s >= -(g-1). All of these are >= 1. So every B-bottom (a "peak") lies strictly above the adjacent A-bottoms ("valleys").
145	
146	At level k the cone map is the coboundary δ of a graph G_k:
147	- vertices: the A's whose bottom is <= k;
148	- edges: the B's whose bottom is <= k;
149	- (Da)_B is the sum of the values at the A's adjacent to B. A B adjacent to only one retained A acts as an edge to a "ground" vertex, where the value is fixed to 0.
150	
151	## 2. The case p > 0
152	**Truncation.** Fix a class i and let s_1 < … < s_n be the elements s ≡ i (mod p) with |s| <= g-1.
153	
154	D: ⊕A → ⊕B is surjective. Indeed, every map is U^e on T^+, which is surjective, and one can solve inductively along the zigzag. So H_*(cone) ≅ ker D, up to a uniform shift.
155	
156	For a kernel element: for s >= g we have V_s = 0, which forces a_s = U^{H_{s-p}} a_{s-p}. For s - p <= -g we have H_{s-p} = 0, which forces a_{s-p} = U^{V_s} a_s. So every a_s outside [-(g-1), g-1] is determined by the a_{s_j}. Hence
157	  ker D ≅ { (a_1,…,a_n) : U^{H_{s_j}} a_j = U^{V_{s_{j+1}}} a_{j+1}, j = 1,…,n-1 }.
158	This is a path graph with valleys x_j (the bottom of A_{s_j}) and peaks y_{j+1} = x_j + H_{s_j} = x_{j+1} + V_{s_{j+1}}. If n = 0 the module is T^+.
159	
160	**Positions.** Solving x(s+p) - x(s) = V_{-s} - V_{s+p} = V_s + s - V_{s+p} gives
161	  x(s) = s(s-p)/(2p) - V_s,
162	and therefore the peak between s and s+p is at
163	  y = x(s) + V_{-s} = s(s+p)/(2p) = (m^2 - p^2/4)/(2p), where m = s + p/2.
164	The peak levels do not depend on K.
165	
166	**Module structure.** At level k, ker D is the space of functions on the vertices of G_k that are constant along its edges, i.e. functions on the connected components of G_k. U acts by restriction from G_k to G_{k-1}.
167	- For large k, G_k is connected, so the module has one tower, with bottom at min_j x_j.
168	- Restriction from level k+1 to level k fails to be surjective by exactly the number of edges (peaks) at level k+1. G_k is a subforest of a path, so each new edge joins two different components.
169	- Hence the finite summands have their tops at the levels {y - 1 : y a peak}. There are n-1 of them, counted with multiplicity.
170	
171	**Number of summands.** The number of finite summands is max(n_i - 1, 0), where n_i = #{s ≡ i mod p : |s| <= g-1}. The integers in [-(g-1), g-1] are 2g-1 consecutive integers. Since 0 < p < 2g-1, every n_i >= 1, and the n_i are all equal iff p | 2g-1. By (*) they must be equal. So p | 2g-1, p is odd, and n := (2g-1)/p >= 3.
172	
173	The class of t (|t| <= (p-1)/2) is then {t + kp : |k| <= (n-1)/2}, and its peaks are at m = t + (k + 1/2)p for k = -(n-1)/2, …, (n-3)/2.
174	- **Class 0:** m ∈ {±p/2, ±3p/2, …, ±(n-2)p/2}. Each peak level occurs with even multiplicity.
175	- **Class 1:** two of the m's would give equal m^2 only if m = -m', i.e. 2 + (k + k' + 1)p = 0, which is impossible for p >= 3. So all n-1 >= 2 top levels are distinct.
176	
177	A translation cannot turn a multiset with all multiplicities even into one with all multiplicities 1. This contradicts (*).
178	
179	## 3. The case p = -q < 0
180	**Truncation.** I use the Ozsvath–Szabo truncation of the cone [lit]: cancel A_s against B_s for s >= g (v_s is an isomorphism there), and A_s against B_{s-q} for s <= -g (h_s is an isomorphism there).
181	
182	In class i, let s_1 < … < s_n be the elements with |s| <= g-1. What remains is the zigzag
183	  B_{s_1-q} ← A_{s_1} → B_{s_1} ← A_{s_1+q} → … → B_{s_n}.
184	It has n A's (valleys) and n+1 B's (peaks); the two end B's are ground edges.
185	- If n = 0, exactly one B survives and the module is T^+.
186	- Every A carries even (A-)parity and every B odd parity, and U preserves parity. So H = ker D ⊕ coker D as F[U]-modules.
187	
188	**Positions.** Solving x(s+q) - x(s) = V_s - V_{-(s+q)} gives
189	  x(s) = -s(s+q)/(2q) - V_s,
190	and the bottom of B_t is at
191	  b(t) = -t(t+q)/(2q) = -(u^2 - q^2/4)/(2q), where u = t + q/2.
192	Again the peak levels do not depend on K.
193	
194	**Module structure.** G_k together with the ground vertex is a subgraph of a single cycle.
195	- **Coker.** coker δ_k = H^1(G_k ∪ ground, ground) = H^1(G_k ∪ ground), which is 0 until the cycle closes at level M = max peak and F from then on. So the B-parity part is a single tower with bottom at M.
196	- **Ker.** ker δ_k is the space of functions on the components of G_k that do not touch ground; it is entirely finite. Its tops lie at {y - 1 : y a peak}, with one copy of M - 1 removed: the edge that closes the cycle does not merge two components.
197	- **Number of summands.** dim ker U on the ker part is n_i: one summand is born at each valley. By (*) the n_i must be equal. That forces q | 2g-1, because if q > 2g-1 some classes have n_i = 0 and others n_i = 1. So n = (2g-1)/q is odd and q >= 3 is odd. The class of t has the B-midpoints u = t + (k + 1/2)q for k = -(n+1)/2, …, (n-1)/2.
198	
199	The invariant used here is the multiset of top levels of the finite summands, measured relative to the tower bottom. Both live in fixed parities, and these relative offsets are preserved by any graded isomorphism.
200	- **Class 0:** u ∈ {±q/2, …, ±nq/2}. The maximal peak (|u| = q/2) occurs twice, so its value survives once after removing one copy; every other value occurs twice.
201	- **Class 1:** all |u| are distinct (as in §2), so all values are distinct.
202	- **If n >= 3:** class 0 has a repeated top level and class 1 does not. Contradiction.
203	- **If n = 1:** both classes have a single finite summand. Its top lies 1 level below the tower bottom in class 0, but |b(1-q) - b(1)| + 1 = 2 levels below in class 1, since the two u's differ in u^2 by 2q. Contradiction.
204	
205	(For n = 1 the finite summand of class s is F[U]/U^{V_{|s|}}, and its top is |s| + 1 levels below the tower bottom. The sizes V_{|s|} alone might coincide across classes; the positions cannot.)
206	
207	This proves the Theorem in both cases. ∎

|p|·rank π1(B) + rank π1(Ã) <= 2g.

## 2. Statement and proof

**Theorem (CB).** Assume the following.
- K ⊂ S^3 is a fibred knot with fibre F, where F is compact, connected and orientable, of genus g >= 1, with ∂F = K.
- p ≠ 0 is an integer, and n := |p|.
- Y := S^3_p(K) ≅ A # B, where B is an integer homology sphere and B ≇ S^3.

Then n·rank π1(B) + rank π1(Ã) <= 2g. Here Ã is the n-fold cyclic cover of A induced by H_1(A) ≅ Z/n. In particular n <= g.

**Cited facts (from memory, all standard).**
- (G) Grushko–Neumann: rank(G1 * G2) = rank G1 + rank G2 for finitely generated groups.
- (P) Perelman (the Poincaré conjecture): a closed simply connected 3-manifold is S^3.
- (VK) Seifert–van Kampen: π1(M1 # M2) = π1(M1) * π1(M2), and H_1(M1 # M2) = H_1(M1) ⊕ H_1(M2).
- (F) Fibred knots: the exterior M_K = S^3 \ N(K) is the mapping torus of a monodromy h: F → F, which may be taken to be the identity near ∂F.
  - H_1(M_K) = Z, generated by the meridian μ. The isomorphism is given by intersection number with a fibre.
  - Every class carried by F maps to 0 in H_1(M_K), since a curve in F can be pushed off F.
  - The longitude λ = ∂F is null-homologous in M_K.

- Write Y = A° ∪_S B°, where S is the splitting sphere and A°, B° are the punctured summands.
- By (VK), H_1(A) ⊕ H_1(B) = Z/n and H_1(B) = 0, so H_1(A) ≅ Z/n.
- π1(B°) = π1(B) is perfect, so φ kills it. Hence q^{-1}(B°) is n disjoint copies of B°.
- φ restricted to π1(A°) = π1(A) is the abelianization of A, so it is onto. Hence q^{-1}(A°) is connected: it is the n-fold cyclic cover of A°, that is, Ã minus n balls (each removed ball lifts to n balls).
- S is simply connected, so it lifts to n spheres. Each of these spheres joins the single A-piece to one B-copy.
- The gluing graph is therefore a tree (a star), so Y_n ≅ Ã # (#_n B).
- By (VK) and (G): rank π1(Y_n) = rank π1(Ã) + n·rank π1(B).
- π1(B) is nontrivial by (P), since B ≠ S^3. It is perfect, so it is not cyclic: a cyclic perfect group is trivial. Hence rank π1(B) >= 2.
- (Perelman-free alternative: Heegaard genus is additive under connected sum (Haken). Closed 3-manifolds of genus <= 1 are S^3, S^1×S^2 and lens spaces. Applying this to B and Y_n gives the Heegaard-genus version of the same inequality.)

- Orientations and the sign ε of Lemma B are never used.

- step 1: Gabai; Gordon–Luecke, "only integral surgeries can yield reducible manifolds";
- step 2: the shape theorem, from the literature on reducible surgeries;
- step 3: the run's Heegaard Floer theorem.

Step 3 forces p >= 2g-1 (negative p is excluded because p < 2g-1). (CB) gives p <= g. Together these give g = 1 and p <= 1, which contradicts p = rs >= 6.

# Answer to round5_q1: the statement (CB)

## 1. Verdict

**(CB) is PROVED.** The sharper form is proved too:

  |p|·rank π1(B) + rank π1(Ã) ≤ 2g,

and since rank π1(B) ≥ 2, this gives |p| ≤ g.

The planner's sketch is correct. I checked every step and found no gap, but several steps needed justification that the sketch leaves out. The proof below supplies it. The proof works for either sign of p and uses only fibredness, not the L-space hypothesis.

## 2. Cited theorems (all cited from memory)

- **(Grushko–Neumann.)** If G1 and G2 are finitely generated groups, then rank(G1 * G2) = rank G1 + rank G2. Only "≥" is needed; that is Grushko's theorem. Rank means the minimal number of generators.
- **(Perelman.)** A closed simply connected 3-manifold is homeomorphic to S^3.
  - Perelman-free alternative: rank can be replaced by Heegaard genus throughout. Heegaard genus is additive under connected sum (Haken's lemma). Closed manifolds of Heegaard genus ≤ 1 are S^3, lens spaces and S^1×S^2, so an integer homology sphere B ≠ S^3 has genus ≥ 2. An open book with page F gives a Heegaard splitting of genus 2g.
- **Van Kampen's theorem**, and the standard facts about covering spaces and fibre bundles over S^1.

## 3. Proof of (CB)

**Setting.**
- Y = S^3_p(K) = M_K ∪ V. Here M_K = S^3 \ N(K) and V is a solid torus whose meridian is glued to the curve α = pμ + λ on T = ∂M_K. The sign or orientation of α plays no role.
- K is fibred: there is a fibration f: M_K → S^1 with fibre F (connected, genus g, one boundary component) and monodromy h.
- Assume Y ≅ A # B with H_1(B) = 0 and B ≢ S^3. Then H_1(A) ≅ H_1(Y) ≅ Z/|p|.
- If |p| = 1, then |p| ≤ g holds trivially. The argument below also works in that case (Y_p = Y).

**Step 0 (the cover).** Let φ: π1(Y) → H_1(Y) = Z/|p| be abelianization, and let Y_p → Y be the connected |p|-fold covering with group ker φ.

**Step 1 (lower bound: Y_p ≅ Ã # (#_{|p|} B)).**
1. Write Y = A° ∪_S B°, where S is a 2-sphere and A°, B° are the summands with an open ball removed.
2. By van Kampen, π1(Y) = π1(A°) * π1(B°).
3. φ restricted to π1(B°) factors through H_1(B°) = H_1(B) = 0, so it is trivial. Since φ is onto and kills π1(B°), its restriction to π1(A°) is onto.
4. Covering theory then gives:
   - The preimage of B° is |p| disjoint copies of B°, each mapped homeomorphically.
   - The preimage of A° is connected. It is the cover of A° with group ker(π1(A°) → Z/|p|). That is Ã minus |p| balls, where Ã → A is the |p|-fold cyclic cover induced by π1(A) = π1(A°) → H_1(A) ≅ Z/|p|, and the removed ball of A lifts to |p| balls.
   - S lifts to |p| spheres, each separating one copy of B° from the connected piece.
5. The gluing graph is a star, hence a tree. So Y_p ≅ Ã # B # ... # B (|p| copies of B), and π1(Y_p) ≅ π1(Ã) * π1(B)^{*|p|}.
6. By Grushko–Neumann, rank π1(Y_p) = rank π1(Ã) + |p|·rank π1(B).
7. B is not S^3, so by Perelman π1(B) ≠ 1. Also π1(B) is perfect, because H_1(B) = 0. A nontrivial cyclic group is not perfect. Hence π1(B) is not cyclic, and rank π1(B) ≥ 2.
8. Therefore rank π1(Y_p) ≥ 2|p|.

**Step 2 (upper bound: rank π1(Y_p) ≤ 2g).**
1. *φ on M_K.* H_1(M_K) = Z⟨μ⟩, and λ = 0 there. Also H_1(Y) = H_1(M_K)/⟨pμ+λ⟩ = Z/|p| with μ ↦ 1. So φ restricted to π1(M_K) is the composite π1(M_K) → Z → Z/|p|.

4. *M̃ is fibred.* f̃: M̃ → S^1 is a fibre bundle with fibre F, because the fibre over z is f^{-1}(q(z)). (It is the mapping torus of h^{|p|}.)

6. *The boundary torus.* φ(μ) = 1 generates Z/|p|, so π1(T) → Z/|p| is onto, and T has a single preimage torus T̃ = ∂M̃.
7. *The solid torus.* The meridian α of V meets μ once, so μ is a longitude of V. Hence the core of V is homologous to ±μ in Y and maps onto Z/|p|. So V has a single preimage Ṽ, which is a solid torus (the connected |p|-fold cover of V).
8. *The meridian disc.* The meridian disc D of V is simply connected, so it lifts. A lift D̃ is a properly embedded disc in Ṽ whose boundary α̃ is a closed lift of α. Since π1(T̃) → π1(T) is injective and α is essential, α̃ is essential in T̃. So D̃ is a meridian disc of Ṽ.

**Step 3 (combine).** Steps 1 and 2 give

  2|p| ≤ |p|·rank π1(B) + rank π1(Ã) = rank π1(Y_p) ≤ 2g,

so |p| ≤ g, along with the sharper form. ∎

**Points checked.**
- The cover of B° is trivial because H_1(B) = 0 (Step 1, item 3).
- The lifted slope satisfies f̃_*(α̃) = ±1 (Step 2, item 10). No intersection-number bookkeeping is needed.
- Neither the sign of p nor any orientation convention enters, since only |p| and ±1 appear.
- The case p < 0 is covered by the same argument.

**Sanity checks.**
- T(2,3) with p = ±1: the bound |p| ≤ g = 1 holds and is attained.
- T(r,s) with p = rs: here the summand B is absent (the result is L(r,s) # L(s,r), with no homology-sphere summand), so (CB) does not apply. This is consistent: rs > g.

## 4. Does the chain (steps 1–5) answer the problem?

Yes, conditionally. Given (CB) and the inputs it relies on, the chain gives "no: at most two prime summands" for surgeries on L-space knots. The logic is sound:
- step 3 forces p ≥ 2g − 1 (for either sign of p, since every negative p is < 2g − 1);

4. The restriction of φ to π1(B°) factors through H_1(B) = 0, so it is trivial.
5. Each component of q^{-1}(B°) is a connected cover of B° corresponding to a subgroup containing the whole of π1(B°). So each component maps homeomorphically onto B°.
6. Hence q^{-1}(B°) consists of n disjoint copies of B°.

**Lifting A°.**
7. The restriction of φ to π1(A°) is the abelianization of π1(A) followed by the isomorphism H_1(A) → H_1(Y). So it is onto Z/n.
8. Hence q^{-1}(A°) is connected. It is the n-fold cyclic cover of A° induced by H_1(A) ≅ Z/n.

9. S is simply connected, so it lifts to n disjoint spheres, and the removed ball of A lifts to n balls.
10. So q^{-1}(A°) is Ã minus n open balls.
11. The gluing pattern is a star: one copy of Ã° is joined by one sphere to each of the n copies of B°. The star is a tree, so no S^1×S^2 summands appear.

2. B is not homeomorphic to S^3, so π1(B) ≠ 1 by Perelman.
3. π1(B) is perfect, since its abelianization H_1(B) is 0.
4. A cyclic group is abelian, and a perfect abelian group is trivial. So π1(B) is not cyclic, and rank π1(B) >= 2.
5. Hence rank π1(Y_n) >= 2n.

# Answer to round5_q5

## 1. Verdicts

- **(C1): PROVED.** The proof is in Section 2. One clarification: I do not identify the monodromy beyond saying it is h^{|p|} composed with some power of the boundary twist. Nothing downstream uses more than that.
- **(C2): PROVED.** The proof is in Section 3.
- **(CB): PROVED** for every nonzero p and every integer homology sphere B ≠ S^3, prime or not. The proof is in Section 4. It also gives the sharper form |p|·rank π1(B) + rank π1(Ã) ≤ 2g.
- **Surrounding derivation:** I found no logical flaw, conditional on the cited inputs. Section 5 lists them; the "shape theorem" is the one to double-check.

Notation: K ⊂ S^3 is fibred, M_K = S^3 \ int N(K) is its exterior, F is the fibre (genus g ≥ 1, ∂F connected), h is the monodromy with h = id on a collar of ∂F, μ is the meridian, λ = ∂F is the longitude, and n = |p| ≥ 1. On ∂M_K we have α = pμ + λ, Y = M_K ∪_α V, and q: Y_n → Y is the covering for the kernel of φ: π1(Y) → H_1(Y) ≅ Z/n.

## 2. Proof of (C1)

**(a) H_1(Y).** H_1(Y) = H_1(M_K)/⟨α⟩ = Z⟨μ⟩/⟨pμ⟩ = Z/n, since λ = 0 in H_1(M_K). So φ restricted to M_K is π1(M_K) → H_1(M_K) = Z → Z/n, sending μ to 1. The covering Y_n is connected because φ is onto.

**(b) Preimage of M_K.** The fibration M_K → S^1 induces π1(M_K) → Z. Its value on μ is ±1, because μ meets F once. Since H_1(M_K) = Z⟨μ⟩, this map is the abelianization up to sign.

So π1(M_K) → Z/n is onto, and q^{-1}(M_K) is connected. It is the cover for the kernel of π1(M_K) → Z → Z/n, which is the pull-back of the n-fold cover S^1 → S^1. That pull-back is the mapping torus M(h^n) = F × [0,n] / (x,n) ~ (h^n(x),0). Its fibres are lifts of F, and each restricts homeomorphically onto F.

**(c) Preimage of ∂M_K = T.** π1(T) → Z/n is onto (μ ↦ 1), so there is a single lift T̃, an n-fold cover of T. The image of H_1(T̃) in H_1(T) is {aμ + bλ : n | a}. A basis is μ̃ = nμ (the closed lift of the n-th power of μ) and λ̃ = λ, a lift of ∂F. The lift λ̃ is closed because λ ↦ 0 in Z/n. T̃ = ∂M(h^n), and the boundaries of the lifted fibres are parallel copies of λ̃ foliating T̃.

**(d) Preimage of the filling torus V.** On ∂V, the curve μ satisfies α·μ = λ·μ = ±1. So the core of V is homologous in V to μ, and π1(V) → Z/n is onto. Hence q^{-1}(V) = Ṽ is a single solid torus, the connected n-fold cover of V.

A meridian disc D of V lifts to n disjoint discs, since D is simply connected. Each lift is a meridian disc of Ṽ, and its boundary is a closed lift of α. In H_1(T̃), with the identification of (c), this class is α = pμ + λ = sgn(p)·μ̃ + λ̃. Therefore the meridian m̃ of Ṽ satisfies m̃·λ̃ = ±1, for both signs of p.

**(e) The circle direction does not matter.** The circle direction of the mapping torus at ∂F is the curve t = {x} × S^1 for x ∈ ∂F, which is closed because h = id near ∂F. A priori t = μ + kλ for some k. The argument does not use k: only m̃·λ̃ = ±1 is needed. (Its lift is t̃ = nμ + nkλ, and m̃ = t̃ + (unit)·λ̃ up to the conventions, but this is not used.)

**(f) The open book.** Since m̃·λ̃ = ±1, λ̃ is a longitude of Ṽ. Choose a homeomorphism Ṽ ≅ S^1 × D^2 such that:
- S^1 × {1} goes to λ̃;
- {1} × ∂D^2 goes to m̃;
- the foliation of T̃ by the boundaries ∂F̃_θ of the lifted fibres, parametrised by θ ∈ S^1, goes to the foliation by the circles S^1 × {e^{iθ}}.

This is possible because both are foliations of the torus by parallel circles of the same longitude class, with a transverse circle meeting each leaf once. The transverse circle may be taken to be m̃, since m̃·λ̃ = ±1.

Then each page F̃_θ extends by the annulus S^1 × {r e^{iθ} : 0 ≤ r ≤ 1}. This gives an open book on Y_n with page F (via the lift F̃_θ ≅ F) and connected binding S^1 × {0}. Its monodromy is h^n composed with a power of the boundary Dehn twist, which is not needed below. This proves the first part of (C1).

**(g) Heegaard splitting and rank.** Write the pages as F_θ, θ ∈ [0,1]. Let H_1 be the union of the pages with θ ∈ [0,1/2], and H_2 the union of those with θ ∈ [1/2,1]; both contain the binding.

Each H_i is homeomorphic to F × [0,1] with the vertical segments over ∂F collapsed. That is homeomorphic to F × I, a handlebody of genus 2g, because F is a surface with nonempty boundary and π1(F) is free of rank 2g. Then H_1 ∩ H_2 = ∂H_1 = ∂H_2 = F_0 ∪ F_{1/2}, a closed surface of genus 2g. So Y_n has a Heegaard splitting of genus 2g.

By van Kampen, π1(Y_n) is a quotient of π1(H_1), which is free of rank 2g. So rank π1(Y_n) ≤ 2g. ∎

## 3. Proof of (C2)

Let S ⊂ Y be the reducing sphere, so that Y = A° ∪_S B°, where A° and B° are the summands minus open balls.

**B° lifts trivially.** The composite π1(B°) → π1(Y) → Z/n factors through H_1(B°) = H_1(B) = 0. So the covering restricted to the connected, locally path-connected set B° is trivial: q^{-1}(B°) is n disjoint copies of B°.

**The preimage of A° is connected.** By Mayer–Vietoris, H_1(Y) = H_1(A°) ⊕ H_1(B°) = H_1(A). So π1(A°) → Z/n is onto, and q^{-1}(A°) is connected. It is the cover of A° induced by π1(A°) = π1(A) → H_1(A) ≅ Z/n. This cover extends over the removed ball, which lifts to n balls, and the extension is Ã. Hence q^{-1}(A°) = Ã minus n open balls.

**Gluing.** S is simply connected, so it lifts to n spheres. Each sphere bounds exactly one copy of B° on one side and the connected piece Ã° on the other. The gluing graph has n + 1 vertices and n edges and is connected, so it is a tree. Gluing punctured manifolds along spheres according to a tree gives the connected sum of the capped-off pieces. Orientations are pulled back by q, and the covering is a local orientation-preserving homeomorphism. Hence Y_n ≅ Ã # B # ... # B, with n copies of B. ∎

## 4. Proof of (CB)

Cited theorems (from memory):
- **Grushko–Neumann:** rank(G_1 * G_2) = rank G_1 + rank G_2.
- **Perelman (Poincaré conjecture):** a closed simply connected 3-manifold is S^3.

Suppose B is an integer homology sphere with B ≠ S^3. By Perelman, π1(B) ≠ 1. Since H_1(B) = 0, π1(B) is perfect. A nontrivial cyclic group is abelian and therefore not perfect, so π1(B) is not cyclic and rank π1(B) ≥ 2.

By van Kampen, the connected sum in (C2) gives π1(Y_n) = π1(Ã) * π1(B)^{*n}. By Grushko–Neumann and (C1):

rank π1(Ã) + n·rank π1(B) = rank π1(Y_n) ≤ 2g.

Hence 2n ≤ 2g, that is, |p| ≤ g. ∎

This covers both signs of p, and B need not be prime.

**Alternative via Heegaard genus.** The same bound follows from Haken additivity of Heegaard genus and the fact that the Heegaard genus of B is at least 2. Genus-0 and genus-1 Heegaard splittings give only S^3, lens spaces and S^1 × S^2.

**Sanity check.** Take the (n,1)-cable K = C_{n,1}(J) of a fibred knot J of genus g(J) ≥ 1. Then K is fibred of genus n·g(J), and its slope-n surgery is L(n,1) # S^3_{1/n}(J). Here Ã = S^3, and the inequality reads 2n ≤ n·rank π1(B) ≤ 2n·g(J), which is consistent. So |p| ≤ g is attained when g(J) = 1.

## 5. The surrounding derivation

The answer to the surrounding problem is **yes**: a surgery on an L-space knot in S^3 has at most two prime summands. This is conditional on the cited inputs below, which I state from memory and did not check here.

**Step 1: reduction to integral slopes.**
- K is nontrivial. Surgery on the unknot gives a lens space, S^1 × S^2 or S^3, each of which is prime.
- Slope 0 (Gabai): S^3_0(K) is irreducible for nontrivial K, and is not S^1 × S^2.
- Non-integral slopes (Gordon–Luecke): non-integral surgeries on nontrivial knots are irreducible.
- Mirroring: replacing K by its mirror, we may assume K is a positive L-space knot; p may then have either sign.

**Step 2: shape theorem (cited, unverified here).** With three or more prime summands, Y = L_1 # L_2 # Y_3, where L_1 and L_2 are lens spaces of coprime orders r, s ≥ 2 with rs = |p|, and Y_3 is an integer homology sphere not equal to S^3. I attribute this to Howie ("Can Dehn surgery yield three connected summands?", which uses the Scott–Wiegold conjecture) and related work of Sayari / Valdez-Sánchez, but I am not certain of the exact attribution and statement. This is the input to verify.

**Step 3: Heegaard Floer input.** L_1 # L_2 is an L-space of order rs ≥ 6 ≥ 3. By the stated Heegaard Floer theorem, p ≥ 2g − 1, which also forces p > 0.

**Step 4: fibredness.** L-space knots are fibred (Ni; Ghiggini for genus 1).

**Step 5: apply (CB).** (CB) with A = L_1 # L_2 and B = Y_3 gives p ≤ g. Together with p ≥ 2g − 1 this gives g ≤ 1 and p ≤ 1, which contradicts p = rs ≥ 6.

So the chain is valid. A remark: Step 5 could also use the sharper bound from Lemma A, namely rank π1(Y_p) ≥ 2p + (r−1)(s−1), but it is not needed.

**Remaining open or unverified items:**
- the exact statement and attribution of the shape theorem;
- the Heegaard Floer theorem "p < 2g − 1 excludes L # Y′", which was proved earlier in this run and not re-checked here.

# round5_q3 — answer

## 1. Verdict

**(CB) is PROVED**, in its sharper form, for every fibred K of genus g >= 1 (with one-component fibre boundary) and every nonzero integer p, of either sign:

  |p|·rank π1(B) + rank π1(Ã) <= 2g,  and hence |p| <= g.

The planner's sketch is correct. Below I check every step and write it out in full. The upper bound uses only a group-theoretic argument; no open-book identification and no sign convention is needed.

Throughout, N := |p| >= 1.

## 2. Cited results (from memory)

- **(Grushko–Neumann)** If G1 and G2 are finitely generated groups, then rank(G1 * G2) = rank G1 + rank G2.
- **(Seifert–van Kampen for connected sums)** π1(M1 # M2) ≅ π1(M1) * π1(M2). This holds because the splitting sphere is simply connected.
- **(Poincaré conjecture, Perelman)** A closed simply connected 3-manifold is homeomorphic to S^3.
  - This can be avoided. Use Heegaard genus instead, with Haken's lemma (Heegaard genus is additive under connected sum) and the classification of manifolds of genus <= 1. See Remark 3.6.
- **(Fibration structure)** If M fibres over S^1 with connected fibre F and monodromy ψ, then π1(M) ≅ π1(F) ⋊ Z. The map π1(M) → Z is induced by the fibration, equivalently by algebraic intersection with a fibre, and its kernel is the image of π1(F).

## 3. Proof of (CB)

**Setting.**
- Y = S^3_p(K) = M_K ∪ V, where M_K is the knot exterior, T = ∂M_K = ∂V, and the meridian disc of V is bounded by α = pμ + λ.
- M_K fibres over S^1 with fibre F (genus g, ∂F = λ) and monodromy h.
- H_1(M_K) = Z⟨μ⟩. The class of a loop is its algebraic intersection with F. Every loop in F can be pushed off F, so π1(F) → H_1(M_K) is zero.
- H_1(Y) = Z⟨μ⟩/(pμ + λ) = Z/N, because λ = 0 in H_1(M_K).
- Let φ: π1(Y) → H_1(Y) = Z/N be abelianization. This is onto. Let q: Y_N → Y be the connected N-fold cyclic cover with group ker φ.

### 3.1 Lower bound: Y_N ≅ Ã # (N copies of B)

1. Fix a homeomorphism Y ≅ A # B. Let S be the splitting sphere, so Y = A° ∪_S B°, where A° and B° are A and B with one open ball removed.
2. π1(Y) = π1(A) * π1(B) and H_1(Y) = H_1(A) ⊕ H_1(B) = H_1(A). So H_1(A) ≅ Z/N.
3. φ restricted to π1(B°) = π1(B) factors through H_1(B) = 0, so it is trivial. Hence q^{-1}(B°) is N disjoint copies of B°, each mapped homeomorphically onto B°.
4. S is simply connected, so q^{-1}(S) is N disjoint spheres.
5. φ restricted to π1(A°) = π1(A) is the surjection π1(A) → H_1(A) ≅ Z/N. Hence q^{-1}(A°) is connected. It is the N-fold cover of A° induced by this map, which is Ã minus N open balls: the removed ball lifts to N balls.
6. So Y_N is Ã minus N balls, with one copy of B° glued to each boundary sphere. The gluing graph is a star, so it is a tree. Hence Y_N ≅ Ã # B # … # B, with N copies of B.
7. By van Kampen and Grushko–Neumann (all groups here are finitely generated, since they are π1 of closed manifolds):
   rank π1(Y_N) = rank π1(Ã) + N·rank π1(B).
8. B is a homology sphere and B ≠ S^3, so π1(B) ≠ 1 by Perelman, and π1(B) is perfect. A nontrivial cyclic group has nontrivial abelianization, so π1(B) is not cyclic. Hence rank π1(B) >= 2.

(If N = 1 the cover is trivial, Ã = A, and the argument still holds; A may be S^3.)

### 3.2 Upper bound: rank π1(Y_N) <= 2g

1. **The exterior lifts to a mapping torus.** φ on π1(M_K) is the composite π1(M_K) → H_1(M_K) = Z → Z/N, where μ ↦ 1. Its kernel is the preimage of NZ. So E := q^{-1}(M_K) is connected and is the N-fold cyclic cover of M_K dual to F, namely the mapping torus of h^N. E fibres over S^1 with fibre F̃, a homeomorphic lift of F. So π1(E) = π1(F̃) ⋊ ⟨t⟩, with t ↦ 1 under the fibration map π: π1(E) → Z.
2. **The boundary lifts to one torus.** φ(μ) generates Z/N and μ lies in π1(T), so π1(T) → Z/N is onto. Hence T̃ := q^{-1}(T) is a single torus, and q|: T̃ → T has degree N.
3. **The solid torus lifts to one solid torus.** μ meets α once on T, so μ is isotopic in V to the core of V. Hence φ maps π1(V) onto Z/N, and Ṽ := q^{-1}(V) is a single solid torus with ∂Ṽ = T̃.
4. **The filling curve.** The meridian disc D of V is simply connected, so it lifts to N discs. Let β ⊂ T̃ be the boundary of one of them. Then q maps β with degree 1 onto α, and Y_N = E ∪_{T̃} Ṽ is the Dehn filling of E along β.
5. **Intersection numbers multiply by the degree.** For a degree-N covering f: T̃ → T of tori, f_*a · f_*b = N(a·b). Two facts follow:
   - Each component of F̃ ∩ T̃ is a lift of λ; call one of them λ̃. Then q_*λ̃ = λ.
   - Since q_*β = α, we get N(β·λ̃) = α·λ = (pμ + λ)·λ = ±p. Hence β·λ̃ = ±1.
6. **β is a once-around loop.** π restricted to π1(T̃) is algebraic intersection with F̃ ∩ T̃, a union of parallel copies of λ̃, one per fibre. So π(β) = ±(β·λ̃) = ±1. Hence, for any basepoint path, β represents an element t^{±1}w in π1(E) with w ∈ π1(F̃).
7. **Conclusion.** By van Kampen, π1(Y_N) = π1(E)/⟨⟨β⟩⟩. In this quotient t = w^{∓1}, which lies in the image of π1(F̃). Hence π1(Y_N) is generated by the image of π1(F̃), a free group of rank 2g. So rank π1(Y_N) <= 2g.

### 3.3 Conclusion

Combining 3.1 and 3.2:

  N·rank π1(B) + rank π1(Ã) = rank π1(Y_N) <= 2g.

Since rank π1(B) >= 2, this gives 2N <= 2g, that is, |p| <= g. ∎

### 3.4 Points checked, as the task requested

- **The lifted filling slope.** It is β with β·λ̃ = ±1, for either sign of p. The identification β = ±μ̃ + λ̃ is not needed; only β·λ̃ = ±1 is used.
- **B° lifts trivially.** This uses only H_1(B) = 0.
- **The case p < 0.** It is covered, since only N = |p| and α·λ = ±p enter. Orientation conventions enter only through signs, which are irrelevant to the argument.
- **The cases p = ±1** are trivial consequences: the bound reads 1 <= g.

### 3.5 Sanity checks

- **T(2,3), p = 1.** Y is the Poincaré sphere and the bound is tight: 2 = 2.
- **T(r,s), p = rs.** Y_N = #(r-1)(s-1) S^1×S^2, which has rank 2g.

### 3.6 Remark: a Perelman-free variant

Use Heegaard genus h(·) in place of rank.
- Upper bound: h(Y_N) <= 2g. By 3.2 (with β·λ̃ = ±1), Y_N is the closed manifold of an open book with page F̃, and the two halves F̃ × [0,1/2] and F̃ × [1/2,1] are genus-2g handlebodies.
- Additivity: h(Y_N) = h(Ã) + N·h(B), by Haken's lemma.
- Lower bound: h(B) >= 2, since closed manifolds of genus <= 1 are S^3, lens spaces and S^1×S^2.

The rank argument above already suffices; this variant only removes the dependence on Perelman.

## 4. Does the chain (steps 1–5) then answer "at most two prime summands"?

**Arithmetic of steps 3–5.**
- Suppose Y = S^3_p(K) = L1 # L2 # Y3 for a positive nontrivial L-space knot K of genus g, as in step 2.
- Then A = L1 # L2 is an L-space with |H_1| = |p| = rs >= 6, and B = Y3 is a homology sphere other than S^3.
- (CB) gives |p| <= g.
- If p < 2g-1, step 3 gives a contradiction. This includes every p < 0.
- Otherwise 2g-1 <= p <= g, so g <= 1 and p <= 1, contradicting p >= 6.

So, granted steps 1–3, the answer is **yes: at most two prime summands**. Step 4 is valid: L-space knots are fibred (Ni; Ghiggini), and (CB) uses only fibredness.

# Answer to round5_q8: the statement (CB)

## Verdict

**(CB) is PROVED**, in the sharper form

  |p|·rank π1(B) + rank π1(Ã) ≤ 2g,  and hence |p| ≤ g.

It is proved for every nonzero integer p of either sign, every fibred knot with fibre of genus g ≥ 1, and every decomposition A # B with B an integer homology sphere other than S^3. A itself may be reducible, and A may be S^3.

The planner's sketch is correct. Below I write it out in full and check each delicate point: the lifted slope, the trivial cover of B°, the sign of p, and the boundary behaviour of the monodromy. Orientations play no role, because only ranks of groups appear.

## Cited theorems (stated from memory)

- **(G) Grushko–Neumann theorem.** For finitely generated groups G and H, rank(G * H) = rank G + rank H. Here rank means the minimal number of generators.
- **(P) Perelman's theorem (Poincaré conjecture).** A closed simply connected 3-manifold is homeomorphic to S^3.
- **(SvK) Seifert–van Kampen theorem.** We use two consequences.
  - π1(M1 # M2) ≅ π1(M1) * π1(M2).
  - If a solid torus V is glued to a 3-manifold M along a torus boundary component T, then π1(M ∪ V) ≅ π1(M)/⟨⟨m⟩⟩, where m is the meridian of V viewed as an element of π1(T) ⊂ π1(M) (after choosing a path to the basepoint).
- **(F) Mapping-torus structure of fibred knot exteriors.** If K is fibred with fibre F, then the exterior M_K ≅ F × [0,1]/((x,1) ~ (h(x),0)) for a homeomorphism h of F. One may take h to be the identity on ∂F: h|∂F is an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of a circle, so it is isotopic to the identity, and the isotopy can be absorbed in a collar. The fibre boundary ∂F is a longitude λ. The meridian μ meets each fibre exactly once, so the fibration map π1(M_K) → Z is the abelianization, with μ ↦ ±1.

A Perelman-free alternative to (P) is given in Remark 2 at the end of the proof.

## Proof

**Notation.** Let Y = S^3_p(K) = M_K ∪ V, where V is a solid torus with meridian m = pμ + λ. Set n = |p| ≥ 1.

### Step 0: homology

H_1(Y) = Z⟨μ⟩/(p) ≅ Z/n.

Because Y ≅ A # B, we have H_1(Y) ≅ H_1(A) ⊕ H_1(B) = H_1(A), so H_1(A) ≅ Z/n.

Let φ: π1(Y) → Z/n be abelianization. Let Y_n → Y be the connected n-fold cyclic cover with group ker φ.

### Step 1: lower bound, Y_n ≅ Ã # (#_n B)

1. Choose a separating sphere S ⊂ Y with Y = A° ∪_S B°, where A° is A minus an open ball and B° is B minus an open ball. Then π1(Y) = π1(A°) * π1(B°), with π1(A°) = π1(A) and π1(B°) = π1(B).
2. **The cover of B° is trivial.** φ restricted to π1(B°) factors through H_1(B) = 0, so φ is trivial there. Hence the preimage of B° is n disjoint copies of B°, each mapped homeomorphically.
3. **The cover of A° is connected.** φ restricted to π1(A°) is onto, because π1(Y) → H_1(Y) is onto and π1(B°) maps to 0. So the preimage of A° is connected: it is the connected n-fold cyclic cover of A° with group ker(φ|π1(A)).
4. That cover extends over the removed ball, because a ball is simply connected and its boundary sphere lifts to n spheres. So the preimage of A° is Ã minus n balls, where Ã is the n-fold cyclic cover of A induced by H_1(A) ≅ Z/n.
5. **The gluing.** S lifts to n spheres. Each sphere joins the single A-piece to one B-piece. The gluing graph is therefore a star, which is a tree. Hence
   Y_n ≅ Ã # B # ⋯ # B (n copies of B).
6. By (SvK) and (G),
   rank π1(Y_n) = rank π1(Ã) + n·rank π1(B).
7. **rank π1(B) ≥ 2.** π1(B) is perfect, since H_1(B) = 0. It is nontrivial by (P), since B ≠ S^3. A cyclic perfect group is trivial, so π1(B) is not cyclic.
8. Therefore rank π1(Y_n) ≥ 2n + rank π1(Ã) ≥ 2n.

### Step 2: upper bound, rank π1(Y_n) ≤ 2g

1. **The cover of M_K.** φ restricted to π1(M_K) factors as π1(M_K) → H_1(M_K) = Z → Z/n, with μ ↦ 1. By (F), the first map is the fibration map, up to sign.
   - So the preimage of M_K in Y_n is connected.
   - It is the cover with group equal to the preimage of nZ, which is the mapping torus N = F × [0,1]/((x,1) ~ (h^n(x),0)).
   - We have h^n|∂F = id.
2. **π1(N).** Fix x0 ∈ ∂F. Let t be the loop {x0} × [0,1], which is closed because h^n(x0) = x0. Then
   π1(N, x0) = π1(F, x0) ⋊ ⟨t⟩,
   and every element has the form w·t^k with w ∈ π1(F, x0).
3. **The boundary torus.** ∂N = T̃ = ∂F × S^1 is a single torus. This is consistent with the fact that ∂M_K has a single lift, since φ(μ) generates Z/n.
   - π1(T̃, x0) ≅ Z^2, with basis t and ℓ = [∂F]; note ℓ ∈ π1(F).
   - The covering T̃ → ∂M_K has degree n, so it induces an injection H_1(T̃) → H_1(∂M_K).
   - Its image is ker(φ|) = {aμ + bλ : n | a}, using φ(μ) = 1 and φ(λ) = 0 (λ is null-homologous in M_K).
   - The image of t is n(μ + kλ) for some integer k: the loop t projects to n times the circle {x0} × S^1 of ∂M_K, which meets λ once and so has class μ + kλ. The image of ℓ is λ.
4. **The cover of V.** The core of V is isotopic in V to μ, because μ·m = μ·λ = ±1 on ∂V. So the core maps onto Z/n under φ.
   - Hence the preimage of V is a single solid torus Ṽ, the n-fold cover of V.
   - A meridian disc of V lifts homeomorphically, because it is simply connected. So the meridian m̃ of Ṽ is a closed curve on T̃ that projects homeomorphically onto m.
5. **The lifted slope.** m̃ maps to pμ + λ in H_1(∂M_K). By the injectivity in point 3, m̃ is the unique class mapping there, namely
   m̃ = sgn(p)·[t] + (1 − pk)·ℓ,
   since sgn(p)·n(μ + kλ) + (1 − pk)λ = pμ + λ. The coefficient of [t] is ±1, for either sign of p.
6. **The quotient.** By (SvK),
   π1(Y_n) = π1(N)/⟨⟨t^{ε} ℓ^{j}⟩⟩, with ε = ±1 and j = 1 − pk.
   In the quotient t = ℓ^{−εj}, which lies in the image of π1(F). Every element w·t^k therefore lies in the image of π1(F, x0), a free group of rank 2g. So rank π1(Y_n) ≤ 2g.

### Step 3: conclusion

From Steps 1 and 2,

  n·rank π1(B) + rank π1(Ã) = rank π1(Y_n) ≤ 2g.

Since rank π1(B) ≥ 2, this gives 2n ≤ 2g, so |p| ≤ g. ∎

**Remark 1 (sharpness).**
- For K = T(2,3) and p = 1, Y is the Poincaré sphere = S^3 # P. Then 1·2 + 0 = 2 = 2g, so the bound is attained.
- In general Y_n is the closed manifold of the open book (F, h^n τ_∂^{±1}). This is consistent with the planner's checks.

**Remark 2 (avoiding Perelman).** Replace rank by Heegaard genus throughout.
- Heegaard genus is additive under connected sum, by Haken's lemma.
- A closed 3-manifold of Heegaard genus ≤ 1 is S^3, a lens space or S^1×S^2 (Waldhausen; the classical genus-one classification). None of these is an integer homology sphere other than S^3, so g(B) ≥ 2.
- An open book whose page has genus g and one boundary component gives a Heegaard splitting of genus 2g: the two halves are F × [0,1/2] and F × [1/2,1], which are handlebodies of genus 2g. So g(Y_n) ≤ 2g.
- The same inequality follows: 2n ≤ g(Ã) + n·g(B) = g(Y_n) ≤ 2g.

## Does the chain (steps 1–5) answer the problem?

**What holds.**
- Given step 2 (the shape theorem) and step 3 (the Heegaard Floer result proved earlier in the run, which I have not re-verified here), the chain does give "at most two prime summands". After mirroring, K is a positive L-space knot, and Y = L1 # L2 # Y3 with |p| = rs ≥ 6. Step 3 forces p ≥ 2g − 1. (CB), applied with A = L1 # L2 and B = Y3, gives p ≤ g. Hence g ≤ 1, so p ≤ 1, contradicting p ≥ 6.
- Steps 1 and 4 are standard and correctly cited: Gabai, Gordon–Luecke, Ni, Ghiggini.
- If p ≥ 2g − 1, the shape theorem is not needed at all. In that case Y is an L-space, the alternative chain (Howie's Scott–Wiegold theorem) already supplies B, and (CB) gives 2g − 1 ≤ p ≤ g. So K = T(2,3), p = 1, and Y is the Poincaré sphere, which is prime.

**Caveat 1: the alternative chain does not suffice by itself.** For p < 2g − 1, step 3 needs the complementary summand A to be an L-space with |H_1(A)| = |p| ≥ 3. The alternative chain gives only B, not the shape of A. So the shape theorem (step 2) is really needed in that range.

**Caveat 2: the shape theorem is cited from memory.** I recall it as attributed to Howie (via the Scott–Wiegold theorem: π1 of a surgery is weight-one, so at most two summands have nontrivial homology), together with Valdez-Sánchez and Sayari. Its exact statement and attribution — that three summands force exactly two lens spaces of coprime orders and one homology sphere — should be checked against the literature.

Apart from this citation, I see no flaw in the derivation.

# round5_q7: answer

## Verdict on (E): PROVED, assuming the standard tools cited from memory in §0.

The argument follows the planner's route. The details are checked below, and points (i)–(iv) of the task are addressed explicitly in §5.

F = Z/2 throughout. "[lit]" marks a result cited from memory.

## 0. Tools (cited from memory)
- **T1 [lit] Integer surgery formula** (Ozsváth–Szabó, "Knot Floer homology and integer surgeries"). For p ≠ 0, Spin^c(S^3_p(K)) is identified with labels i ∈ Z/|p|. HF^+(S^3_p(K), i) is isomorphic, as a relatively graded F[U]-module, to the homology of the mapping cone D: ⊕_{s≡i} A_s^+ → ⊕_{s≡i} B_s^+, built from v_s: A_s → B_s and h_s: A_s → B_{s+p}. The cone may be truncated as in OS.
  - For an L-space knot, A_s^+ ≅ B_s^+ ≅ T^+, v_s = U^{V_s} and h_s = U^{H_s} with H_s = V_{-s}.
  - The cone may be computed on homology. T^+ is an injective F[U]-module, so every chain map between complexes with homology T^+ is determined, up to homotopy, by its map on homology.
- **T2 [lit] Labels are affine.** The labelling Spin^c(S^3_p(K)) ↔ Z/|p| is affine over H_1(S^3_p(K)) = Z/|p| = ⟨[μ]⟩, and [μ] acts by i ↦ i+1.
- **T3 [lit] Connected sums.**
  - Spin^c(Y1#Y2) = Spin^c(Y1) × Spin^c(Y2), equivariantly for H_1(Y1#Y2) = H_1(Y1) ⊕ H_1(Y2).
  - CF^-(Y1#Y2, (t1,t2)) ≃ CF^-(Y1,t1) ⊗_{F[U]} CF^-(Y2,t2).
  - If L is an L-space, CF^-(L,t) ≃ F[U] (free complex over a PID). Hence HF^+(L#Y'', (t,t'')) ≅ HF^+(Y'',t'') as relatively graded F[U]-modules, up to a degree shift.
- **T4.** The V_s facts stated in (E).

## 1. Fibre invariance (points (i) and (iv))
Suppose S^3_p(K) ≅ L # Y''.
- **Orientation.** If the homeomorphism reverses orientation, replace (L, Y'') by (−L, −Y''). Here −L is again an L-space with |H_1| = a. So assume it preserves orientation.
- **The subgroup H_1(L).** H_1(L) ⊕ H_1(Y'') ≅ Z/|p|, so a divides |p| and |H_1(Y'')| = b := |p|/a. In the cyclic group Z/|p| = ⟨[μ]⟩, the unique subgroup of order a is generated by b[μ].
- **Orbits.** By T3, the Spin^c structures sharing a fixed Y''-component t'' form one H_1(L)-orbit. By T2, these orbits are exactly the cosets i + bZ of labels.
- **Consequence.** By T3, every structure (t, t'') has HF^+ ≅ HF^+(Y'', t'') up to shift. Therefore:

**(★)** For every label i, HF^+(Y, i) ≅ HF^+(Y, i+b) as relatively graded F[U]-modules, up to a degree shift.

Since a ≥ 2, b ≢ 0 mod |p|. Let t be the representative of b mod |p| with 0 < |t| ≤ (|p|−1)/2; this is possible because |p| is odd, as it divides 2g−1. Labels 0 and t lie in the same orbit, so by (★) we compare labels 0 and t. We never need label 0 to be self-conjugate. Only its arithmetic matters: its elements are the multiples of p.

## 2. The invariant (point (ii))
Every module below has the form M = T^+ ⊕ ⊕_l F[U]/U^{e_l}, where U lowers the level by 1.
- The number of finite summands whose top lies at level k is dim coker(U: M_{k+1} → M_k). The tower contributes nothing, because U is onto on T^+.
- Hence the multiset of top levels of the finite summands is an isomorphism invariant. A degree shift translates it.
- In particular, "some level carries ≥ 2 tops" is invariant under isomorphism up to shift.

## 3. Setup common to both signs
Let N = |p| and n := (2g−1)/N. Since N | 2g−1 and N < 2g−1, n is odd and n ≥ 3.

For |c| ≤ (N−1)/2, the elements s ≡ c (mod N) with |s| ≤ g−1 are exactly c + kN for |k| ≤ (n−1)/2:
- |c + kN| ≤ (N−1)/2 + (n−1)N/2 = (nN−1)/2 = g−1;
- for k = ±(n+1)/2 we get |c + kN| ≥ (nN+1)/2 > g−1.

So each class has exactly n such elements.

**Key arithmetic.** Let u = c + (k+½)N and u' = c + (k'+½)N with k ≠ k'. Then u² = u'² only if u = −u', i.e. 2c + (k+k'+1)N = 0. This would give N | 2c; since N is odd, N | c, i.e. c ≡ 0. So for c = t, all the values u² (over distinct k) are distinct.

## 4a. The case p > 0 (N = p)
I use the computation of round2_q3 §2, which I re-checked as follows.
- **Truncation.** The truncated kernel is a path on the n valleys A_{s_j}. The edge between s_j and s_{j+1} = s_j + p has exponents H_{s_j} and V_{s_{j+1}}, both ≥ 1, because s_j ≥ −(g−1) and s_{j+1} ≤ g−1.
- **Surjectivity.** D is surjective, so H ≅ ker D.
- **Positions.** The valley levels x(s) = s(s−p)/(2p) − V_s satisfy x(s+p) − x(s) = s + V_s − V_{s+p} = H_s − V_{s+p}. The peak between s and s+p is at y = s(s+p)/(2p) = (m² − p²/4)/(2p), where m = s + p/2. This level does not depend on K.
- **Kernel at level k.** At level k, ker D is the space of functions on the components of G_k, the subgraph of the path consisting of vertices with bottom ≤ k and edges with bottom ≤ k. Since peaks lie strictly above valleys, every edge of G_k has both endpoints in G_k.
- **Action of U.** U maps level k+1 to level k by restriction. A vertex that is new at level k+1 has all its edges strictly higher, so it is isolated there. Each edge that is new at level k+1 joins two distinct components, because G is a path. Hence dim coker U at level k equals #{peaks at level k+1}.
- **Result.** The tops of the finite summands lie at the levels {y − 1}, one for each of the n−1 peaks.

**Comparison.** For class c, the peaks have m = c + (k+½)p with k = −(n−1)/2, …, (n−3)/2.
- **c = 0:** m ∈ {±p/2, ±3p/2, …, ±(n−2)p/2}. These are nonzero and come in ± pairs, so every top level occurs with even multiplicity. There are n−1 ≥ 2 tops, so some level carries ≥ 2 tops.
- **c = t:** by §3 all n−1 levels are distinct.

This contradicts (★) together with §2.

## 4b. The case p = −N < 0
I use round2_q3 §3, re-checked as follows.
- **Truncation.** Cancel the tails A_s ↔ B_s for s ≥ g and A_s ↔ B_{s−N} for s ≤ −g. Each tail is a quotient complex (respectively a subcomplex) in which every edge is an isomorphism, so it is acyclic. What remains is B_{s_1−N} ← A_{s_1} → B_{s_1} ← … → B_{s_n}: n valleys and n+1 peaks, with the two end B's acting as edges to a "ground" vertex. All exponents are ≥ 1.
- **Splitting.** Computed on homology, H = ker D ⊕ coker D as F[U]-modules, because U preserves the A- and B-parts.
- **Positions.** The peak at B_{t'} lies at level −(u² − N²/4)/(2N), where u = t' + N/2.
- **Coker part.** G_k ∪ {ground} is a subgraph of a single cycle. The coker part is H^1 of that graph, which gives a single tower starting at the maximal peak level M.
- **Ker part.** The ker part consists of functions on the ungrounded components. The same restriction argument applies, so its tops lie at {y − 1 : y a peak}, with one copy of M − 1 removed: exactly one edge, at level M, closes the cycle instead of merging two components.

**Comparison.** For class c, the peaks have u = c + (k+½)N with k = −(n+1)/2, …, (n−1)/2.
- **c = 0:** u ∈ {±N/2, ±3N/2, …, ±nN/2}. After removing one copy of the top level for |u| = N/2, each level with |u| ∈ {3N/2, …, nN/2} still occurs twice. This set is nonempty because n ≥ 3.
- **c = t:** by §3 the n+1 peak levels are distinct, so the n remaining tops are distinct.

This again contradicts (★) together with §2. ∎

## 5. Checklist
- **(i) Labels and orbits.** Affineness (T2), together with uniqueness of the order-a subgroup of a cyclic group, gives that the H_1(L)-orbits are the cosets i + bZ. Self-conjugacy of label 0 is never used; only the facts that its elements are ≡ 0 mod N and that t ≢ 0 are used.
- **(ii) The invariant.** The multiset of top levels, counted by dim coker U per level, is an invariant of graded F[U]-modules up to shift (§2).
- **(iii) Both signs.** Both signs of p are done (§4a, §4b).
- **(iv) Hypotheses used:**
  - a ≥ 2, so that t ≢ 0;
  - N | 2g−1, so that every class has the same n elements, and N is odd, which drives the key arithmetic of §3;
  - N < 2g−1, so that n ≥ 3: this is needed for ≥ 2 tops when p > 0, and for a doubled level when p < 0.

  Nothing about Y'' is used beyond T3.
- **Not covered.** N = 2g−1, i.e. n = 1, is not covered by this argument. When p > 0 that surgery is an L-space. When p < 0, round2_q3 handles it only for a = |p|. (E) excludes this case anyway.

## 6. Status
- **Proved:** Theorem (E), modulo the cited tools T1–T4. These are the integer surgery formula as a relatively graded isomorphism together with its truncation, the affine labelling, the Künneth formula for CF^-, and the facts about V_s for L-space knots.
- **Not part of this task:** the other links of chain B (Howie, Gordon–Luecke, the bound |p| ≤ g).

# Answer to round5_q6: the cover bound (CB)

## 1. Verdict

**(CB) is PROVED, in its sharper form, for every nonzero integer p, of either sign.** The proof follows the named route (Heegaard genus). It does not use the Poincaré conjecture or Grushko's theorem.

**Theorem.** Let K ⊂ S^3 be a fibred knot. Its fibre F is compact, connected and orientable, of genus g ≥ 1, with one boundary component. Let p ≠ 0 and n = |p|, and suppose Y = S^3_p(K) ≅ A # B, where B is an integer homology sphere with B ≇ S^3. Let Ã be the n-fold cyclic cover of A induced by H_1(A) ≅ Z/n. Then

  g(Ã) + n·g(B) ≤ 2g, and in particular n ≤ g,

where g(·) denotes Heegaard genus.

### Results cited from memory

- **(H) Haken's lemma and additivity** (W. Haken, "Some results on surfaces in 3-manifolds", 1968). Heegaard genus is additive under connected sum of closed orientable 3-manifolds: g(M_1 # M_2) = g(M_1) + g(M_2). Only the inequality "≥" is used, and only for Y_p ≅ Ã # nB (Step 2). That inequality is the standard corollary of Haken's lemma.
- **(F) Standard facts about fibred knots.**
  - The exterior M_K = S^3 \ int N(K) is homeomorphic to a mapping torus N(h) = F×R/⟨σ⟩, where σ(x,t) = (h(x), t−1).
  - The monodromy h is a homeomorphism of F that is the identity on a collar C ≅ S^1×[0,1] of ∂F = S^1×{0}.
  - ∂F is the Seifert longitude λ.
  - The fibration map M_K → S^1 = R/Z induces the abelianisation π_1(M_K) → H_1(M_K) = Z, up to sign.

Everything else is proved below.

## 2. Proof

Throughout, n = |p| and N(ψ) = F×R/⟨(x,t) ~ (ψ(x), t−1)⟩. Whenever ψ is the identity on ∂F, the boundary ∂N(ψ) = ∂F × (R/Z) is a torus. On this torus, λ is the θ-circle ∂F×{pt} and c is the t-circle {pt}×R/Z.

### Step 1. The covering space.

1. H_1(Y) ≅ Z/n, and it is generated by the meridian μ.
2. Let φ: π_1(Y) → H_1(Y) = Z/n be abelianisation, and let π: Y_p → Y be the connected n-fold cyclic cover with kernel ker φ. When n = 1, Y_p = Y.

### Step 2. Y_p ≅ Ã # (n copies of B).

1. Let S be the splitting sphere, so Y = A° ∪_S B°, where A° and B° are A and B with an open ball removed.
2. **The preimage of B° is n copies of B°.** By Mayer–Vietoris, H_1(Y) = H_1(A°) ⊕ H_1(B°) = H_1(A) ⊕ 0. The map φ restricted to π_1(B°) factors through H_1(B°) = H_1(B) = 0, so it is trivial. Hence π^{-1}(B°) is n disjoint copies, each mapped homeomorphically onto B°.
3. **The preimage of A° is connected.** π_1(A°) → H_1(A°) → H_1(Y) is onto, so π^{-1}(A°) is connected. It is the restriction to A° of the n-fold cyclic cover Ã → A determined by H_1(A) ≅ Z/n.
4. **The removed ball and the sphere.** The removed ball is simply connected, so its preimage in Ã is n disjoint balls. Hence π^{-1}(A°) = Ã minus n open balls. Since S is simply connected, it lifts to n disjoint spheres.
5. **Gluing.** Each copy of B° has exactly one boundary sphere, glued to one of the n distinct boundary spheres of π^{-1}(A°). The gluing graph is a star, which is a tree, so
   Y_p ≅ Ã # B # ⋯ # B (n copies of B).
6. **Applying (H).** By (H), g(Y_p) ≥ g(Ã) + n·g(B).

### Step 3. g(B) ≥ 2.

1. **Genus 0.** A genus-0 Heegaard splitting is two 3-balls glued along their boundary. By the Alexander trick this is S^3.
2. **Genus 1.** A genus-1 splitting is V_1 ∪_f V_2 with V_1, V_2 solid tori. Let m_2 be the meridian of V_2 and let f(m_2) = a·ℓ_1 + b·m_1 in H_1(∂V_1), where ℓ_1 is a longitude and m_1 the meridian of V_1. Then H_1 = H_1(V_1)/⟨a⟩ = Z/a, with Z when a = 0.
3. If H_1 = 0 then a = ±1, so f(m_2) is isotopic to a longitude of V_1. Attaching a 2-handle to V_1 along a longitude gives a 3-ball, and V_2 is that 2-handle plus a 3-ball. So the manifold is a ball union a ball, which is S^3.
4. So every integer homology sphere of Heegaard genus ≤ 1 is S^3. Since B ≇ S^3, g(B) ≥ 2.

### Step 4. Y_p is obtained from N(h^n) by filling along a slope meeting ∂F once.

1. **The preimage of M_K.** Write Y = M_K ∪_∂ V, with V a solid torus whose meridian is glued to α = pμ + λ. The composite π_1(M_K) → H_1(M_K) = Z⟨μ⟩ → Z/n is onto, and by (F) it is induced by the fibration. So π^{-1}(M_K) is the connected cover F×R/⟨σ^n⟩. Since σ^n(x,t) = (h^n(x), t−n), rescaling t by 1/n identifies this cover with N(h^n).
2. **The boundary torus.** On ∂M_K the curve c meets λ once, so c = ±μ + kλ for some integer k. Orient c so that c = μ + kλ.
3. The fibration map sends c to a generator of π_1(S^1). So ∂M_K has a single preimage T̃ = ∂F × (R/nZ). This is the boundary torus ∂N(h^n), with basis λ̃ (the θ-circle, mapping to λ) and c̃ (the t-circle, mapping to n·c).
4. So π_*: H_1(T̃) → H_1(∂M_K) is injective, with image span{n·c, λ}.
5. **Rewriting the filling slope.** α = pμ + λ = p·c + (1 − pk)·λ = (p/n)·(n·c) + (1 − pk)·λ.
6. **The preimage of V.** Let β be a curve on ∂V meeting α once, so β is isotopic in V to the core. Then β = aμ + bλ with a ≡ ±1 (mod p), so the core represents a generator of H_1(Y). Hence π^{-1}(V) is a single solid torus Ṽ.
7. Meridian discs of V are simply connected, so they lift to meridian discs of Ṽ. Their boundaries are closed lifts of α in T̃.
8. **The lifted slope.** Each lift is a simple closed curve whose class γ satisfies π_*γ = α. Since π_* is injective, γ = ±(ε·c̃ + (1 − pk)·λ̃), where ε = p/n = ±1. Reversing the orientation of the t-direction if p < 0, we get:
   Y_p ≅ N(h^n) ∪ (solid torus with meridian c̃ + m·λ̃), for some integer m.
9. This settles the sign question raised in the task: the case p < 0 is treated exactly like p > 0. All that matters is that the lifted slope has intersection number ±1 with λ̃ = ∂F. That holds because intersection numbers multiply by the covering degree n on the n-fold cover T̃ → ∂M_K.

### Step 5. Filling a mapping torus along c + mλ gives an open book with page F.

1. **The setting.** Let ψ be a homeomorphism of F that is the identity on the collar C = S^1_θ × [0,1]_s, with s = 0 at ∂F. For the case at hand take ψ = h^n.
2. **The twist.** Choose a continuous function ρ: [0,1] → [0,1] with ρ = 1 on [0,1/2] and ρ(1) = 0. Define Φ on F×[0,1] by
   - Φ(θ,s,t) = (θ − 2πm·t·ρ(s), s, t) on C×[0,1];
   - Φ = id elsewhere.
3. Φ restricts to the identity on F×{0}. On F×{1} it restricts to a map T: F → F supported in s ∈ [1/2, 1]. Indeed, for s ≤ 1/2 the map is rotation by 2πm, which is the identity.
4. Let ψ' = ψ ∘ T^{-1}. Then ψ' = id on the half collar s ≤ 1/2. Moreover Φ descends to a homeomorphism N(ψ) → N(ψ'), where N(·) is the [0,1]-model F×[0,1]/((x,1) ~ (ψ(x),0)). The required identity is ψ'(T x) = ψ(x).
5. **Action on the boundary.** On the boundary (s = 0), Φ is (θ,t) ↦ (θ − 2πm·t, t). It fixes λ and sends c + mλ to c. Hence
   N(ψ) ∪_{c+mλ} (solid torus) ≅ N(ψ') ∪_{c} (solid torus).
6. **This is the open book.** Let OB(F,ψ') = F×[0,1]/~, where (x,1) ~ (ψ'(x),0) and (x,t) ~ (x,t') for x ∈ ∂F. In OB(F,ψ'), the image of {s ≤ 1/2} × [0,1] is S^1_θ × (([0,1/2]_s × S^1_t) with s = 0 collapsed) = S^1 × D^2. Its meridian is the t-circle c. Its complement is N(ψ') with a collar shrunk, so OB(F,ψ') ≅ N(ψ') ∪_c (solid torus).
7. Combining with Step 4, Y_p ≅ OB(F, ψ') for some homeomorphism ψ' of F that fixes ∂F.

### Step 6. An open book with page F gives a Heegaard splitting of genus 2g.

1. In Q = OB(F,ψ'), let H_1 be the image of F×[0,1/2] and H_2 the image of F×[1/2,1].
2. **Each half is a handlebody.** Each half is (F×I)/(collapse {x}×I for x ∈ ∂F). This quotient is homeomorphic to F×I: on (collar × I) it is S^1 × (a square with one side collapsed), which is S^1 × (a triangle), and that is homeomorphic to S^1 × (a square), compatibly with the rest.
3. F is a disc with 2g bands attached, so F×I is a 3-ball with 2g 1-handles, i.e. a handlebody of genus 2g.
4. **The common boundary.** H_1 ∪ H_2 = Q. The intersection H_1 ∩ H_2 is the image of F×{1/2} ∪ F×{0}, using F×{1} = F×{0} via ψ'. These two copies of F are glued along the binding ∂F, giving a closed surface of genus 2g, which equals ∂H_1 = ∂H_2.
5. So Q has a Heegaard splitting of genus 2g, and g(Y_p) ≤ 2g.

### Step 7. Conclusion.

Steps 2, 3 and 6 give

  2n ≤ g(Ã) + n·g(B) ≤ g(Y_p) ≤ 2g,

so n = |p| ≤ g. ∎

**Remarks on the proof.**
- **Hypotheses actually used.** We used p ≠ 0 (so that H_1(Y) is finite, cyclic and generated by μ), that K is fibred with fibre of genus g, and that B is a homology sphere ≇ S^3. The hypothesis g ≥ 1 is not used; when g = 0, K is the unknot and Y is a lens space, which has no such decomposition.
- **Sanity checks, all consistent.**
  - K = T(2,3), p = 1: Y is the Poincaré sphere = S^3 # Y, and 1 ≤ 1 (tight).
  - Torus knots T(r,s) with p = rs: Y_p = #_{(r−1)(s−1)} S^1×S^2, which has Heegaard genus (r−1)(s−1) = 2g. This case has no homology-sphere summand B, so (CB) does not apply.

## 3. Does the chain of steps 1–5 answer the question?

**Conditionally yes.** The arithmetic runs as follows.
1. Suppose Y = S^3_p(K) has ≥ 3 prime summands, with K a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g and p integral.
2. By the cited shape theorem, Y = L_1 # L_2 # Y_3 with rs = |p| ≥ 6 and Y_3 a homology sphere ≇ S^3.
3. The Floer theorem gives p ≥ 2g − 1.
4. Ni's theorem (L-space knots are fibred) together with (CB), applied with A = L_1 # L_2 and B = Y_3, gives p ≤ g.
5. Hence 2g − 1 ≤ g, so g ≤ 1 and p ≤ 1. This contradicts p = rs ≥ 6.

(CB) alone already gives the weaker conclusion rs ≤ g.

**Caveats. These are external inputs that I did not and could not verify here.**

1. **The shape theorem.** The chain needs the cited result that ≥ 3 prime summands forces exactly the shape L_1 # L_2 # Y_3: two lens spaces of coprime orders and a homology sphere ≇ S^3. From memory, a result of this type is due to J. Howie (and to L. Valdez-Sánchez for the related case). The chain is only as good as that citation.
   - In particular, (CB) needs some summand to be a homology sphere ≇ S^3.
   - It is the shape theorem that rules out three summands with nontrivial pairwise-coprime H_1. Nothing in (CB) does.
2. **The Floer theorem.** The "already-proved Heegaard Floer theorem" (p ≥ 2g − 1 in this situation) is taken from earlier rounds. I did not re-check it.
3. **The reduction steps.** The reduction to integral slopes (Gordon–Luecke: non-integral surgery on a nontrivial knot is irreducible), the case of slope 0 (Gabai: 0-surgery is prime/irreducible) and the passage to the mirror are standard. Ni's theorem (L-space knots are fibred) is quoted correctly.

I found no flaw in the logic of the chain, given those inputs. The answer to the problem is "yes, at most two prime summands", conditional on the cited shape theorem and the earlier Floer-theoretic theorem.

## 4. Status summary

- **Proved:** (CB) in the sharper form g(Ã) + |p|·g(B) ≤ 2g, for all p ≠ 0. This relies only on Haken's lemma (additivity of Heegaard genus) and standard facts about fibred knots, both cited from memory.
- **Not re-verified here (external inputs to the chain):** the shape theorem for ≥ 3 summands, and the Floer bound p ≥ 2g − 1.
- **Open:** nothing further within (CB) itself.

content.content:
Does a 3-manifold obtained by Dehn surgery on an L-space knot have at most two prime summands?----
# Notes (planner memory)

## Round 1 (plan)
- Goal: posed claim as stated. Expected answer YES. Memory: Hom–Lidman–Zufelt MRL 2015 likely proves it; Greene JDG 2015 related; Matignon–Sayari |p| <= 2g-1 for non-cable reducible slopes; Howie <= 3 summands.
- Cables: reducible slope mn can exceed 2g-1 (C_{2,3}(T(2,3)): 6 > 5).

## Round 2 (plan)
- Round 1 answers were all short, all just cite HLZ from memory (statement uncertain). Screened all OK. Nothing proved. Do not commission more recollection queries.
- My check: hat-cone rank per class for positive L-space knot, p>0: 2n_i-1 (n_i>=1) else 1, n_i = #{s≡i mod p, |s|<=g-1}. Script /tmp/cone.py (truncated cone gives +2 artifact; subtract 2). Recorded as OPEN ledger line (round2_plan).
- Consequence: L1#L2#Y3 => all ranks equal => p>=2g-1 or p | 2g-1 with quotient >=3 (odd). Lens summand => rank fn translation invariant => same dichotomy. Remaining: kill p|2g-1 (p<2g-1), negative p, and L-space regime (Y3 L-space ZHS, d(Y3) unknown).
- Round 2 queries (all attempt): q1 ledger #2 (reducible => p>=2g-1); q2 #3 L-space regime (d-inv/Casson-Walker/Greene); q3 #3 non-L-space regime (graded modules); q4 topological reduction rigorous (satellites, Howie shape, Matignon–Sayari) = ledger #4.
- Ledger now: #1 GOAL open, #2, #3 open, #4 reduction open (round1_q3), #5 rank formula open (round2_plan).
- Next: if q1+q2+q3+q4 close the chain (with cited standard theorems stated exactly), write PROVED [GOAL] and two verify queries spliced from the answer files. Literature dependence acceptable if statements are standard and exactly stated; flag uncertain ones (GL96 lens summand, Howie shape, Scharlemann satellite statement) for verifier.

# Round 5 summary (after round 4 results)

## Problem and goal
Does every 3-manifold obtained by Dehn surgery on an L-space knot have at most two prime summands? Goal = ledger entry 1 ([GOAL], OPEN): the posed claim (expected answer YES), or a counterexample. Convention: after mirroring, K is a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g, with invariants V_s (V_s >= 0, steps 0/1, V_s = 0 iff s >= g, V_{-s} = V_s + s). L-space knots are fibred (Ni / Ghiggini, cited), with fibre F of genus g and one boundary component, monodromy h.

## Standing results
(Heegaard Floer results hold modulo cited standard tools: Ozsvath–Szabo integer surgery mapping cone, plus and hat, relatively graded, with truncation; for L-space knots A_s = B_s = T^+, v_s = U^{V_s}, h_s = U^{V_{-s}}; Kunneth / connected-sum formula; Ni–Wu d formula; HF of lens spaces.)
1. Ledger 6 (round2_q1 §3): hat ranks per Spin^c class: rank HF-hat(S^3_p(K), i) = 1 for p >= 2g-1, 2n_i - 1 for 0 < p <= 2g-2, 2n_i + 1 for p < 0, n_i = #{s ≡ i mod |p| : |s| <= g-1}. Not on the current line.
2. Ledger 7 (round2_q1 §1–3): if S^3_p(K) = L # Y' with L a lens space of order a >= 2 and Y' ANY closed 3-manifold (b = |p|/a), then HF-hat ranks and HF^+ (up to shift) are invariant under i -> i + b, hence p >= 2g-1 or |p| divides 2g-1; p = ±1 impossible. Used by the alternative chain B below. Not independently checked.
3. Ledger 8 (round2_q3): THEOREM. For a nonzero integer p < 2g-1 (either sign), S^3_p(K) is never L # Y' with L an L-space of order |p| >= 3 and Y' an integer homology sphere. Proof: all classes would carry the same relatively graded HF^+; "level" model of the cone with K-independent peak levels; class 0 (self-conjugate) has even multiplicities of tops, class 1 has distinct tops (p > 0); for p < 0 a repeated top / offset argument. INDEPENDENTLY CHECKED by round4_q10: correct as stated given the cited tools (it supplied the chain-level-to-homology justification; one unused misstatement about module classification).
4. Ledger 9 (round2_q3): Consequence: a three-summand surgery L1 # L2 # Y3 has p >= 2g-1, so Y and Y3 are L-spaces; with Matignon–Sayari (cited) p = 2g-1 for non-cables. (Under the new chain only "p >= 2g-1" is needed.)
5. Ledger 13 (round3_q1): in case (R), the reversed trace glued to sharp negative-definite plumbings gives a smooth negative-definite X with boundary -Y3 and unimodular lattice of rank n containing <-p> ⊕ Λ(Q1) ⊕ Λ(Q2) with index p. Not on the current line.
6. NEW (round4_q2 Lemma 1): in case (R), d(Y3) <= -2 for all (r,s) (lattice X + Ni–Wu + Elkies; uses V_{g-1} >= 1); hence Y3 bounds no negative-definite 4-manifold and Y3 is not S^3 or Σ(2,3,5) oriented as ∂(-E8). Not on the current line.
7. NEW (round4_q3 Lemma 2.1 / round4_q1 §1): no-go for all coprime odd r,s: the formal staircase V' = V(T(r,s)) + 1 on [0, g-1] gives d(S^3_p(K'), i) = d(S^3_{rs}(T(r,s)), i) - 2, i.e. exactly the d-invariants (and torsion, Casson–Walker) of L1 # L2 # S^3_{+1}(T(2,3)); Δ' = Δ_{T(r,s)} + t^{-g}(t-1)(t^p-1). So no invariant of Y alone excludes (R). Generalises ledger 10. Not on the current line.
8. NEW (round4_q9 Lemma A): in case (R), the p-fold cyclic (= universal abelian) cover Y_p of Y = L1 # L2 # Y3 is #_p Y3 # (r-1)(s-1)(S^1×S^2). Planner re-derived: the general version is Y = A # B with B a ZHS gives Y_{|p|} = Ã # (|p| copies of B), Ã the |p|-fold cyclic cover of A.
9. NEW (round4_q9 Lemma B(i)): for a fibred knot, the |p|-fold cyclic cover of S^3_p(K) is obtained from the mapping torus M(h^p) by filling along the lift μ̃ + λ̃ of pμ + λ, which meets ∂F once; so it is the closed manifold of an open book with page F (monodromy h^p τ_∂^ε). Planner re-checked the slope computation (intersection numbers scale by the covering degree: (pμ)·λ = p = p (μ̃·λ̃)).

## Dead ends (each a REFUTED statement with its file)

## Set aside, not refuted
- 4-dimensional lattice route (round3_q1, round4_q2 Lemma 1): gives d(Y3) <= -2; consistent with the split model.
- Graph-of-intersection / Scharlemann-cycle route (round3_q2, round4_q2 Lemmas 2–4, round4_q3 §3, round4_q8): parallel families <= n/2, chains of monodromy iterates, Euler count p <= ē <= 3p with no contradiction; needs a type-(c) sphere with a Scharlemann cycle on the Y3 side (round4_q8 (M'), (M'1), (M'2)).
- Fibration / Morse position / FDTC (round4_q4, q9 Lemma C): c(h) = 1/b, |p - b| <= 1; no contradiction.
- Sutured decomposition along P (round4_q5): [P] = 0 so all-or-nothing; no information.
- Rational genus of K* (round4_q7 Lemma 4): needs K* to minimise Θ in its class (H); open.
- Alexander polynomial obstruction to V_T + 1 (round4_q6 §3): no known restriction applies (see semigroup refutation above).
These are no longer needed if the cover bound below is proved.

## Open gaps
A. The missing statement below (cover bound). B. Ledger 11 (not needed any more). C. Exact statements of the cited topology still used: Gordon–Luecke 1987, Gabai (0-surgery), Ni (L-space knots fibred), the three-summand shape theorem (chain A) or Howie's Scott–Wiegold theorem + Gordon–Luecke 1996 lens summand (chain B); Perelman or Haken additivity for the rank/genus count. D. Chain B also needs the coset extension of ledger 8 (OPEN line this round) and ledger 7 (not independently checked).

## The chain and the missing statement

Chain (chain A; cited entries by ledger number; "cited" = published theorems as listed under gap C):
1. Mirror so K is a positive L-space knot (S^3_r(mK) = -S^3_{-r}(K); orientation reversal preserves the number of prime summands). If K is the unknot every surgery is S^3, a lens space or S^1×S^2, all prime. Let K be nontrivial, genus g >= 1. Slope ∞ gives S^3; slope 0 gives an irreducible manifold (Gabai, cited); a non-integral slope gives an irreducible manifold (Gordon–Luecke 1987, cited); irreducible closed 3-manifolds are prime. So assume p is a nonzero integer and Y = S^3_p(K) has >= 3 prime summands.
2. Cited shape theorem (ledger 4): then Y = L1 # L2 # Y3 with L1, L2 lens spaces of coprime orders r, s >= 2, rs = |p|, and Y3 an integer homology sphere, Y3 ≠ S^3 (Y3 may be taken to be the connected sum of all summands with trivial H_1).
3. L1 # L2 is an L-space (Kunneth) with |H_1| = |p| = rs >= 6 >= 3, so ledger 8 forbids every p < 2g-1: hence p >= 2g-1 (in particular p > 0).
4. K is fibred (Ni, cited) with fibre of genus g. Apply the missing statement with A = L1 # L2, B = Y3: |p| <= g.
5. So 2g-1 <= p <= g, hence g <= 1 and p <= 1, contradicting p = rs >= 6. Hence no surgery on an L-space knot has three or more prime summands: the [GOAL] answer is YES. (No hyperbolicity reduction, satellite theory, Moser or Matignon–Sayari is needed.)
Alternative chain B (removes the "two lens spaces" citation; needs one more OPEN entry): Howie's Scott–Wiegold theorem (π1 has weight one, so it cannot surject onto a free product of three nontrivial cyclic groups) gives at most two summands with nontrivial H_1, hence a summand B, H_1(B) = 0, B ≠ S^3; Gordon–Luecke 1996 gives a lens summand L(a), a >= 2. Missing statement ⇒ |p| <= g (so g >= 2 and |p| < 2g-1). Ledger 7 ⇒ |p| divides 2g-1. The coset extension of ledger 8 (OPEN, round5_plan) ⇒ contradiction.

Missing statement (OPEN, round5_plan; replaces ledger 12 as the chain's missing statement; it implies ledger 12 at once since there p = 2g-1 > g):
(CB) Let K ⊂ S^3 be a fibred knot whose fibre is a compact connected orientable surface F of genus g >= 1 with one boundary component, and let p be a nonzero integer. Suppose S^3_p(K) is homeomorphic to a connected sum A # B of closed oriented 3-manifolds, where B is an integer homology sphere not homeomorphic to S^3. Then |p| <= g. (Expected sharper form: |p|·rank π1(B) + rank π1(Ã) <= 2g, where Ã is the |p|-fold cyclic cover of A induced by H_1(A) ≅ Z/|p|.)

Why it should hold (planner sketch):
- Let φ: π1(Y) → H_1(Y) = Z/|p| and Y_p the induced connected |p|-fold cyclic cover. Since H_1(B) = 0, φ kills π1(B°): B° lifts to |p| disjoint copies; A° has connected preimage (π1(A°) → H_1(A) = H_1(Y) onto). Lifting the splitting sphere gives Y_p ≅ Ã # (|p| copies of B).
- Grushko–Neumann: rank π1(Y_p) = rank π1(Ã) + |p|·rank π1(B). B ≠ S^3 ZHS ⇒ π1(B) nontrivial (Perelman) and perfect, so not cyclic: rank >= 2. Hence rank π1(Y_p) >= 2|p|. (Perelman-free alternative: Heegaard genus g(B) >= 2 since genus <= 1 manifolds are S^3, lens spaces, S^1×S^2; Haken additivity of Heegaard genus.)
- Y = M_K ∪ V. H_1(M_K) = Z<μ> → Z/|p| onto, so the preimage of M_K is the |p|-fold cyclic cover M(h^{|p|}) of the mapping torus, fibred with fibre F; π1 generated by π1(F) (free, rank 2g) and a lift t of μ^{|p|}. ∂M_K lifts to one torus with H_1 basis μ̃ (↦ |p|μ), λ̃ = ∂F (↦ λ); the filling slope pμ + λ has trivial φ-image, lifts to closed curves of class ±μ̃ + λ̃ (H_1 of the lift injects), and μ̃·λ̃ = 1 since intersection numbers multiply by the degree. V lifts to one solid torus (its core represents a generator). So π1(Y_p) = π1(M(h^{|p|}))/<<t^{±1}·∂F>>, generated by π1(F): rank <= 2g. (Equivalently Y_p is an open book with page F, Heegaard genus <= 2g.)
- Combine: 2|p| <= 2g.
