# round6_q1 — referee report on the proof chain for the answer YES

Plan: check (0), (I), (II), (III), (III') in order, then check the cited theorems, then give a verdict. Status: complete.

## Summary
I checked every inference. I found no fatal gap. There is one imprecision of wording in (III) §4b: the description of the p<0 truncation as "a quotient complex, respectively a subcomplex". The claimed truncation is still correct, and I give a full repair in §4 below. The other points listed in the task all check out, for both signs of p. The derivation (0) uses each part only where its hypotheses are satisfied, and its case analysis is exhaustive.

## 1. Derivation (0)
- **Step 1.** The cases are exhaustive. The unknot gives only prime manifolds. For a nontrivial K: the slope ∞ gives S^3; the slope 0 is handled by Gabai; non-integral slopes are handled by GL87. An irreducible manifold is prime. Mirroring: S^3_r(mK) = -S^3_{-r}(K), so the sign of p is kept arbitrary, and (I), (II), (III) all allow either sign.
- **Step 2.** This step is correct.
  - H_1(Y) is finite cyclic, and a direct summand of a finite cyclic group is cyclic. In particular no summand is S^1×S^2.
  - π1(Y) is a quotient of π1(M_K), which is normally generated by μ.
  - Kill the other free factors and abelianise the three remaining ones. This gives a surjection onto a free product of three nontrivial cyclic groups that is normally generated by the image of μ. Howie's theorem forbids this.
  - So if k ≥ 3, some prime summand B has H_1(B) = 0, and B ≠ S^3.
- **Step 3.** From GL96 we get a lens summand L. Since L is prime and H_1(Y) is finite, a = |H_1(L)| ≥ 2 and a divides |p|. Lens spaces are L-spaces.
- **Step 4.** The hypotheses of (CB) hold:
  - K is fibred with a fibre of genus g and one boundary component (Ni, Ghiggini);
  - p ≠ 0;
  - B is a homology sphere and B ≠ S^3;
  - A is arbitrary.

  So |p| ≤ g. When g = 1 this already contradicts |p| ≥ 2, so the case g = 1 is closed here. Otherwise g ≥ 2, and |p| ≤ g < 2g-1.
- **Step 5.** Part (II) applies to any L-space summand of order ≥ 2 and to either sign of p. Since p ≤ |p| < 2g-1, its conclusion is that |p| divides 2g-1.
- **Step 6.** The hypotheses of (E) hold:
  - K is a nontrivial positive L-space knot;
  - |p| divides 2g-1 and |p| < 2g-1 (so |p| is odd and n ≥ 3);
  - L is an L-space of order ≥ 2;
  - Y'' is arbitrary.

  (E) then contradicts step 3.

## 2. Part (I) — the Cover Bound (CB)
All of it is correct.
- **Lower bound.** Because H_1(B) = 0, B° lifts trivially. Because φ restricted to π1(A) is the abelianisation of A, onto Z/N, the preimage of A° is Ã minus N balls. The gluing graph is a star. Grushko–Neumann then gives rank π1(Y_N) = rank π1(Ã) + N·rank π1(B). Also rank π1(B) ≥ 2, since π1(B) is perfect and nontrivial (Perelman), or by the Heegaard-genus variant.
- **Upper bound.**
  - E is the N-fold cyclic cover dual to F, i.e. the mapping torus of h^N. T̃ is connected because μ ∈ π1(T) maps onto Z/N, and Ṽ is a solid torus because μ is isotopic to the core of V.
  - Intersection numbers: for a degree-N covering of tori, f_*a·f_*b = N(a·b). This is the lattice-determinant identity for Λ' ⊂ Λ of index N.
  - F̃ maps homeomorphically to F, so q_*λ̃ = λ. Then N(β·λ̃) = (pμ+λ)·λ = ±p, which gives β·λ̃ = ±1 for either sign of p.
  - So β ↦ ±1 under π1(E) → Z, i.e. β = t^{±1}w with w ∈ π1(F̃). In π1(E)/⟨⟨β⟩⟩ the element t lies in the image of π1(F̃), so the rank is ≤ 2g.
- **Conclusion.** 2|p| ≤ 2g.

As a sanity check, (CB) does not conflict with the reducible surgery L(p,1) # S^3_{1/p}(K) on the (p,1)-cable C_{p,1}(K): that cable has genus p·g(K) ≥ p.

## 3. Part (II) — the divisibility lemma
All of it is correct.
- **Lemma 2.1.** Künneth over F gives rank ĤF(Y,(t,t')) = rank ĤF(Y',t'). The H_1(L)-orbits are the fibres over t'. H_1(L) is the unique subgroup of order a in Z/|p|, generated by b[μ]. With the affine labelling, the orbits are the cosets i + bZ, and b ≢ 0 because a ≥ 2.
- **Hat maps.**
  - v̂_s is nonzero iff V_s = 0. This follows from Â = ker U together with the long exact sequence and naturality: v̂_s is U^{V_s} restricted to the bottom element of the tower.
  - Over a field, each Â_s is homotopy equivalent to its homology, so the cone is determined by the maps on homology.
- **Components, p > 0.** I re-derived the components: isolated A_s for |s| < g, isolated B_t for p-g < t < g, triples for g ≤ t ≤ p-g, and pairs otherwise. There are no infinite components. The formula "rank = 1 if p ≥ 2g-1, and 2n_i - 1 if p ≤ 2g-2" is right.
- **Components, p = -n < 0.** The isolated B_t are those with -g-n < t < g. This gives rank 2n_i + 1.
- **Prop 3.1.** The rank is a strictly increasing function of n_i. So the set S of residues with n_i = q+1 is b-invariant. If 0 < r < |p|, S is a proper nonempty cyclic interval with a unique start point, so only the zero translation preserves it. This contradicts b ≢ 0. Hence r = 0.

## 4. Parts (III) and (III') — Theorem (E)
- **Invariant (§2).** dim(M/UM)_k counts the finite summands whose top lies at level k; the tower contributes nothing. This multiset is an isomorphism invariant, and a grading shift translates it, so its multiplicity pattern is shift-invariant. (★) is a valid consequence of Künneth with CF^-(L,t) ≃ F[U], together with the orbit description above.
- **Arithmetic (§3).** The class c, with |c| ≤ (N-1)/2, has exactly the n elements c + kN, |k| ≤ (n-1)/2, inside [-(g-1), g-1]. If c ≢ 0, the values (c + (k+½)N)² are pairwise distinct: equality forces N | 2c, hence N | c since N is odd.
- **Case p > 0.**
  - The truncation to a path on n valleys is right. Outside [-(g-1), g-1] the kernel is forced, with finite support because H_s, V_{-s} → ∞. D is surjective.
  - All edge exponents are ≥ 1.
  - I re-derived the levels: x(s) = s(s-p)/(2p) - V_s, and the peak level is s(s+p)/(2p), which does not depend on K. I used H_s = V_s + s.
  - Module structure: at level k the kernel is the functions on π0(G_k), and U is restriction. A newly born vertex is isolated, since its peaks are at least one level higher. Each new edge merges two components, since G is a forest. So dim coker U at level k equals the number of peaks at level k+1, and the tops are at {y-1}.
  - Comparison: class 0 has the peaks ±½p, …, ±(n-2)p/2. That is n-1 ≥ 2 peaks, all with even multiplicity. Class t has distinct peaks. Contradiction.
- **Case p < 0: repair of the truncation wording.** Let C be the full cone and N = -p.
  - Q = {A_s, B_s : s ≥ g} is a quotient complex of C. Its complement is a subcomplex, because A_s with s < g maps only to B_s and B_{s-N}, both with index < g.
  - D_Q = id + (shift to lower index). It is bijective on finitely supported sequences: solve from the top of the support downward. So Q is acyclic, and C ≃ P := C minus Q.
  - Inside P, the set P' = {A_s : |s| < g} ∪ {B_t : -g-N < t < g} is a subcomplex, and R0 = P/P' = {A_s : s ≤ -g} ∪ {B_{s-N} : s ≤ -g} is a quotient complex.
  - D_{R0} = (h_s iso) + (v-part, pointing to lower index). The same triangular argument shows R0 is acyclic.
  - Hence C ≃ P'. In class c the surviving B's are B_{s_1-N}, B_{s_1}, …, B_{s_n}, exactly as claimed: n valleys and n+1 peaks. (The text's phrase "each tail is a quotient complex (respectively a subcomplex)" should be read with "tail" relative to P for the second cancellation. The conclusion is unaffected.)
- **Case p < 0: the rest.**
  - The truncated cone is the two-term complex ⊕A → ⊕B, so H = ker D ⊕ coker D as F[U]-modules.
  - The edge exponents H_{s_1} and V_{s_n} at the ground ends are ≥ 1.
  - The B-levels are b(t) = -t(t+N)/(2N). I checked b(s) - b(s-N) = V_s - H_s = -s.
  - The graph together with the ground vertex is one cycle. The coker part is a single tower starting at the maximal peak M.
  - Ker part: each new edge lowers the count of non-ground components by 1, except exactly one edge at level M, which closes the cycle. So the tops are {y-1} with one copy of M-1 removed, n tops in all.
  - Comparison: class 0 has u = ±½N, …, ±(n/2)N. After one copy of the maximum is removed, every level with |u| ≥ 3N/2 is still doubled, and such levels exist because n ≥ 3. Class t has n+1 distinct peaks, so after the removal its n tops are distinct. Contradiction.
- **Not used.** The theorem of (III') itself (including its n = 1 analysis) is not used. Its §1–§3 computations are correct as re-derived above.

## 5. Cited theorems (from memory)
- **Gabai.** S^3_0(K) is irreducible for nontrivial K. Correct (Gabai 1987, the Property R paper).
- **GL87.** Gordon–Luecke, "Only integral Dehn surgeries can yield reducible manifolds" (1987). Correct.
- **Howie 2002** (J. Pure Appl. Algebra), proof of the Scott–Wiegold conjecture: a free product of three nontrivial cyclic groups is not the normal closure of one element. Correct, and it is used in exactly this form.
- **GL96.** Gordon–Luecke, "Reducible manifolds and Dehn surgery", Topology 35 (1996): a reducible surgery on a nontrivial knot in S^3 has a (nontrivial) lens-space summand. To my recollection this is a correct statement; it is proved via Scharlemann cycles and is cited this way in the later literature (e.g. Greene; Hom–Lidman–Zufelt). My confidence is moderately high, not certain. The chain needs only the weaker form "some summand is an L-space with |H_1| ≥ 2".
- **Ni / Ghiggini.** Knots whose knot Floer homology has rank 1 in the top Alexander grading are fibred, and L-space knots have this property (Ozsváth–Szabó). Correct.
- **Ozsváth–Szabó facts.**
  - The integer surgery mapping cone is a relatively graded quasi-isomorphism, with its truncation, in the plus and hat versions.
  - The affine labelling has the meridian acting by ±1; the sign is irrelevant here.
  - For staircases, A_s ≃ T^+ with v_s = U^{V_s} and h_s = U^{H_s}, H_s = V_{-s} = V_s + s. The reduction to homology-level maps is standard: pass through the free minus complexes, which are homotopy equivalent to F[U].
  - Künneth for CF^- and for ĤF.

  All of these are correct as used.
- **Consistency with the literature (recalled, uncertain).** Hom–Lidman–Zufelt (2015) show that a reducible surgery on an L-space knot has slope ±(2g-1) and is a lens space # (L-space homology sphere). If recalled correctly, this would give the same answer YES independently. The chain's intermediate conclusions are consistent with it.

## 6. Verdict
VERDICT: the chain proves the claim exactly as stated (given the cited theorems). The only defect is a wording imprecision in the p<0 truncation of (III) §4b; it is repaired in §4 above and does not affect the argument.

Answer to the problem: **YES.** Every 3-manifold obtained by Dehn surgery on an L-space knot has at most two prime summands. The bound is sharp, e.g. S^3_6(T(2,3)) = L(2,1) # L(3,2).

**Proved:** the full chain (0)–(III), modulo the cited published theorems listed in §5.

**Open:** nothing is open for the stated question. The only residual uncertainty is my recalled form of GL96, and the chain needs only the weak form stated in §5.

=== END OF ANSWER round6_q1 ===
# round6_q2 — referee report on the proof chain for entry 28 (answer YES)

Plan: check (0), (I), (II), (III), (III') line by line; then the external citations; then give the verdict.
Status: finished. All tasks 1–5 are done below.

## 1. The derivation (0)

- **Step 1.**
  - The unknot gives only S^3, S^1×S^2 and lens spaces.
  - Slope ∞ gives S^3. Slope 0 is irreducible by Gabai. Non-integral slopes are irreducible by GL87.
  - Irreducible closed 3-manifolds other than S^3 are prime.
  - The mirror reduction holds: S^3_r(mK) = −S^3_{−r}(K), and orientation reversal preserves the number of prime summands. If K has a nontrivial L-space surgery at slope r < 0, then mK has one at −r > 0. Afterwards both signs of p must be handled, and they are (I, II, III all treat p < 0).
  - The V_s facts for a positive L-space knot are the standard ones (staircase complex; V_{−s} = V_s + s by symmetry).
  - The case analysis is exhaustive: slopes ∞, 0, non-integral, nonzero integer.
- **Step 2.** Correct.
  - Each H_1(P_i) is a direct summand of Z/|p|, so it is finite cyclic. No summand can be S^1×S^2.
  - The map π1(Y) = *π1(P_i) → π1(P_1)*π1(P_2)*π1(P_3) → H_1(P_1)*H_1(P_2)*H_1(P_3) is onto.
  - π1(Y) is normally generated by μ, so the image is normally generated by one element. This contradicts Howie if all three H_1 are nontrivial.
  - Only finite cyclic factors occur, which is the case Howie proved.
  - So some prime summand B is a ZHS with B ≠ S^3.
- **Step 3.** Correct, given GL96.
  - The lens summand L is not S^1×S^2, since H_1(Y) is finite. So a = |H_1(L)| ≥ 2, and a divides |p| because H_1(L) is a direct summand of Z/|p|.
  - Lens spaces are L-spaces.
- **Step 4.** The hypotheses of (CB) hold: K is fibred with one-boundary fibre of genus g ≥ 1 (Ni/Ghiggini), p is a nonzero integer, and B is a ZHS ≠ S^3. So |p| ≤ g.
  - With |p| ≥ 2 this gives g ≥ 2, and then g < 2g−1.
  - The case g = 1 is closed here: |p| ≤ 1 contradicts |p| ≥ 2.
- **Step 5.** Prop 3.1 gives "p ≥ 2g−1 or |p| divides 2g−1". Since p ≤ |p| ≤ g < 2g−1, we get |p| | 2g−1, and |p| < 2g−1. It follows that |p| is odd.
- **Step 6.** All hypotheses of (E) hold:
  - K is a nontrivial positive L-space knot;
  - p ≠ 0, of either sign;
  - |p| divides 2g−1 and |p| < 2g−1;
  - L is an L-space of order a ≥ 2;
  - Y'' is arbitrary.

  The contradiction is valid.

## 2. Part (I), the Cover Bound — correct

**3.1 (the cover splits).**
- φ is trivial on π1(B°), because H_1(B) = 0. So B° lifts to N copies.
- φ|π1(A°) is the abelianisation π1(A) → H_1(A) ≅ Z/N. So q^{-1}(A°) = Ã minus N balls.
- The gluing pattern is a star, hence a tree. So Y_N ≅ Ã # N·B.
- Grushko–Neumann gives the rank formula.
- rank π1(B) ≥ 2: π1(B) is perfect, nontrivial (Poincaré conjecture), and so not cyclic.

**3.2 (the upper bound).** I checked each step.
- **The exterior lifts to a mapping torus.** φ|π1(M_K) factors through H_1(M_K) = Z → Z/N with μ ↦ 1. So E is the connected N-fold cyclic cover dual to F, i.e. the mapping torus of h^N.
- **T and V lift to single pieces.** T̃ is connected because φ(μ) generates. μ·α = μ·λ = ±1, so μ is isotopic in V to the core, and Ṽ is one solid torus whose meridian is β, a homeomorphic lift of α.
- **Intersection numbers.** For a degree-N cover of tori, f_*x·f_*y = N(x·y). Proof: f_*x·z = x·f^!z, where f^! is the transfer; and f^!f_*y = Ny, because deck translations of a torus act trivially on H_1.
- **The sign check.** F̃ maps homeomorphically to F, so F̃∩T̃ = λ̃ is a single curve with q_*λ̃ = λ. Hence N(β·λ̃) = α·λ = ±p, so β·λ̃ = ±1 for **both signs of p**.
- **Generation.** The fibration map sends β to ±1. So β = t^{±1}w with w ∈ π1(F̃), for any choice of basepoint path. In π1(Y_N) = π1(E)/⟨⟨β⟩⟩ the element t lies in the image of π1(F̃), so rank ≤ 2g.
- **(Minor wording.)** "One per fibre" in 3.2.6 is loose: F̃∩T̃ is a single curve. This is harmless.

**Sanity check (mine).** Take the cable C_{p,1}(T(2,3)). It is fibred, of genus p, and S^3_p of it is L(p,1) # S^3_{1/p}(T(2,3)). Here Ã = S^3 and the Brieskorn sphere has rank 2. CB gives 2p ≤ 2p, so the bound is tight and consistent.

**Remark 3.6 (Perelman-free variant).** The variant is also sound. β·λ̃ = ±1 gives an open book with page F̃; Haken additivity of Heegaard genus applies; and a ZHS other than S^3 has Heegaard genus ≥ 2.

## 3. Part (II), Lemma 2.1 and Prop 3.1 — correct

**Fibre invariance.**
- HF-hat(L,t) = F for an L-space, so ranks depend only on t'.
- The H_1(L)-orbits in Spin^c(L)×Spin^c(Y') are the fibres over t'.
- Under an affine labelling over the cyclic group Z/|p|, they are the cosets of the unique subgroup of order a, namely i + bZ. This holds whichever generator acts, so the sign convention is irrelevant.

**Hat cone.**
- Ĥ(A_s) ≅ ker(U on T^+) ≅ F. v̂_s ≠ 0 iff V_s = 0, and ĥ_s ≠ 0 iff s ≤ −g.

**Components for p > 0** (B_t is adjacent to A_t via v and to A_{t−p} via h):
- the isolated A_s with |s| < g;
- the isolated B_t with p−g < t < g;
- the triples with g ≤ t ≤ p−g;
- everything else in pairs.

For p ≤ 2g−2, the interval [−(g−1), p−g] has exactly p elements, one per class. So rank = 2n_i − 1.

**Components for p = −n.** B_t is adjacent to A_t and A_{t+n}. The isolated vertices are A_s with |s| < g and B_t with −g−n < t < g. The B-interval is [−(g−1)−n, −g] ∪ [−(g−1), g−1], and the first part holds one element per class. So rank = 2n_i + 1.

**Interval argument.** A proper nonempty cyclic interval has a unique start point, so it is invariant under no nontrivial translation. This also covers |p| > 2g−1 (q = 0, r = 2g−1). The conclusion "|p| | 2g−1 unless p ≥ 2g−1" is correct.

## 4. Parts (III)/(III'), Theorem (E) — correct

**Invariant.**
- The function k ↦ dim(M/UM)_k, taken up to translation, is an isomorphism invariant of graded F[U]-modules up to a shift. The tower contributes nothing.
- All finite summands lie in the A-part (see p < 0 below). So the relative shift between the A- and B-gradings in the cone is irrelevant.

**p > 0.**
- **Kernel.** Kernel elements are determined by the valleys A_{s_j}, |s_j| ≤ g−1, through the forced tail relations. The forced tail values eventually vanish because H_s and V_{−s} grow, so finite support is fine.
- **Exponents.** All exponents on the path are ≥ 1.
- **Positions.** I recomputed x(s) = s(s−p)/(2p) − V_s and the peak level y = s(s+p)/(2p).
- **Level graph.** At level k, an edge imposes a_j = a_{j+1} exactly when k ≥ y.
- **Cokernel of U.** U is restriction. New vertices are isolated, and in a path each new edge merges two components. So dim coker U at level k is #{peaks at level k+1}.
- **Comparison.**
  - Class 0 has m = ±(j+½)p for 0 ≤ j ≤ (n−3)/2: each level has even multiplicity, and n−1 ≥ 2.
  - Class t has distinct m². Equality would force 2t + (k+k'+1)N = 0, so N | t (N odd), i.e. t ≡ 0.

**p = −N < 0.**
- **Truncation.** I checked it directly. The middle piece M = {A_{s_1..s_n}, B_{s_1−N..s_n}} is a subcomplex, and C/M is the direct sum of the two tails. Each tail is acyclic (paired by isomorphisms; I checked injectivity and surjectivity for finitely supported chains). So M ≃ C.

# Referee report on chain A (round6_q3)

Plan: (1) check (0), (I), (II) line by line; (2) assess the cited shape theorem (S) and try to derive the weaker form from Howie (Scott–Wiegold) + Gordon–Luecke 1996; (3) give a verdict. Where (S) cannot be derived, supply a repair.

Summary of findings:
- (0), (I) and (II) are correct, for both signs of p. I found no errors, only a few cosmetic points.
- (S) in full, and even the weaker form "Y = A # B with A an L-space, |H_1(A)| = |p| >= 3, B a ZHS other than S^3", does **not** follow from (a) Howie and (b) Gordon–Luecke 1996 alone. Exactly one case is missing: two summands with nontrivial H_1. In that case GL96 makes one of them a lens space, but nothing makes the other an L-space.
- That case can be closed by a small generalisation (II') of part (II). (II') uses the "coset" invariance HF^+(Y,t+h) ≅ HF^+(Y,t) for h ∈ H_1(lens summand). That invariance is an immediate consequence of the connected-sum formula and the spin^c labelling of the surgery formula. With it, the claim is proved from correctly stated published theorems (cited from memory). However, the repaired chain no longer avoids GL96 or the coset step, so it is no longer independent of the main chain.

---

## 1. Check of the derivation (0)

- Step 1. Unknot surgeries give S^3, S^1×S^2 or lens spaces, all with at most one prime summand. ∞-surgery gives S^3. For nontrivial K, 0-surgery is irreducible (Gabai), so prime. Non-integral surgeries are irreducible (Gordon–Luecke 1987). Mirroring S^3_r(mK) = -S^3_{-r}(K) preserves the number of prime summands. So we may take K a nontrivial positive L-space knot and p a nonzero integer. Correct.
- Step 2 uses (S): r, s >= 2 coprime gives rs >= 6. Correct given (S).
- Step 3. A = L1 # L2 is an L-space: rank HF-hat is multiplicative and |H_1| is multiplicative. Y3 is a ZHS. So (II) applies. For p < 0 the hypothesis p < 2g-1 is automatic, so p < 0 is excluded outright; for p > 0 we get p >= 2g-1. Correct.
- Step 4. Ni: K is fibred, the fibre is a minimal-genus Seifert surface of genus g, and that g is the g in the V_s facts. CB with B = Y3 (a ZHS ≠ S^3) gives p <= g. Correct.
- Step 5. 2g-1 <= p <= g forces g <= 1, hence p <= 1 < 6. Contradiction. Correct.

**Conclusion:** (0) is a valid deduction from (S), (I) and (II).

## 2. Check of (I), the Cover Bound

I checked every step. All are correct. Notes:

- **3.1, step 5.** The connected N-fold cover of A° = A minus a ball, induced by π1(A) → Z/N, is Ã minus N balls: the ball is simply connected, so it lifts to N balls. Correct.
- **3.1, step 8.** π1(B) is perfect and nontrivial. A nontrivial perfect group is not cyclic, so rank >= 2. Correct. Here B may be the connected sum of all ZHS summands; that is fine.
- **3.2, step 3.** α·μ = ±1, so μ is a longitude of V and hence isotopic to its core. So π1(V) → Z/N is onto and Ṽ is a single solid torus. Correct.
- **3.2, step 5.** For a degree-N covering of tori, f_*a · f_*b = N(a·b), since det f_* = N. ∂F̃ maps homeomorphically to λ because F̃ → F is a homeomorphism. Then N(β·λ̃) = α·λ = ±p gives β·λ̃ = ±1. Correct for both signs.
- **3.2, step 6.** Cosmetic: the fibration E → S^1 restricts on T̃ to a circle fibration with fibres the curves ∂F̃_θ. The induced map π1(T̃) → Z is algebraic intersection with **one** fibre λ̃, not with "a union of parallel copies". The conclusion π(β) = ±1 is right. Since ker π = π1(F̃), β represents t^{±1}w with w ∈ π1(F̃). Correct.
- **3.2, step 7.** Filling kills β, so t ≡ w^{∓1} and π1(Y_N) is a quotient of the free group π1(F̃) of rank 2g. Correct.
- **3.3.** 2N <= N·rank π1(B) <= 2g gives |p| = N <= g. Correct for both signs. Nothing in the argument uses the sign of p.
- **3.6 (Perelman-free variant).** Since β·λ̃ = ±1, the filling is an open book with page F̃, giving a genus-2g Heegaard splitting. Haken additivity, plus the classification of manifolds of Heegaard genus <= 1, gives h(B) >= 2 (B is a prime-decomposition piece ≠ S^3 with finite H_1). Correct.

## 3. Check of (II), the Heegaard Floer theorem

**§0 (reduction).** For an L-space L, CF^-(L,s) is a free complex with homology F[U], so it is homotopy equivalent to F[U]. By the Künneth formula, HF^+(L#Y', s#t) ≅ HF^+(Y',t) up to grading shift. Since H_1(Y') = 0, all |p| classes have isomorphic HF^+ up to shift.

The invariants used are:
- the degree of the tower bottom;
- the multiset of tops of finite summands, read off from M/UM (T^+ is U-divisible, so it contributes nothing to M/UM).

Under a shift, these are translated. The number of finite summands and the multiplicity pattern are therefore invariants. Correct.

**§1 (level model).** A map U^e from a tower with bottom x preserves levels iff the target bottom is x + e. Checked. The exponents used are V_s (s <= g-1) and H_s = V_{-s} (s >= -(g-1)), all >= 1. Hence every B present at level k has both adjacent A's present. "Ground" edges arise only at the truncated ends. Correct.

**§2 (p > 0, p < 2g-1).** All points check:
- D is surjective, so H = ker D.
- Truncation. Values outside [-(g-1), g-1] are forced recursively:
  - Going up from s >= g lands in [g-p, g-1] ⊂ [-(g-1), g-1].
  - Going down from s <= -g lands in [-(g-1), p-g] ⊂ [-(g-1), g-1].
  - No B_s has both V_s = 0 and H_{s-p} = 0: that would need p >= 2g.
  - Kernel elements are finitely supported, since the exponents grow.
  - So ker D is the path model. Correct.
- x(s) = s(s-p)/(2p) - V_s satisfies the recursion; verified by direct substitution. The peak is y = s(s+p)/(2p) = (m^2 - p^2/4)/(2p). Correct.
- Module structure. U acts as restriction H^0(G_{k+1}) → H^0(G_k). New vertices at level k+1 are isolated. Each new edge joins distinct components (subforest of a path), so dim(M/UM)_k = #{peaks at level k+1}. Tops are at y-1; there are n-1 finite summands. Correct.
- Counting. 2g-1 consecutive integers and p < 2g-1 give n_i >= 1 for every class, and the n_i are all equal iff p | 2g-1. Then p and n are odd and n >= 3.
- Class 0 peaks are symmetric (m ↦ -m), so all multiplicities are even.
- Class 1: m = -m' would need 2 + (k+k'+1)p = 0, which is impossible for p >= 3. So class 1 has n-1 >= 2 distinct values. Contradiction. Correct.

**§3 (p = -q < 0).** I re-derived the truncation as follows.
- Q1 = {A_s, B_s : s >= g} and Q2 = {A_s : s <= -g} ∪ {B_t : t <= -g-q} are quotient complexes. Their complement, the middle part, is a subcomplex.
- Q1 and Q2 do not interact.
- Each is acyclic: it is triangular with invertible diagonal (v_s, resp. h_s, are the identity on T^+), and a finitely supported right-hand side can be solved recursively.
- So H(cone) ≅ H(middle).

The middle part per class is ground – B_{s_1-q} – A_{s_1} – … – A_{s_n} – B_{s_n} – ground: n A's and n+1 B's. If n = 0 it is exactly one B. Checked.

H = ker D ⊕ coker D as F[U]-modules holds automatically for a two-term complex; the parity remark is not even needed.

Further checks:
- x(s) = -s(s+q)/(2q) - V_s and b(t) = -t(t+q)/(2q): verified.
- Coker part: H^1 of a subgraph of a cycle, giving a single tower with bottom at the maximal peak M. U is an isomorphism there.
- Ker part = H^0(X_k, ground). Each new edge imposes one independent condition, except that the increase of b_1 at level M removes exactly one: in Euler-characteristic terms, (#new edges) − Δb_1. So the tops are {y-1}, with one copy of M-1 removed. Each A carries exactly one bottom, so there are n finite summands.
- If q > 2g-1, the n_i take both values 0 and 1. Otherwise they are equal iff q | 2g-1.
- n >= 3: class 0 has a repeated top, class 1 has none. Correct.
- n = 1: class t's finite top lies |t|+1 levels below the tower bottom. Check: the two peaks differ by ((t+q/2)^2 - (t-q/2)^2)/(2q) = t. So class 0 and class 1 differ.
- This offset is an invariant of relatively graded modules: real degrees are 2·level, with one uniform odd shift for B-type elements, the same in every class. Correct.

**Extension to |p| = 2 (used below).**
- p = 2 < 2g-1 (g >= 2): 2 ∤ 2g-1, so the n_i differ.
- p = -2: either q = 2 > 2g-1 (g = 1), giving n_i ∈ {0,1} with both values occurring, or 2 ∤ 2g-1.

So the Theorem of (II) holds verbatim for |p| >= 2.

**Verdict on (I) and (II):** correct as stated, given the cited Heegaard Floer tools: the integer surgery formula with relative gradings, the V_s facts for L-space knots, and the Künneth formula.

## 4. The shape theorem (S): what the literature gives (from memory)

All statements in this section are from memory, and I flag my confidence.

- **Gordon–Luecke 1987** (confident): reducible surgeries on knots in S^3 have integral slope.
- **Gordon–Luecke 1996**, "Reducible manifolds and Dehn surgery", Topology 35 (confident): if surgery on a nontrivial knot in S^3 is reducible, it has a lens-space summand (≠ S^3, S^1×S^2). In particular, ±1-surgeries (ZHS) are irreducible.
- **Howie 2002**, JPAA 173 (confident): proves the Scott–Wiegold conjecture — a free product of three nontrivial cyclic groups is not the normal closure of one element.
- **Howie**, "Can Dehn surgery yield three connected summands?" (≈2010) (moderately confident): if some surgery with parameter r on K yields more than two summands, then |r| is bounded in terms of the bridge number b, I believe |r| <= b-2. I believe its introduction records the known consequence that such a surgery has the form "two lens spaces # a ZHS". I cannot reliably recall whether the "both are lens spaces" part is proved there, or in Valdez-Sánchez or Sayari (Sayari, JKTR ≈2009, bounds the slope of a reducible surgery by the bridge number). So **the attribution of (S) is unverified**.
- **Hom–Lidman–Zufelt**, "Reducible surgeries and Heegaard Floer homology" (MRL ≈2015) (moderately confident): if an L-space knot has a reducible surgery S^3_p(K), then p = 2g(K)-1. I do not reliably recall what they state about the number or type of summands. If it is as I recall, the CB argument of (I) closes the problem at once: p = 2g-1 <= g gives g <= 1, so p = 1, which GL96 excludes. But I do not rely on this.

### 4.1 What (a) Howie and (b) GL96 give

**Lemma 1.** Let K be nontrivial and Y = S^3_p(K), p ≠ 0, with prime decomposition Y = Y_1 # … # Y_k, k >= 3. Then:
1. at most two Y_i have nontrivial H_1, and those that do have cyclic H_1 of coprime orders whose product is |p|;
2. at least one Y_i is a ZHS ≠ S^3;
3. at least one Y_i is a lens space L(r,·) with r >= 2, and |p| >= 2.

*Proof.*
- H_1(Y) = Z/|p| = ⊕ H_1(Y_i), so each H_1(Y_i) is cyclic, and their orders are coprime with product |p|. No summand is S^1×S^2, since H_1(Y) is finite.
- π1(Y) is the normal closure of one element, the core of the filling (equivalently, the image of the meridian μ, since π1(S^3 \ K) is normally generated by μ). Normal generation by one element passes to quotients. π1(Y) = *π1(Y_i) surjects onto *H_1(Y_i).
- If three of the H_1(Y_i) were nontrivial, then projecting away the other factors gives a quotient that is a free product of three nontrivial cyclic groups normally generated by one element. This contradicts (a). This proves 1.
- Since k >= 3, some Y_i has H_1 = 0. It is ≠ S^3 because it is a prime-decomposition piece. This proves 2.
- 3 is (b), and r >= 2 gives |p| >= 2. ∎

**Consequences.**
- **Case α: exactly one summand has nontrivial H_1.** It must be the GL lens space L, with |H_1(L)| = |p|. Then Y = L # B with B the connected sum of the others, a ZHS ≠ S^3. This is the needed weaker form, except that |p| may be 2; §3 shows (II) also covers |p| = 2.
- **Case β: exactly two summands Y_1, Y_2 have nontrivial H_1,** of coprime orders r, s >= 2. GL96 makes one of them, say Y_1, a lens space. **Nothing in (a), (b) and standard facts makes Y_2 an L-space** (or a lens space). The weaker form needs A = Y_1 # Y_2 to be an L-space, so it is not obtained.
  - Taking A = Y_1 alone fails, because |H_1(Y_1)| = r < |p|.
  - Taking A = Y_1 # Y_2 needs Y_2 to be an L-space.

  So in case β, (S) — specifically "L2 is a lens space" — is used essentially and is not derivable from (a) and (b). **This is the gap.**
- **Case γ:** no summand has nontrivial H_1, so |p| = 1. Excluded by GL96.

### 4.2 Repair of case β

Proving Y_2 is a lens space is not needed. The ingredient is invariance of HF^+ under translation by H_1(Y_1).

**Lemma 2 (coset invariance).** If Y = L # Y'' with L a lens space of order r, then HF^+(Y, t+h) ≅ HF^+(Y,t) up to shift for every h ∈ H^2(L) ⊂ H^2(Y).

*Proof.* Spin^c(Y) = Spin^c(L) × Spin^c(Y''), equivariantly for H^2(Y) = H^2(L) ⊕ H^2(Y''). Adding h changes only the L-component. HF^+(L,·) ≅ T^+ for every spin^c structure, and the Künneth formula applies as in (II) §0. ∎

In the Ozsváth–Szabó cone, label i ∈ Z/p corresponds to a spin^c structure t_i, and i ↦ t_i is affine over an isomorphism Z/p ≅ H^2(Y) taking 1 to a generator: consecutive labels differ by the restriction of the generator of H^2(W) = Z, which restricts to a generator of H^2(Y). (Cited from memory, standard.)

The subgroup H^2(L) of order r is the multiples of s := |p|/r. So in case β: **HF^+(Y,i) ≅ HF^+(Y,i+s) up to shift for all i, with s | p and 2 <= s <= |p|/2.**

**Theorem (II').** Let K be a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g, and p a nonzero integer with p < 2g-1. Let s | p with 0 < s < |p|. Then it is not true that HF^+(S^3_p(K), i) ≅ HF^+(S^3_p(K), i+s) up to shift for every i.

*Proof.* Reuse the computations of (II).

1. **The counts n_i must be s-invariant.** n_i takes at most two values. The set of classes with the larger value is an arc of length ℓ = (2g-1) mod |p|, or, when -p > 2g-1, an arc of length 2g-1. An arc of length 0 < ℓ < |p| in Z/|p| is not invariant under a nonzero translation, since its first element would be moved. So ℓ = 0, i.e. |p| divides 2g-1, and |p| and n = (2g-1)/|p| are odd.
2. **p > 0.** Here n >= 3. Compare class 0 with class s. The peaks of class s are m = s + (k+1/2)p. A coincidence m = -m' would need p | 2s, hence p | s since p is odd, which is impossible. So class s has n-1 >= 2 distinct tops, while class 0 has only even multiplicities. Contradiction.
3. **p = -q < 0, n >= 3.** The same argument applies with u = s + (k+1/2)q: class 0 has a repeated top and class s does not.
4. **p = -q < 0, n = 1.** Class s's finite top is s+1 >= 2 levels below the tower bottom, while class 0's is 1 level below. (Here 0 < s <= q/3 < q/2, so s is the representative of the class.) Contradiction. ∎

**Theorem (YES).** Every manifold obtained by Dehn surgery on an L-space knot in S^3 has at most two prime summands.

*Proof.* Reduce as in (0), step 1, and suppose k >= 3 prime summands.
- Lemma 1 gives a ZHS ≠ S^3 summand B and |p| >= 2.
- Ni and CB give 2 <= |p| <= g, so g >= 2 and p <= g < 2g-1.
- Case α: by (II), extended to |p| >= 2 in §3, with A the lens space, this is impossible.
- Case β: by Lemmas 1 and 2 and (II'), with s = |p|/r, this is impossible.
- Case γ is excluded by GL96. ∎

Cited (from memory): Gabai; GL87; GL96; Howie (Scott–Wiegold); Ni; Perelman (or Haken plus the Heegaard genus <= 1 classification); the OS integer surgery formula with relative gradings and its spin^c labelling; the Künneth formula; the V_s facts for L-space knots.

This repaired chain is complete given these citations, but it uses GL96 and the coset step. So it is essentially the main chain's route (with CB), and not the independent confirmation chain A was meant to be.

## 5. Status

- **Proved here (given the citations):**
  - correctness of (0), (I) and (II);
  - extension of (II) to |p| = 2;
  - Lemma 1, Lemma 2 and Theorem (II');
  - hence the answer YES, by the repaired argument in 4.2.
- **Not established:** that (S), or its weaker form, follows from Howie + GL96. It does not in case β, and I cannot confirm from memory that (S) is a published theorem, or who proved it.
- **Open (for chain A as an independent route):** whether in case β the second non-ZHS summand must be a lens space (or an L-space) for a surgery on a knot in S^3.

VERDICT: gap — chain A is correct given (S), but (S), and even its weaker form, is not derivable from Howie's Scott–Wiegold theorem together with Gordon–Luecke 1996. Its attribution could not be verified. The gap is case β: two non-ZHS summands, where only one is known to be a lens space. It is closed in §4.2 by the coset invariance (Lemma 2) and the generalisation (II'). That yields a complete proof of YES, but not one independent of GL96 and the coset step.

    20	## 1. p = ±1 is impossible
    21	Y would be an integer homology sphere. A lens summand of order a ≥ 2 would make |H_1(Y)| divisible by a, which is impossible. So |p| ≥ 2.
    22	
    23	## 2. Fibre invariance
    24	Write Y = L # Y' with |H_1(L)| = a ≥ 2 and |H_1(Y')| = b. Then ab = |p| and gcd(a,b) = 1.
    25	
    26	Each lens space has HF-hat(L,t) = F. So rank HF-hat(Y,(t,t')) = rank HF-hat(Y',t') does not depend on t. Likewise HF^+(Y,(t,t')) ≅ HF^+(Y',t') up to a grading shift of d(L,t).

    32	## 3. Hat ranks (this proves the planner's hint, and the negative-slope analogue)

    40	- {A_s} for |s| < g;
    41	- {B_t} for p−g < t < g;

# Surgery on an L-space knot has at most two prime summands

## Answer

**Yes.** Throughout, "L-space knot" means a knot K in S^3 such that some surgery S^3_r(K) with r ∈ Q is an L-space. The answer covers every slope r ∈ Q ∪ {∞}.

**Theorem.** Let K ⊂ S^3 be an L-space knot and r ∈ Q ∪ {∞}. Then S^3_r(K) has at most two prime summands.

The bound is sharp. By Moser, S^3_6(T(2,3)) ≅ L(2,1) # L(3,2), which has two summands. More generally, an L-space cable C_{a,b}(J) gives L(a,b) # S^3_{b/a}(J) at the cabling slope ab.

**Status.** The proof below is complete, given the published theorems listed in §0. Those theorems are cited from memory, and their exact wording was not checked against the sources. During the run, two independent referee passes checked the whole chain (§§1–5), for both signs of the slope, and found no substantive gap. The one citation recalled with less than full certainty is the wording and attribution of Gordon–Luecke 1996 (§0, item 4). Only the weak form stated there is used. Nothing beyond the citations is left open. §7 describes other routes, and §8 lists the dependencies.

---

## 0. Conventions and cited results

F = Z/2. Here M_K is the exterior of K, μ and λ are its meridian and Seifert longitude, and g = g(K).

**Mirroring.** S^3_r(mK) ≅ −S^3_{−r}(K), and reversing orientation does not change the number of prime summands. If K has a nontrivial L-space surgery at a negative slope, then mK has one at a positive slope. So we may assume K is a *positive* L-space knot, meaning it has an L-space surgery at some positive slope. The slope p is then an arbitrary integer of either sign, and both signs are treated below.

Cited theorems (from memory):

1. **Gabai (1987).** For a nontrivial knot K, S^3_0(K) is irreducible.
2. **Gordon–Luecke (1987).** If S^3_r(K) is reducible for a nontrivial K, then r is an integer.
3. **Howie (2002), the Scott–Wiegold conjecture.** A free product of three nontrivial cyclic groups is not the normal closure of a single element.
4. **Gordon–Luecke (1996), "Reducible manifolds and Dehn surgery".** If a surgery on a nontrivial knot in S^3 is reducible, one of its prime summands is a lens space other than S^3 and S^1×S^2. *Only this weak consequence is used:* some prime summand L is an L-space with |H_1(L)| ≥ 2.
5. **Ni; Ghiggini (for g = 1).** An L-space knot is fibred. Its fibre is a minimal-genus Seifert surface F, of genus g, with one boundary component.
6. **Grushko–Neumann.** rank(G_1 * G_2) = rank G_1 + rank G_2 for finitely generated groups. Also van Kampen: π_1(M_1 # M_2) ≅ π_1(M_1) * π_1(M_2).
7. **Perelman.** A closed simply connected 3-manifold is S^3. This can be avoided; see Remark 3.4.
8. **Ozsváth–Szabó surgery package.** Let K be a positive L-space knot of genus g ≥ 1 and p ≠ 0 an integer.
   - (a) *Integers V_s.* There are integers V_s (s ∈ Z) with V_s ≥ 0, V_s − V_{s+1} ∈ {0,1}, V_s = 0 iff s ≥ g, and V_{−s} = V_s + s. Put H_s := V_{−s}, so H_s = 0 iff s ≤ −g.
   - (b) *Integer surgery mapping cone, plus version.* Spin^c(S^3_p(K)) is labelled by Z/|p|. For each label i, HF^+(S^3_p(K), i) is isomorphic, as a relatively graded F[U]-module, to the homology of the cone of D = Σ(v_s + h_s): ⊕_{s≡i} A_s^+ → ⊕_{s≡i} B_s^+ (direct sums). Here v_s: A_s → B_s and h_s: A_s → B_{s+p}, and these maps are homogeneous. For a positive L-space knot, H_*(A_s^+) ≅ H_*(B_s^+) ≅ T^+ := F[U,U^{−1}]/U·F[U]. On homology, v_s = U^{V_s} and h_s = U^{H_s}. The cone may be computed from these homology-level maps, because T^+ is an injective F[U]-module.
   - (c) *Hat version.* The same holds for ĤF with Â_s, B̂_s: each has homology F, v̂_s is nonzero (an isomorphism) iff V_s = 0, and ĥ_s is nonzero iff H_s = 0. (This follows from (b): Â = ker U, and the map induced on the bottom element of T^+ is U^{V_s}, resp. U^{H_s}.) Over a field the cone is determined by these homology-level maps.
   - (d) *Affine labelling.* The labelling Spin^c(S^3_p(K)) ↔ Z/|p| is affine over H_1(S^3_p(K)) = Z/|p| = ⟨[μ]⟩, and [μ] acts by i ↦ i+1. The sign convention does not matter below.
   - (e) *Connected sums.* Spin^c(Y_1 # Y_2) = Spin^c(Y_1) × Spin^c(Y_2), equivariantly for H_1(Y_1) ⊕ H_1(Y_2). Also CF^−(Y_1#Y_2,(t_1,t_2)) ≃ CF^−(Y_1,t_1) ⊗_{F[U]} CF^−(Y_2,t_2), and ĤF(Y_1#Y_2) ≅ ĤF(Y_1) ⊗ ĤF(Y_2) on each spin^c structure. If L is an L-space, then CF^−(L,t) ≃ F[U], so HF^+(L#Y'',(t,t'')) ≅ HF^+(Y'',t'') as relatively graded F[U]-modules up to a shift, and rank ĤF(L#Y'',(t,t'')) = rank ĤF(Y'',t''). Lens spaces are L-spaces.

---

## 1. Reduction

Suppose S^3_r(K) has at least three prime summands. We derive a contradiction.

- If K is the unknot, its surgeries are S^3, S^1×S^2 and lens spaces, each with at most one prime summand.
- So K is nontrivial. Slope ∞ gives S^3, and slope 0 gives an irreducible manifold by Gabai.
- By Gordon–Luecke 1987, a non-integral slope also gives an irreducible manifold. An irreducible closed 3-manifold other than S^3 is prime.

So r = p is a nonzero integer. After mirroring (§0), K is a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g ≥ 1 and p ≠ 0 has either sign. Write

  Y = S^3_p(K) = P_1 # ⋯ # P_k, with every P_i prime and k ≥ 3.

H_1(Y) = Z/|p| is finite. So no P_i is S^1×S^2, and each H_1(P_i) is a direct summand of Z/|p|, hence finite cyclic.

## 2. Two topological consequences

**Lemma 2.1 (a homology-sphere summand).** Some P_i is an integer homology sphere B ≠ S^3.

*Proof.*
- π_1(M_K) is normally generated by μ, and π_1(Y) is a quotient of it, so π_1(Y) is normally generated by one element.
- Suppose three summands, say P_1, P_2, P_3, had nontrivial H_1. Then π_1(Y) = π_1(P_1) * ⋯ * π_1(P_k) maps onto π_1(P_1) * π_1(P_2) * π_1(P_3), by killing the other factors, and then onto H_1(P_1) * H_1(P_2) * H_1(P_3).
- That target is a free product of three nontrivial cyclic groups, and it is normally generated by the image of one element. This contradicts Howie's theorem.
- So at most two summands have nontrivial H_1. Since k ≥ 3, some P_i has H_1 = 0, and P_i ≠ S^3 because it is a prime summand. ∎

Write Y ≅ A # B, where B is this homology sphere and A is the sum of the other summands.

**Lemma 2.2 (an L-space summand).** Y ≅ L # Y'', where L is a lens space with a := |H_1(L)| ≥ 2. Hence a divides |p| and |p| ≥ 2.

*Proof.* By Gordon–Luecke 1996 (weak form), some prime summand is a lens space L ≠ S^3, S^1×S^2, so a ≥ 2. Also H_1(L) is a direct summand of Z/|p|. ∎

## 3. The cover bound

**Proposition 3.1 (cover bound).** Let K ⊂ S^3 be fibred with fibre F of genus g and one boundary component, and let p ≠ 0 be an integer. If S^3_p(K) ≅ A # B with B an integer homology sphere other than S^3, then

  |p|·rank π_1(B) + rank π_1(Ã) ≤ 2g, and hence |p| ≤ g.

Here N := |p| and Ã is the connected N-fold cyclic cover of A defined below.

*Setup.*
- Y = S^3_p(K) = M_K ∪_T V, where the meridian disc of the solid torus V is bounded by α = pμ + λ on T = ∂M_K.
- H_1(M_K) = Z⟨μ⟩. The class of a loop is its algebraic intersection number with F, and λ = 0 in H_1(M_K). So H_1(Y) = Z/N.
- Let φ: π_1(Y) → H_1(Y) = Z/N be the abelianisation, which is onto, and let q: Y_N → Y be the connected N-fold cyclic cover with group ker φ.

**3.2 Lower bound: Y_N ≅ Ã # (N copies of B).**
1. Let S be the splitting sphere, so Y = A° ∪_S B°, where ° means one open ball removed.
2. π_1(Y) = π_1(A) * π_1(B), and H_1(A) = H_1(Y) ≅ Z/N because H_1(B) = 0.
3. φ restricted to π_1(B°) = π_1(B) factors through H_1(B) = 0. So q^{−1}(B°) is N disjoint copies of B°, each mapped homeomorphically onto B°.
4. S is simply connected, so q^{−1}(S) is N spheres.
5. φ restricted to π_1(A°) = π_1(A) is the surjection π_1(A) → H_1(A) ≅ Z/N. So q^{−1}(A°) is connected: it is the induced N-fold cyclic cover Ã of A with N balls removed (the removed ball lifts to N balls).
6. Y_N is therefore Ã minus N balls, with a copy of B° glued to each boundary sphere. The gluing graph is a star, hence a tree, so Y_N ≅ Ã # B # ⋯ # B with N copies of B.
7. By van Kampen and Grushko–Neumann, rank π_1(Y_N) = rank π_1(Ã) + N·rank π_1(B).
8. π_1(B) is perfect (H_1(B) = 0) and nontrivial (Perelman, since B ≠ S^3). A nontrivial cyclic group has nontrivial abelianisation, so π_1(B) is not cyclic, and rank π_1(B) ≥ 2.

If N = 1 the cover is trivial and Ã = A. Nothing changes.

**3.3 Upper bound: rank π_1(Y_N) ≤ 2g.**
1. *The exterior lifts to a mapping torus.* On π_1(M_K), φ is the composite π_1(M_K) → H_1(M_K) = Z → Z/N with μ ↦ 1. So E := q^{−1}(M_K) is connected and is the N-fold cyclic cover dual to F. It is the mapping torus of h^N, where h is the monodromy, and it fibres over S^1 with fibre F̃, a homeomorphic lift of F. So π_1(E) = π_1(F̃) ⋊ ⟨t⟩, and the fibration map π: π_1(E) → Z has kernel π_1(F̃) and sends t ↦ 1.
2. *The boundary lifts to one torus.* μ ∈ π_1(T) maps onto a generator of Z/N. So T̃ := q^{−1}(T) is one torus, and q|: T̃ → T has degree N.
3. *The solid torus lifts to one solid torus.* μ meets α once, so μ is isotopic in V to the core of V. Hence π_1(V) maps onto Z/N, and Ṽ = q^{−1}(V) is one solid torus with ∂Ṽ = T̃.
4. *The filling curve.* The meridian disc of V lifts to N discs. Let β ⊂ T̃ be the boundary of one of them. Then q maps β homeomorphically onto α, so q_*[β] = [α]. Y_N = E ∪ Ṽ is the Dehn filling of E along β.
5. *Intersection numbers.* For a degree-N covering f: T̃ → T of tori, f_*x · f_*y = N(x·y). This follows from the transfer f^!: f_*x·z = x·f^!z and f^! f_* = N, since deck transformations of a torus act trivially on H_1.
   - F̃ ∩ T̃ = ∂F̃ is a single curve λ̃ with q_*[λ̃] = [λ].
   - Hence N(β·λ̃) = α·λ = (pμ+λ)·λ = ±p, so β·λ̃ = ±1. This holds for either sign of p.
6. *β goes once around.* On π_1(T̃), the map π is algebraic intersection with the fibre boundary λ̃. So π(β) = ±1, and β represents t^{±1}w for some w ∈ π_1(F̃), for any choice of basepoint path.
7. *Conclusion.* By van Kampen, π_1(Y_N) = π_1(E)/⟨⟨β⟩⟩. In this quotient t = w^{∓1} lies in the image of π_1(F̃). So π_1(Y_N) is generated by the image of π_1(F̃), which is free of rank 2g, and rank π_1(Y_N) ≤ 2g.

Combining 3.2 and 3.3: 2N ≤ N·rank π_1(B) ≤ rank π_1(Y_N) ≤ 2g, so |p| ≤ g. ∎

*Sanity checks.*
- T(2,3) with p = 1 gives the Poincaré sphere, and the bound is tight: 2 = 2.
- The cable C_{p,1}(J), with p ≥ 2 and J nontrivial, has p-surgery L(p,1) # S^3_{1/p}(J). Its genus is p·g(J) ≥ p, which is consistent with the bound.

**Remark 3.4 (avoiding Perelman).** Replace rank by Heegaard genus h.
- Since β·λ̃ = ±1, Y_N is the closed manifold of an open book with page F̃, so h(Y_N) ≤ 2g.
- By Haken's lemma, h(Y_N) = h(Ã) + N·h(B).
- h(B) ≥ 2, since closed manifolds of Heegaard genus ≤ 1 are S^3, S^1×S^2 and lens spaces.

## 4. Heegaard Floer input

In this section K is a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g, and p ≠ 0. Suppose S^3_p(K) ≅ L # Y'', where L is an L-space with a = |H_1(L)| ≥ 2. If the homeomorphism reverses orientation, replace (L, Y'') by (−L, −Y''); −L is again an L-space of the same order. Put b := |p|/a, which is not ≡ 0 mod |p|.

**Lemma 4.1 (coset invariance).** For every label i, HF^+(S^3_p(K), i) ≅ HF^+(S^3_p(K), i+b) as relatively graded F[U]-modules up to a degree shift. Also rank ĤF(S^3_p(K), i) = rank ĤF(S^3_p(K), i+b).

*Proof.*
- H_1(L) is the unique subgroup of order a in Z/|p| = ⟨[μ]⟩, namely ⟨b[μ]⟩.
- By 8(e), the spin^c structures with a fixed Y''-component t'' form one H_1(L)-orbit, and they all have HF^+ ≅ HF^+(Y'',t'') up to shift (resp. hat rank equal to rank ĤF(Y'',t'')).
- By 8(d), the H_1(L)-orbits are exactly the cosets i + bZ of labels. ∎

For a label class i, let n_i := #{s ≡ i (mod |p|) : |s| ≤ g−1}.

**Proposition 4.2 (hat ranks).**
- If 0 < p ≤ 2g−2, then rank ĤF(S^3_p(K), i) = 2n_i − 1.
- If p ≥ 2g−1, the rank is 1 for every class.
- If p = −n < 0, the rank is 2n_i + 1.

*Proof.* By 8(c), the hat cone in class i is a graph complex with one copy of F at each vertex. Each edge is either an isomorphism or zero. A finite connected component in which every edge is an isomorphism, A's mapping to B's, contributes homology of rank 1 if it has an odd number of vertices and 0 if even.

*Case p > 0.*
- The edge A_s–B_s (v̂_s) is present iff s ≥ g. The edge A_s–B_{s+p} (ĥ_s) is present iff s ≤ −g.
- The components are:
  - isolated A_s with |s| < g;
  - isolated B_t with p−g < t < g (neither v̂_t nor ĥ_{t−p} is present);
  - triples {A_{t−p}, B_t, A_t} with g ≤ t ≤ p−g (rank 1);
  - everything else in pairs (rank 0).
- So rank = n_i + #{t ≡ i : p−g < t < g} + #{t ≡ i : g ≤ t ≤ p−g}.
- If p ≥ 2g−1, every class gets rank 1, since the 2g−1+... count telescopes: [−(g−1), g−1] = [−(g−1), p−g] ∪ ... reduces to one surviving vertex per class.
- If p ≤ 2g−2, the third set is empty. [−(g−1), p−g] contains exactly one element of each class, so #{t ≡ i in (p−g, g−1]} = n_i − 1, and rank = 2n_i − 1.

*Case p = −n < 0.* Now h_s goes to B_{s−n}.
- The edge B_{s−n}–A_s is present iff s ≤ −g, and A_s–B_s iff s ≥ g. Everything else pairs off.
- The isolated vertices are A_s with |s| < g, and B_t with −g−n < t < g.
- The interval (−g−n, g) is [−(g−1)−n, −g] ∪ [−(g−1), g−1], and the first part holds one element per class. So rank = n_i + (n_i + 1). ∎

(The case p ≥ 2g−1 is not used below. The reader may check it directly from the component list.)

**Proposition 4.3 (divisibility).** If S^3_p(K) ≅ L # Y'' with L an L-space of order a ≥ 2, then p ≥ 2g−1 or |p| divides 2g−1.

*Proof.*
- Suppose p < 2g−1. By 4.2 the hat rank is a strictly increasing function of n_i.
- Write 2g−1 = Q|p| + r with 0 ≤ r < |p|. The integers in [−(g−1), g−1] are 2g−1 consecutive integers. So n_i = Q+1 on a set S of r cyclically consecutive residues, and n_i = Q elsewhere.
- By Lemma 4.1 the hat rank is invariant under i ↦ i+b, so S is invariant under translation by b ≢ 0.
- If 0 < r < |p|, then S is a proper nonempty cyclic interval. It has exactly one start point (x ∈ S with x−1 ∉ S), and a translation preserving S must fix that start point. That is impossible for b ≢ 0.
- So r = 0, i.e. |p| divides 2g−1. ∎

**Theorem 4.4 (Theorem E).** Let K be a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g, and p a nonzero integer with |p| dividing 2g−1 and |p| < 2g−1. Then S^3_p(K) is not homeomorphic to L # Y'' for any L-space L with |H_1(L)| ≥ 2 and any closed oriented 3-manifold Y''.

*Proof.* Let N := |p| and n := (2g−1)/N. Both are odd, and n ≥ 3. Suppose such a splitting exists.

**(i) The invariant.** Every module below has the form M = T^+ ⊕ ⊕_l F[U]/U^{e_l}.
- The number of finite summands whose top lies in degree k is dim coker(U: M_{k+1} → M_k). The tower contributes nothing, since U is onto on T^+.
- So the multiset of top degrees of the finite summands is an isomorphism invariant, and a degree shift translates it.
- Let t be the representative of b with 0 < |t| ≤ (N−1)/2; this exists since N is odd. By Lemma 4.1, labels 0 and t have isomorphic HF^+ up to shift. Hence:

  (★) the top multisets of classes 0 and t agree up to a translation.

**(ii) Arithmetic.**
- For |c| ≤ (N−1)/2, the elements s ≡ c with |s| ≤ g−1 are exactly c + kN for |k| ≤ (n−1)/2. Indeed |c+kN| ≤ (N−1)/2 + (n−1)N/2 = g−1, while |k| = (n+1)/2 gives |c+kN| ≥ (nN+1)/2 > g−1.
- *Key fact.* Let u = c + (k+½)N and u' = c + (k'+½)N with k ≠ k'. If u² = u'², then u = −u', so 2c + (k+k'+1)N = 0. Hence N | 2c, and N | c since N is odd, so c = 0. Thus for c = t all the values u² are distinct.

**(iii) Level model.** Use 8(b). Record each tower T^+ by its *bottom level*; U lowers level by 1. Regrade each B so that the cone maps preserve levels. A map U^e from a tower with bottom x then lands in a tower with bottom x+e. Under this regrading:
- an A-element at level k maps to the B-element at level k in each adjacent B present at level k;
- a B is "present at level k" iff its bottom is ≤ k;
- since all exponents are ≥ 0, every present B has its adjacent A's present.

At level k the cone map is therefore the coboundary δ_k: F^{vertices} → F^{edges} of a graph G_k. Its vertices are the A's with bottom ≤ k, and its edges are the B's with bottom ≤ k, each B joining its adjacent A's. U acts on the A-part (kernel) by restriction from G_{k+1} to G_k. The cone's relative grading is homogeneous, so all B-levels are shifted from A-levels by one uniform amount, the same in every class.

**(iv) Case p > 0.**
- In class c, the A's and B's form one infinite path ⋯ A_{s−p} — B_s — A_s — B_{s+p} — ⋯. The bottoms solve x(s+p) − x(s) = H_s − V_{s+p} (B_{s+p} receives U^{H_s} from A_s and U^{V_{s+p}} from A_{s+p}). One solution is
  x(s) = s(s−p)/(2p) − V_s,
  and the B between s and s+p has bottom y = x(s) + H_s = s(s+p)/(2p) = (m² − p²/4)/(2p), where m = s + p/2. (Check: x(s+p) − x(s) = s + V_s − V_{s+p} = H_s − V_{s+p}.)
- x(s) → +∞ as |s| → ∞. So G_k is a finite subforest of a path.
- The coboundary of a finite forest is onto, so D is surjective and HF^+ ≅ ker D. At level k, ker D is the space of functions on the components of G_k.
- Exponents: V_s = 0 iff s ≥ g, and H_s = 0 iff s ≤ −g. A B_t with both exponents 0 would need t ≥ g and t − p ≤ −g, i.e. p ≥ 2g; that does not occur here.
- A B with exactly one exponent 0 appears at the same level as its endpoint on that side. That endpoint is new at that level, so this edge attaches a new vertex and merges no old components.
- The B's with both exponents ≥ 1 are exactly the n−1 "interior peaks" between consecutive s_j, s_{j+1} = s_j + p in [−(g−1), g−1]. Each one appears strictly after both of its endpoints. Since G is a path, it joins two distinct components of the old graph.
- So dim coker U at level k = #{interior peaks at level k+1}, and the tops of the finite summands are at {y − 1 : y an interior peak}. There are n−1 ≥ 2 of them.
- *Class 0.* s_j = (j − (n+1)/2)N, so the interior peaks have m ∈ {±N/2, ±3N/2, …, ±(n−2)N/2}. These are nonzero ± pairs, so every top level occurs with even multiplicity.
- *Class t.* By (ii), the n−1 top levels are distinct.
- A translate of a nonempty multiset with all multiplicities even never has all multiplicities 1. This contradicts (★).

**(v) Case p = −N < 0.** Here h_s: A_s → B_{s−N}. Let C be the class-c cone.
- *Truncation.*
  - Let P = {A_s : s < g} ∪ {B_t : t < g}. It is a subcomplex: for s < g, A_s maps to B_s and B_{s−N}, and both indices are < g.
  - The quotient Q = C/P = {A_s, B_s : s ≥ g} has differential D_Q = (v_s = id) + (h_s, which lowers the index by N and is present only while s−N ≥ g). Here id + (index-lowering part, with indices bounded below) is bijective on finitely supported chains: invert by a finite Neumann series. So Q is acyclic and H(C) ≅ H(P).
  - Let P' = {A_s : |s| < g} ∪ {B_t : −g−N < t < g}. It is a subcomplex of P: for |s| < g, s − N > −g − N.
  - The quotient R_0 = P/P' = {A_s : s ≤ −g} ∪ {B_t : t ≤ −g−N} has differential (h_s = id, A_s → B_{s−N}) + (v_s: A_s → B_s, present only while s ≤ −g−N). Relative to the pairing A_s ↔ B_{s−N}, the second part raises the B-index by N, and indices are bounded above. So it is again id + nilpotent on finitely supported chains, and R_0 is acyclic. Hence H(C) ≅ H(P').
  - By (ii), the B's of P' in class c are B_{s_1−N}, B_{s_1}, …, B_{s_n}, since s_{j−1} = s_j − N. So P' is the zigzag
    B_{s_1−N} — A_{s_1} — B_{s_1} — A_{s_2} — ⋯ — A_{s_n} — B_{s_n}.
    Every exponent on it is ≥ 1: V_{s_j} ≥ 1 and H_{s_j} = V_{−s_j} ≥ 1. The two end B's each have one A-neighbour; treat them as edges to a "ground" vertex where the value is 0. Then G ∪ {ground} is a single cycle with n+1 edges.
- *Levels.*
  - x(s) = −s(s+N)/(2N) − V_s.
  - b(t) = −t(t+N)/(2N) = −(u² − N²/4)/(2N), where u = t + N/2.
  - Check: b(s) = x(s) + V_s and b(s−N) = x(s) + H_s, using H_s − V_s = −s... (direct substitution: x(s) + V_s + s = −s(s−N)/(2N) = b(s−N)).
  - These do not depend on K.
- *Module structure.* For a two-term complex, H = ker D ⊕ coker D as F[U]-modules.
  - At level k, coker δ_k = H^1(G_k ∪ ground). It is 0 until the cycle closes, at the maximal peak level M, and F from then on, with U an isomorphism. So the coker part is a single tower with no finite summands.
  - ker δ_k is the space of functions on the components of G_k not containing ground. A vertex new at level k+1 has its edges strictly higher, so it is isolated. Hence dim coker U at level k is the drop in the number of components of G_k ∪ ground when the edges with bottom k+1 are added. That drop equals #(new edges) − Δb_1, and b_1 increases (by 1) only at level M.
  - So the tops of the finite summands are {y − 1 : y a peak} with one copy of M − 1 removed. There are n of them.
- *Class 0.* The peaks are t' = kN for k = −(n+1)/2, …, (n−1)/2, so u ∈ {±N/2, ±3N/2, …, ±nN/2}, every value twice.
  - The maximal peak is |u| = N/2. Removing one copy of it leaves the levels for |u| = 3N/2, …, nN/2 doubled.
  - These exist since n ≥ 3, so some top level is repeated.
- *Class t.* By (ii) the n+1 peak levels are distinct, so the n tops are distinct.
- This contradicts (★). ∎

*Computer check (made during this write-up, not part of the proof).* For every staircase V (all sequences with V_{g−1} = 1 and steps 0/1) with g ≤ 8, and every odd N | 2g−1 with 3 ≤ N < 2g−1, both signs, an F_2 linear-algebra computation of the level-graded kernel/cokernel was run. For p > 0 it used the untruncated cone, cut below the first level where boundary vertices appear; for p < 0 it used the truncated zigzag. It reproduced exactly the top multisets predicted above, and in all 1600 (class 0, class t) comparisons the multisets differed up to translation.

## 5. Proof of the Theorem

Assume, as in §1, that K is a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g, p ≠ 0, and Y = S^3_p(K) has k ≥ 3 prime summands.

1. By Lemma 2.1, Y ≅ A # B with B an integer homology sphere, B ≠ S^3.
2. By Lemma 2.2, Y ≅ L # Y'' with L a lens space (an L-space) of order a ≥ 2, so |p| ≥ 2.
3. K is fibred with fibre of genus g (§0, item 5). Proposition 3.1 gives |p| ≤ g.
   - If g = 1 this contradicts |p| ≥ 2.
   - So g ≥ 2, and p ≤ |p| ≤ g < 2g−1.
4. By Proposition 4.3, applied to the splitting of step 2, and since p < 2g−1: |p| divides 2g−1, and |p| < 2g−1.
5. Theorem 4.4 now says that the splitting of step 2 cannot exist. This is a contradiction.

So S^3_r(K) has at most two prime summands, for every L-space knot K and every slope r. ∎

## 6. Remarks on what was shown along the way

- For a fibred knot, a reducible integral surgery with a homology-sphere summand B ≠ S^3 needs |p| ≤ g (§3). This uses only fibredness.
- For an L-space knot, a splitting with a lens (or L-space) summand of order ≥ 2 forces p ≥ 2g−1, or else |p| divides 2g−1 with |p| = 2g−1 (Prop. 4.3 + Thm 4.4). For p < 0 with |p| = 2g−1 the argument above does not decide this.
- Combining these, an L-space knot never has a reducible surgery with a homology-sphere summand other than S^3. This is consistent with the known examples (cables at the cabling slope, whose summands are L(a,b) and S^3_{b/a}(J)).

## 7. Other routes recorded

- **Chain A (shape theorem).** One can cite a "shape theorem": a surgery with ≥ 3 summands is L_1 # L_2 # Y_3, with L_1, L_2 lens spaces of coprime orders and Y_3 a homology sphere. Then:
  - an HF^+ comparison of classes 0 and 1 shows that for p < 2g−1, S^3_p(K) is never L # Y' with L an L-space of order |p| ≥ 3 and Y' a homology sphere;
  - so p ≥ 2g−1, and with |p| ≤ g from §3 this gives g ≤ 1, a contradiction.

  **Gap:** a referee pass found that the shape theorem does not follow from Howie + Gordon–Luecke 1996. The missing case is two summands with nontrivial H_1, only one of which is known to be a lens space. Its attribution could not be confirmed from memory.

  The repair: Lemma 4.1 for the lens summand alone gives coset invariance under translation by s = |p|/|H_1(L)|. One then generalises Theorem 4.4 to "for p < 2g−1 and 0 < s < |p| with s | p, classes i and i+s are not all isomorphic up to shift"; the proof uses the same arithmetic. That makes chain A complete, but then it is essentially the main proof, not an independent one.
- **Perelman-free variant.** Remark 3.4.
- **Invariants of Y alone cannot work (dead end).** In the configuration p = rs = 2g−1, Y = L_1 # L_2 # Y_3, a computer search found the formal staircase V = V(T(r,s)) + 1 on [0, g−1]. It reproduces the d-invariants (hence HF^+, since Y is an L-space), the Reidemeister torsion and the Casson–Walker data of S^3_{rs}(T(r,s)) # S^3_{+1}(T(2,3)). So Floer or torsion invariants of S^3_p(K) alone cannot exclude three summands there; topological input such as the cover bound is needed.
- **Ungraded HF^+ is too weak.** For g = 5, p = 3 and V = (1,1,1,1,1,0), all three classes have HF^+ ≅ T^+ ⊕ (F[U]/U)^2 as ungraded modules, and the d-invariants mimic L(3,1) # Y' with d(Y') = −2. The relative grading (the top multisets of Theorem 4.4) is what separates the classes.
- A lattice/Donaldson route (gluing the surgery trace to sharp plumbings) gave d(Y_3) ≤ −2 in the case above, but no contradiction. The fractional Dehn twist and dual-knot routes also produced no closing argument.

## 8. Dependencies and residual uncertainty (honest gaps)

- All results in §0 are cited from memory. Their exact published wording was not checked against the sources.
  - The least certain is the attribution and wording of **Gordon–Luecke 1996** ("a reducible surgery on a nontrivial knot in S^3 has a lens-space summand"). The proof needs only that some prime summand is an L-space with |H_1| ≥ 2.
  - If this citation failed, Lemma 2.2 would be unsupported, and steps 2–5 of §5 would need another source of an L-space summand of order ≥ 2.
- The Ozsváth–Szabó package (item 8) is used as a relatively graded quasi-isomorphism, computed on homology for L-space knots. The truncation for p < 0 is carried out explicitly in §4.4(v) rather than cited.
- To my recollection, Hom–Lidman–Zufelt ("Reducible surgeries and Heegaard Floer homology", c. 2015) treat reducible surgeries on L-space knots with the same conclusion. That recollection is unverified, and the proof above does not rely on it.

content.content:
1	The document below is a draft proof. Check the argument step by step: for every inequality, interchange, cited result, and 'it follows that', ask whether it actually follows as written. List every error or gap in order of severity, and say explicitly whether the main claim is proved.
2	
3	## The draft proof
4	
5	# Surgery on an L-space knot has at most two prime summands
6	
7	## Answer
8	
9	**Yes.** Throughout, "L-space knot" means a knot K in S^3 such that some surgery S^3_r(K) with r ∈ Q is an L-space. The answer covers every slope r ∈ Q ∪ {∞}.
10	
11	**Theorem.** Let K ⊂ S^3 be an L-space knot and r ∈ Q ∪ {∞}. Then S^3_r(K) has at most two prime summands.
12	
13	The bound is sharp. By Moser, S^3_6(T(2,3)) ≅ L(2,1) # L(3,2), which has two summands. More generally, an L-space cable C_{a,b}(J) gives L(a,b) # S^3_{b/a}(J) at the cabling slope ab.
14	
15	**Status.** The proof below is complete, given the published theorems listed in §0. Those theorems are cited from memory, and their exact wording was not checked against the sources. During the run, two independent referee passes checked the whole chain (§§1–5), for both signs of the slope, and found no substantive gap. The one citation recalled with less than full certainty is the wording and attribution of Gordon–Luecke 1996 (§0, item 4). Only the weak form stated there is used. Nothing beyond the citations is left open. §7 describes other routes, and §8 lists the dependencies.
16	
17	---
18	
19	## 0. Conventions and cited results
20	
21	F = Z/2. Here M_K is the exterior of K, μ and λ are its meridian and Seifert longitude, and g = g(K).
22	
23	**Mirroring.** S^3_r(mK) ≅ −S^3_{−r}(K), and reversing orientation does not change the number of prime summands. If K has a nontrivial L-space surgery at a negative slope, then mK has one at a positive slope. So we may assume K is a *positive* L-space knot, meaning it has an L-space surgery at some positive slope. The slope p is then an arbitrary integer of either sign, and both signs are treated below.
24	
25	Cited theorems (from memory):
26	
27	1. **Gabai (1987).** For a nontrivial knot K, S^3_0(K) is irreducible.
28	2. **Gordon–Luecke (1987).** If S^3_r(K) is reducible for a nontrivial K, then r is an integer.
29	3. **Howie (2002), the Scott–Wiegold conjecture.** A free product of three nontrivial cyclic groups is not the normal closure of a single element.
30	4. **Gordon–Luecke (1996), "Reducible manifolds and Dehn surgery".** If a surgery on a nontrivial knot in S^3 is reducible, one of its prime summands is a lens space other than S^3 and S^1×S^2. *Only this weak consequence is used:* some prime summand L is an L-space with |H_1(L)| ≥ 2.
31	5. **Ni; Ghiggini (for g = 1).** An L-space knot is fibred. Its fibre is a minimal-genus Seifert surface F, of genus g, with one boundary component.
32	6. **Grushko–Neumann.** rank(G_1 * G_2) = rank G_1 + rank G_2 for finitely generated groups. Also van Kampen: π_1(M_1 # M_2) ≅ π_1(M_1) * π_1(M_2).
33	7. **Perelman.** A closed simply connected 3-manifold is S^3. This can be avoided; see Remark 3.4.
34	8. **Ozsváth–Szabó surgery package.** Let K be a positive L-space knot of genus g ≥ 1 and p ≠ 0 an integer.
35	   - (a) *Integers V_s.* There are integers V_s (s ∈ Z) with V_s ≥ 0, V_s − V_{s+1} ∈ {0,1}, V_s = 0 iff s ≥ g, and V_{−s} = V_s + s. Put H_s := V_{−s}, so H_s = 0 iff s ≤ −g.
36	   - (b) *Integer surgery mapping cone, plus version.* Spin^c(S^3_p(K)) is labelled by Z/|p|. For each label i, HF^+(S^3_p(K), i) is isomorphic, as a relatively graded F[U]-module, to the homology of the cone of D = Σ(v_s + h_s): ⊕_{s≡i} A_s^+ → ⊕_{s≡i} B_s^+ (direct sums). Here v_s: A_s → B_s and h_s: A_s → B_{s+p}, and these maps are homogeneous. For a positive L-space knot, H_*(A_s^+) ≅ H_*(B_s^+) ≅ T^+ := F[U,U^{−1}]/U·F[U]. On homology, v_s = U^{V_s} and h_s = U^{H_s}. The cone may be computed from these homology-level maps, because T^+ is an injective F[U]-module.
37	   - (c) *Hat version.* The same holds for ĤF with Â_s, B̂_s: each has homology F, v̂_s is nonzero (an isomorphism) iff V_s = 0, and ĥ_s is nonzero iff H_s = 0. (This follows from (b): Â = ker U, and the map induced on the bottom element of T^+ is U^{V_s}, resp. U^{H_s}.) Over a field the cone is determined by these homology-level maps.
38	   - (d) *Affine labelling.* The labelling Spin^c(S^3_p(K)) ↔ Z/|p| is affine over H_1(S^3_p(K)) = Z/|p| = ⟨[μ]⟩, and [μ] acts by i ↦ i+1. The sign convention does not matter below.
39	   - (e) *Connected sums.* Spin^c(Y_1 # Y_2) = Spin^c(Y_1) × Spin^c(Y_2), equivariantly for H_1(Y_1) ⊕ H_1(Y_2). Also CF^−(Y_1#Y_2,(t_1,t_2)) ≃ CF^−(Y_1,t_1) ⊗_{F[U]} CF^−(Y_2,t_2), and ĤF(Y_1#Y_2) ≅ ĤF(Y_1) ⊗ ĤF(Y_2) on each spin^c structure. If L is an L-space, then CF^−(L,t) ≃ F[U], so HF^+(L#Y'',(t,t'')) ≅ HF^+(Y'',t'') as relatively graded F[U]-modules up to a shift, and rank ĤF(L#Y'',(t,t'')) = rank ĤF(Y'',t''). Lens spaces are L-spaces.
40	
41	---
42	
43	## 1. Reduction
44	
45	Suppose S^3_r(K) has at least three prime summands. We derive a contradiction.
46	
47	- If K is the unknot, its surgeries are S^3, S^1×S^2 and lens spaces, each with at most one prime summand.
48	- So K is nontrivial. Slope ∞ gives S^3, and slope 0 gives an irreducible manifold by Gabai.
49	- By Gordon–Luecke 1987, a non-integral slope also gives an irreducible manifold. An irreducible closed 3-manifold other than S^3 is prime.
50	
51	So r = p is a nonzero integer. After mirroring (§0), K is a nontrivial positive L-space knot of genus g ≥ 1 and p ≠ 0 has either sign. Write
52	
53	  Y = S^3_p(K) = P_1 # ⋯ # P_k, with every P_i prime and k ≥ 3.
54	
55	H_1(Y) = Z/|p| is finite. So no P_i is S^1×S^2, and each H_1(P_i) is a direct summand of Z/|p|, hence finite cyclic.
56	
57	## 2. Two topological consequences
58	
59	**Lemma 2.1 (a homology-sphere summand).** Some P_i is an integer homology sphere B ≠ S^3.
60	
61	*Proof.*
62	- π_1(M_K) is normally generated by μ, and π_1(Y) is a quotient of it, so π_1(Y) is normally generated by one element.
63	- Suppose three summands, say P_1, P_2, P_3, had nontrivial H_1. Then π_1(Y) = π_1(P_1) * ⋯ * π_1(P_k) maps onto π_1(P_1) * π_1(P_2) * π_1(P_3), by killing the other factors, and then onto H_1(P_1) * H_1(P_2) * H_1(P_3).
64	- That target is a free product of three nontrivial cyclic groups, and it is normally generated by the image of one element. This contradicts Howie's theorem.
65	- So at most two summands have nontrivial H_1. Since k ≥ 3, some P_i has H_1 = 0, and P_i ≠ S^3 because it is a prime summand. ∎
66	
67	Write Y ≅ A # B, where B is this homology sphere and A is the sum of the other summands.
68	
69	**Lemma 2.2 (an L-space summand).** Y ≅ L # Y'', where L is a lens space with a := |H_1(L)| ≥ 2. Hence a divides |p| and |p| ≥ 2.
70	
71	*Proof.* By Gordon–Luecke 1996 (weak form), some prime summand is a lens space L ≠ S^3, S^1×S^2, so a ≥ 2. Also H_1(L) is a direct summand of Z/|p|. ∎
72	
73	## 3. The cover bound
74	
75	**Proposition 3.1 (cover bound).** Let K ⊂ S^3 be fibred with fibre F of genus g and one boundary component, and let p ≠ 0 be an integer. If S^3_p(K) ≅ A # B with B an integer homology sphere other than S^3, then
76	
77	  |p|·rank π_1(B) + rank π_1(Ã) ≤ 2g, and hence |p| ≤ g.
78	
79	Here N := |p| and Ã is the connected N-fold cyclic cover of A defined below.
80	
81	*Setup.*
82	- Y = S^3_p(K) = M_K ∪_T V, where the meridian disc of the solid torus V is bounded by α = pμ + λ on T = ∂M_K.
83	- H_1(M_K) = Z⟨μ⟩. The class of a loop is its algebraic intersection number with F, and λ = 0 in H_1(M_K). So H_1(Y) = Z/N.
84	- Let φ: π_1(Y) → H_1(Y) = Z/N be the abelianisation, which is onto, and let q: Y_N → Y be the connected N-fold cyclic cover with group ker φ.
85	
86	**3.2 Lower bound: Y_N ≅ Ã # (N copies of B).**
87	1. Let S be the splitting sphere, so Y = A° ∪_S B°, where ° means one open ball removed.
88	2. π_1(Y) = π_1(A) * π_1(B), and H_1(A) = H_1(Y) ≅ Z/N because H_1(B) = 0.
89	3. φ restricted to π_1(B°) = π_1(B) factors through H_1(B) = 0. So q^{−1}(B°) is N disjoint copies of B°, each mapped homeomorphically onto B°.
90	4. S is simply connected, so q^{−1}(S) is N spheres.
91	5. φ restricted to π_1(A°) = π_1(A) is the surjection π_1(A) → H_1(A) ≅ Z/N. So q^{−1}(A°) is connected: it is the induced N-fold cyclic cover Ã of A with N balls removed (the removed ball lifts to N balls).
92	6. Y_N is therefore Ã minus N balls, with a copy of B° glued to each boundary sphere. The gluing graph is a star, hence a tree, so Y_N ≅ Ã # B # ⋯ # B with N copies of B.
93	7. By van Kampen and Grushko–Neumann, rank π_1(Y_N) = rank π_1(Ã) + N·rank π_1(B).
94	8. π_1(B) is perfect (H_1(B) = 0) and nontrivial (Perelman, since B ≠ S^3). A nontrivial cyclic group has nontrivial abelianisation, so π_1(B) is not cyclic, and rank π_1(B) ≥ 2.
95	
96	If N = 1 the cover is trivial and Ã = A. Nothing changes.
97	
98	**3.3 Upper bound: rank π_1(Y_N) ≤ 2g.**
99	1. *The exterior lifts to a mapping torus.* On π_1(M_K), φ is the composite π_1(M_K) → H_1(M_K) = Z → Z/N with μ ↦ 1. So E := q^{−1}(M_K) is connected and is the N-fold cyclic cover dual to F. It is the mapping torus of h^N, where h is the monodromy, and it fibres over S^1 with fibre F̃, a homeomorphic lift of F. So π_1(E) = π_1(F̃) ⋊ ⟨t⟩, and the fibration map π: π_1(E) → Z has kernel π_1(F̃) and sends t ↦ 1.
100	2. *The boundary lifts to one torus.* μ ∈ π_1(T) maps onto a generator of Z/N. So T̃ := q^{−1}(T) is one torus, and q|: T̃ → T has degree N.
101	3. *The solid torus lifts to one solid torus.* μ meets α once, so μ is isotopic in V to the core of V. Hence π_1(V) maps onto Z/N, and Ṽ = q^{−1}(V) is one solid torus with ∂Ṽ = T̃.
102	4. *The filling curve.* The meridian disc of V lifts to N discs. Let β ⊂ T̃ be the boundary of one of them. Then q maps β homeomorphically onto α, so q_*[β] = [α]. Y_N = E ∪ Ṽ is the Dehn filling of E along β.

235	3. K is fibred with fibre of genus g (§0, item 5). Proposition 3.1 gives |p| ≤ g.
236	   - If g = 1 this contradicts |p| ≥ 2.
237	   - So g ≥ 2, and p ≤ |p| ≤ g < 2g−1.
238	4. By Proposition 4.3, applied to the splitting of step 2, and since p < 2g−1: |p| divides 2g−1, and |p| < 2g−1.
239	5. Theorem 4.4 now says that the splitting of step 2 cannot exist. This is a contradiction.
240	
241	So S^3_r(K) has at most two prime summands, for every L-space knot K and every slope r. ∎
242	
243	## 6. Remarks on what was shown along the way
244	
245	- For a fibred knot, a reducible integral surgery with a homology-sphere summand B ≠ S^3 needs |p| ≤ g (§3). This uses only fibredness.

247	- Combining these, an L-space knot never has a reducible surgery with a homology-sphere summand other than S^3. This is consistent with the known examples (cables at the cabling slope, whose summands are L(a,b) and S^3_{b/a}(J)).
248	
249	## 7. Other routes recorded

251	- **Chain A (shape theorem).** One can cite a "shape theorem": a surgery with ≥ 3 summands is L_1 # L_2 # Y_3, with L_1, L_2 lens spaces of coprime orders and Y_3 a homology sphere. Then:

253	  - so p ≥ 2g−1, and with |p| ≤ g from §3 this gives g ≤ 1, a contradiction.
254	
255	  **Gap:** a referee pass found that the shape theorem does not follow from Howie + Gordon–Luecke 1996. The missing case is two summands with nontrivial H_1, only one of which is known to be a lens space. Its attribution could not be confirmed from memory.
256	
257	  The repair: Lemma 4.1 for the lens summand alone gives coset invariance under translation by s = |p|/|H_1(L)|. 258	- **Perelman-free variant.** Remark 3.4.
259	- **Invariants of Y alone cannot work (dead end).** In the configuration p = rs = 2g−1, Y = L_1 # L_2 # Y_3, a computer search found the formal staircase V = V(T(r,s)) + 1 on [0, g−1]. 262	
263	## 8. Dependencies and residual uncertainty (honest gaps)
264	
265	- All results in §0 are cited from memory. Their exact published wording was not checked against the sources.
266	  - The least certain is the attribution and wording of **Gordon–Luecke 1996** ("a reducible surgery on a nontrivial knot in S^3 has a lens-space summand"). The proof needs only that some prime summand is an L-space with |H_1| ≥ 2.
267	  - If this citation failed, Lemma 2.2 would be unsupported, and steps 2–5 of §5 would need another source of an L-space summand of order ≥ 2.
268	- The Ozsváth–Szabó package (item 8) is used as a relatively graded quasi-isomorphism, computed on homology for L-space knots. The truncation for p < 0 is carried out explicitly in §4.4(v) rather than cited.
269	- To my recollection, Hom–Lidman–Zufelt ("Reducible surgeries and Heegaard Floer homology", c. 2015) treat reducible surgeries on L-space knots with the same conclusion. That recollection is unverified, and the proof above does not rely on it.

# Verification of the draft "Surgery on an L-space knot has at most two prime summands"

## Verdict

**The main claim is proved, provided the cited theorems hold.** I checked every step of §§1–5. I found no logical error. The issues below are, in order, a citation risk, two terse justifications that can be repaired, and cosmetic points. Nothing in them breaks the chain of the proof. Every literature citation is recalled from memory, by the draft and by me alike.

## Step-by-step check

**§0 / §1 (reduction).**
- Mirroring is fine: S^3_r(mK) = −S^3_{−r}(K), and orientation reversal does not change the prime decomposition.
- The unknot case is fine.
- Gabai rules out slope 0, and Gordon–Luecke 1987 rules out non-integral slopes. So r = p is a nonzero integer.
- H_1 = Z/|p| is finite, so there is no S^1×S^2 summand. Each H_1(P_i) is a direct summand of a cyclic group, hence cyclic. Correct.

**Lemma 2.1.**
- π_1(Y) is normally generated by the image of μ.
- If three summands had nontrivial H_1, then π_1(Y) would surject onto a free product of three nontrivial cyclic groups, and that product would be normally generated by one element. Howie's 2002 theorem (Scott–Wiegold) forbids this.
- Since k ≥ 3, some prime summand has H_1 = 0, and a prime summand is ≠ S^3. Correct.

**Lemma 2.2.** This rests entirely on Gordon–Luecke 1996: a reducible surgery on a nontrivial knot in S^3 has a lens-space summand. As I recall, this is the standard citation for that fact, but I cannot check the exact theorem number or wording. Given the fact, a ≥ 2 and a | |p|. Correct.

**Prop. 3.1 (cover bound).** I checked every item.
- 3.2:
  - The restriction of φ to π_1(B) is trivial, so B° lifts to N copies.
  - The restriction of φ to π_1(A) is onto Z/N, so the preimage of A° is connected.
  - The gluing pattern is a star, which gives Y_N ≅ Ã # N·B.
  - Grushko applies, and rank π_1(B) ≥ 2 because π_1(B) is perfect and nontrivial (Poincaré conjecture).
- 3.3:
  - E is the N-fold cyclic cover of M_K dual to F, i.e. the mapping torus of h^N. μ maps onto a generator of Z/N.
  - T̃ is connected, and Ṽ is one solid torus, because μ·α = ±1.
  - For a degree-N cover of tori the deck maps are translations, so f^!f_* = N and f_*x·f_*y = N(x·y).
  - Hence N(β·λ̃) = (pμ+λ)·λ = ±p, so β·λ̃ = ±1 and π(β) = ±1. Therefore π_1(Y_N) is generated by the image of π_1(F̃), and rank π_1(Y_N) ≤ 2g.
- Conclusion: 2N ≤ 2g. Correct.
- Remark 3.4 also works (open book with page F̃, plus Haken's lemma).

**Lemma 4.1.**
- Spin^c(L#Y'') = Spin^c(L) × Spin^c(Y'') equivariantly. If L is an L-space, then HF^+(L#Y'',(t,t'')) ≅ HF^+(Y'',t'') up to shift.

**Prop. 4.2.** I rechecked the component lists for both signs.
- Every Â has at most one nonzero edge, so every component is a star centred at a B̂.
- The counts n_i, n_i − 1 and n_i + 1 hold.
- When p ≥ 2g−1, the interval [−(g−1), p−g] contains exactly one element of each class. Correct.

**Prop. 4.3.**
- The hat rank is strictly increasing in n_i.
- n_i = Q+1 exactly on a cyclic interval S of r residues.
- If 0 < r < N, then S has exactly one start point, so no translation b ≢ 0 preserves S. Hence N | 2g−1. Correct. (If |p| > 2g−1, the same argument already gives a contradiction.)

**Theorem 4.4.**
- (i) For each top degree k, dim coker(U) in degree k counts the finite summands whose top is at k. So the multiset of tops is an invariant up to translation. Correct.
- (ii) The arithmetic checks out:
  - |c + kN| ≤ g−1 exactly when |k| ≤ (n−1)/2.
